title: Release
content:
A framework theme or plugin cannot simply be zipped from its Git checkout. The checkout has no vendor/, the editor scripts are not built, and the dependencies are not prefixed. A site with two framework consumers would load one framework for both of them.

wp-app-framework release turns a checkout into a ZIP that runs in any plain WordPress installation, without Composer on the server. It ships all dependencies, including the framework and Twig, prefixed with the project's own namespace in vendor-prefixed/. Several consumers with different framework versions can therefore run side by side.

vendor/bin/wp-app-framework release [--output=<zip>] [--expect-version=<version>] [--package-source=<package>=<directory>]...

In a consumer created as in Getting started, composer release runs the same command. It recognizes a theme or a plugin by the type in its composer.json.

What the release build does

The command works on a copy in the system's temporary directory and never changes your checkout. It runs these steps:

Copy the project. It copies the files Git does not ignore (git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard), so uncommitted changes are included. generated/manifest.php must not exist in the checkout.

Install the dependencies. It runs composer install --no-dev --classmap-authoritative from the lock file, so the release contains exactly the versions you tested.

Prefix the dependencies. Strauss renames every dependency into the project's namespace and rewrites the project's own code to use the new names. Strauss must be in the PATH (the tools images of wp-dev-env and wp-test-env provide it); the release command runs it with PHP and a memory limit of 512 MB, since it parses the large class map of the dependencies.
Then the command patches Twig. Twig's compiler writes class names such as use Twig\Environment; as plain strings into every compiled template, and no prefixing tool rewrites strings. Release\TwigPatcher rewrites exactly these places. It expects each pattern a fixed number of times, so a Twig update that changes them fails the build instead of producing a broken release.

Build the manifest. It builds generated/manifest.php with the prefixed classes (using bin/wp-app-framework-prefixed.php in the prefixed copy) and writes the template version into it, and the image variants the templates ask for into generated/assets/ (with Imagick or GD of the PHP that runs the release). Then it compiles all templates of the project and the framework, as release mode would, and checks the compiled code for names that were not prefixed.

Build the assets. If there is a package.json, it runs npm ci && npm run build, which also builds the editor runtime from vendor/. Then it checks that every built file the framework loads at run time exists, because a missing one would only fail on the page that needs it. The manifest decides which files these are:
The project has	It needs in build/
blocks, post meta or editor scripts in assets/	vendor/wp-app-framework/editor.asset.php (editor runtime)
blocks	vendor/wp-app-framework/canvas.asset.php (canvas styles)
an editor or view script of a block or block support	that script's .asset.php
a document view, an editor script or a shared module in assets/	that script's .asset.php below assets/
view scripts or document views	vendor/wp-app-framework/view.asset.php (view runtime)
settings groups	vendor/wp-app-framework/settings.asset.php (settings page)
post meta	vendor/wp-app-framework/meta-box.asset.php (meta boxes)
assets/styles.css	styles.css
fonts marked for preloading in assets/styles.css	styles.preload.php
Static assets in assets/ and the image variants in generated/assets/ are checked as well. A missing file stops the release with a list of the missing files and what needs them. A project without blocks, post meta, settings and stylesheet needs no package.json; one with them needs a package.json with a build script and a webpack.config.js with the framework's webpack helper.

Remove development files. It removes node_modules/, vendor/, composer.json, composer.lock, package.json, package-lock.json and every path the project marks export-ignore in .gitattributes (use dir/** for directories). Then it checks all PHP files for names of dependencies that were not prefixed, in string literals too. Inside vendor-prefixed/ string literals are not checked, because dependencies mention their own class names in messages.

Write the ZIP. It writes dist/<slug>-<version>.zip, or the file given with --output, with the project directory as root. The slug is the directory name. The version is the Version: header of the theme's or child theme's style.css, or of the plugin's main file <slug>.php. --expect-version makes the build fail if the version differs, which CI uses to compare it with the tag.

A child theme is built without its parent theme. Calls of the parent's public template callables compile without it.

Every step fails with the file, command or setting at fault. On failure the build directory is kept, and its path is printed, so you can look at what went wrong.

Strauss settings

The project declares the Strauss settings in its composer.json. The command cannot add them itself, because extra is part of the lock file's content hash. It checks the values it relies on instead:

"extra": {
    "strauss": {
        "target_directory": "vendor-prefixed",
        "namespace_prefix": "Vendor\\Theme\\Vendor\\",
        "classmap_prefix": "Vendor_Theme_Vendor_",
        "include_root_autoload": true,
        "update_call_sites": ["src", "functions.php"],
        "delete_vendor_packages": false
    }
}

namespace_prefix and classmap_prefix name the prefix for the dependencies. The prefix must not be the project's own namespace, which is Strauss' default.

update_call_sites lists where Strauss rewrites your code to the prefixed names. It must contain the file that boots the framework: functions.php of a theme or child theme, <slug>.php of a plugin.

Leave constant_prefix unset. It would rename the constants that the Symfony polyfills define for PHP itself, such as MB_CASE_UPPER. Twig defines no constants.

Unreleased framework changes

Normally the release uses the framework version from the lock file. To test a release with framework changes that are not released yet, replace the package with a local checkout:

composer release -- --package-source=webcodingcat/wp-app-framework=../wp-app-framework

--package-source=<package>=<directory> copies the checkout's files without those marked export-ignore, like a distribution archive. The output says that the build is not from the lock file. Composer path repositories are not supported, because the temporary copy has no sibling checkouts.

Distribution

The release ZIP is what you hand on – the source checkout never goes to a site. Where it goes depends on what you built.

A plugin that others may use belongs in the plugin directory of WordPress.org. You commit the content of the release ZIP to the plugin's SVN repository. The directory requires every file of a plugin to be under a license compatible with the GPL; the framework, Twig and the release build meet that, as long as your own code does too. Sites built with Bedrock then install the plugin with Composer from a mirror of the directory, such as repo.wp-packages.org, like any other plugin from WordPress.org.

A theme built with the framework cannot go into the theme directory of WordPress.org. Its review requirements forbid custom blocks and custom post types in themes, and blocks are what a framework theme is made of. A theme built for one site therefore lives in that site's repository – in a Bedrock site under web/app/themes/<slug> – and the deployment builds its release there:

cd web/app/themes/my-theme && composer release

The release command works in a subdirectory of another repository: it collects the files of the theme's directory with Git. The deployment then puts the content of the ZIP in place of the theme's source directory. The same applies to a plugin that only one site uses.

Rules:

The release ZIP contains the directory <slug>/ with everything the theme or plugin needs; nothing is installed on the server.

The framework and its dependencies are licensed under the GPL-2.0-or-later; a theme or plugin that ships them must be GPL-compatible as well.

Never deploy the source checkout: it runs in development mode, with unprefixed classes and without the release build's checks.
description: A framework theme or plugin cannot simply be zipped from its Git checkout. The checkout has no vendor/, the editor scripts are not built, and the dependencies are not prefixed. A site with two framework consumers would load one framework for both of them. wp-app-framework release turns a checkout into a ZIP that runs in any plain WordPress installation, without Composer on the server. It ships all dependencies, including the framework and Twig, prefixed with the project's own namespace in vendor-prefixed/. Several consumers with different framework versions can therefore run side by side. In a consumer created as in Getting started, composer release runs the same command. It recognizes a theme or a plugin by the type in its composer.json.

title: Concepts
content:
This page explains the ideas that the rest of the documentation relies on: who uses the framework, what happens in the build and what happens at run time, and how a block travels from a PHP class to the page and to the editor. You don't need it to follow Getting started, but the guides make more sense once you know it.

Consumers and instances

The framework is a Composer library. A project that includes it is a consumer. There are three kinds:

a theme, which boots the framework with Theme::boot();

a plugin, which boots it with Plugin::boot(__FILE__);

a child theme with code of its own (blocks, hooks, REST routes), which boots it with ChildTheme::boot(). A child theme that only overrides templates and adjusts theme.json needs no framework code at all.

Every consumer that boots creates its own instance of the framework. Instances are strictly separated, so everything with a global name is derived from one of two names of the consumer.

The namespace names what your content and data refer to. You choose it once in composer.json, as extra.wp-app-framework.namespace, for example sections. Your blocks are registered as sections/hero, your REST routes live under sections/v1, your WP-CLI commands under wp sections, your settings are stored in options such as sections_general, and your post types, taxonomies and meta keys are named sections_event and the like. These names end up in posts and in the database, so they must stay the same for as long as the content exists.

The names you give in attributes follow two patterns. Names that become part of a database name – post types, taxonomies, settings groups, meta classes, tables – consist of lowercase letters, digits and _, because they are joined to the namespace with _ (sections_event). Names that become part of a block name, a hook or a command – blocks, variations, cron events and tasks, WP-CLI commands – consist of lowercase letters, digits and - (sections/hero, wp sections import-events).

The slug is the directory name of the theme or plugin. It names the technical parts: the REST route of the editor, the script handles, the JavaScript global window.wpAppFramework[slug], the cache directory wp-content/cache/{slug}/ and the init action wp_app_framework/init/{slug}. The directory name can change when a theme or plugin is installed under another name; that's why no content depends on it.

Two consumers that boot with the same slug or the same namespace are an error.

The separation goes further in a release. Each consumer ships its own copy of the framework and its dependencies, prefixed with its own namespace. A theme built with framework 0.6 and a plugin built with 0.7 load different classes and don't interfere with each other. The flip side is that instances cannot pass framework objects to each other. When a plugin wants to offer something to the theme, it does so through a public interface made of WordPress filters named after its slug (see Plugins).

Build and run time

You declare almost everything with PHP attributes: #[Hook] on a method registers a hook, #[RestRoute] a REST route, #[Block] a block, #[TemplateFunction] a Twig function, #[SettingsGroup] a group of settings, #[PostType] a post type, #[Table] a database table. Nothing reads these attributes while WordPress handles a request in production. Instead, a build step reads them once and writes a manifest: plain PHP data listing the hooks, routes, blocks with their attribute schemas, template functions, settings and the services with their constructor dependencies.

This has two benefits. First, mistakes surface early. A REST route without a permission, a constructor parameter the container cannot fill, a template function with the name of a Twig built-in – each is a build error naming the class at fault, not a surprise in production. Second, a release does no extra work at run time: it loads the manifest and calls your classes, without reflection, without checking files, and without ever writing into the theme or plugin directory.

You can run the checks yourself at any time with composer build-manifest (see Build).

Development mode and release mode

You don't run the build by hand while you develop. The framework picks one of two modes:

Release mode applies when the consumer contains generated/manifest.php. Only the release build writes that file, so this is what runs on a live site.

Development mode applies otherwise, for example in your Git checkout. The framework builds the manifest itself on the first request and caches it in wp-content/cache/{slug}/manifest/. On each request it checks whether your classes changed in a way that matters – a new attribute, a changed signature – and rebuilds only then. You edit a file and reload the page.

Boot and modes describes both modes in detail.

Services

Your classes don't create each other. Concrete classes in your PSR-4 directories are service candidates (with a few exceptions such as enums and attribute classes), and the framework's container creates them when needed, passing other services into their constructors. A class that has a hook, a REST route, a template function or filter, or a block is an entry point; everything it needs is created for it, and only when the hook fires, the route is called or the block renders. See Services.

How a block works

Blocks show how these pieces fit together. A block consists of three files next to each other:

src/Block/Teaser/
├── Teaser.php             the block: #[Block] and a render() method
├── TeaserAttributes.php   the attributes as a typed class
└── Teaser.twig            the markup

Two optional scripts can sit next to them: Teaser.editor.js extends the block in the editor (see Editor), Teaser.view.js gives it behavior on the page (see Front-end scripts).

In the build, the framework reads the attribute class and derives the attribute schema from its constructor: types, defaults, the allowed values of enums, and which attributes are content. There is no block.json. On init the framework registers the block with register_block_type(), and WordPress passes the definition to the block editor by itself.

In the post content, the block is stored as a comment with its attributes as JSON:

<!-- wp:my-theme/teaser {"title":"Summer party","highlighted":true} /-->

On the front end, WordPress calls the framework when it renders the block. The framework cleans the attributes against their schema, turns them into an instance of your attribute class, and calls your block's render() method, which renders the Twig template.

In the editor, the framework's editor runtime asks the server to render the block from the same template. The template marks editable elements with field('title'). In the editor these marks become attributes on the element, and the runtime replaces the marked elements with text editors, image pickers and inner blocks. Content editors type into the real markup; there is no second template for the editor. Typing does not re-render the block, but every other change, such as a different option in the inspector, does.

With #[Cache], the front end renders the block once and reads its HTML from the cache until a tag of the block is invalidated or the entry expires. The editor always renders it fresh.

With a front-end script, the block also gets behavior on the page. The framework loads the script only on pages that render the block and starts one instance of its class per block. In the editor, a Preview button in the block's toolbar shows the front-end markup and runs the script on it.

TeaserAttributes.php ──build──▶ attribute schema ──▶ register_block_type()
                                                         │
             post content: <!-- wp:my-theme/teaser {…} /-->
                                                         │
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────┐
     front end: render() → Teaser.twig → HTML         editor: render route → same HTML
                                                        → marked fields become editors

Blocks and Editor go into the details.

src and assets

Each project has two directories for its own files. src/ holds everything that belongs to a PHP class: the classes themselves, their Twig templates and the scripts of blocks, block supports and settings groups, each next to its class (Hero.php, Hero.twig, Hero.editor.js, Hero.view.js, Design.settings.js).

assets/ holds everything that belongs to no PHP class: the stylesheet assets/styles.css (see Styles), scripts for the whole page (*.view.js, see Scripts for the whole page), editor scripts without a block (*.editor.js, see Editor) modules shared between scripts (assets/shared/, see Shared modules) and static files such as images and fonts (see Static assets). The directory is optional and ships with the release like src/.

A script in src/ that sits next to no block or block support class – or a settings script next to no settings group – is a build error. The webpack helper would build it, but the framework would never load it.

Templates in layers

Twig templates live in the src/ directory of each project, next to the code that uses them. A template name is always the full path relative to src/, such as Block/Teaser/Teaser.twig.

When the framework looks for a template, it searches several layers in order. For a theme this is the active child theme's overrides/{theme-slug}/, then the theme's src/, then the framework's src/. A file with the same path on a higher layer wins. That is how a child theme changes the markup of a theme's block without touching its code, and how a theme changes the markup of a plugin's block. See Twig templates.

Errors

The framework never hides a missing prerequisite. Missing prerequisites – a missing build output, an unknown template, a wrong boot method – raise exceptions that name the file, class or parameter at fault.

Errors in your code at run time depend on WP_DEBUG. With WP_DEBUG enabled, exceptions from hooks and blocks are rethrown, so you see them immediately. Without it, they are written to the PHP error log, and the site keeps working: a filter returns its original value, a block renders nothing. REST routes always answer with an error response instead (see REST routes), and WP-CLI commands end with an error message (see WP-CLI commands).

You don't need it to follow Getting started, but the guides make more sense once you know it.

title: Adding a feature
content:
A new feature of the framework touches the same places every time: the attribute or class consumers use, the build, the manifest, the run time, the tests in two repositories, the benchmark and the documentation. This checklist goes through them in order. Architecture explains the chain behind it; src/Hook/ is the smallest complete example.

Before you start

Check the design decisions: is the idea among the rejected alternatives, and does it fit the principles?

Verify the WordPress behavior you build on in the source of WordPress (the wordpress image of wp-test-env has it in /usr/src/wordpress) and note file and line. The same for Twig, Composer, Strauss or a browser API.

Decide the API from the consumer's side first: names, required and optional arguments, enums instead of strings, what is a build error.

The checklist

Attribute or API class in the directory of its area (src/<Area>/): final readonly, public promoted properties for an attribute, a doc comment for the class and every parameter, @api <group> if consumers use it (the groups are in tools/ApiReference/Generator.php), @internal on members only the framework uses.

Collector (<Area>Collector): reads the attribute in the build, checks everything that can be checked and returns plain data. Every mistake is an error message with class, method and parameter. Shared checks of entry points are in src/Manifest/EntryPointInspector.php.

Definition (<Area>Definition): the PHPStan array shapes of that data.

Manifest: call the collector in ManifestBuilder, add the data to the manifest and raise Manifest::FORMAT. If the build reads a new kind of input (a file type, a directory), make it part of the signature or listing hash of the development cache, or changes will not rebuild the manifest.

Registrar (<Area>Registrar): registers the feature from the manifest at run time, called from Instance. No reflection, no file checks, no writes into the consumer; services resolved only when they are needed; errors thrown with WP_DEBUG and logged otherwise.

Unit tests in tests/Unit/<Area>/: the collector with valid fixtures (tests/Fixtures/<Area>Valid/) and a fixture for every build error (<Area>Broken/, with @phpstan-ignore and the reason), the registrar against the WordPress doubles. Add missing doubles to tests/Stubs/ with the real signatures.

JavaScript, if the editor or the front end is involved: the runtime modules in assets/, Vitest tests next to them, the declarations in types/ if consumers import something new.

Test consumer: use the feature in theme-dev-test (and in plugin-dev-test or theme-dev-test-child if plugins or child themes behave differently), with a browser spec, a render case, a WP-CLI or a lifecycle check – whatever proves it in WordPress. List new specs in its README; update the expected output of composer build-manifest there.

Benchmark: if the feature runs on requests, add a scenario to theme-bench, so the next benchmark (run on request) measures it; bin/bench --coverage shows that the scenario reaches the code.

Texts for editors (see Conventions): new texts in PHP or the scripts with the text domain wp-app-framework, then php tools/translations and the German translation; new texts consumers write in attributes are translated where they reach WordPress or the editor (I18n\Translator) and listed by wp-app-framework pot (I18n\AttributeTexts).

Documentation: the guide page of the area (or a new one, linked in docs/rspress.config.mjs), with what it is for, how it works, an example and the rules; Upgrading if anything a consumer relies on changes; these development pages if conventions, tests or pipelines change.

Checks before the commit: composer lint, npm run lint, the documentation build (it fails on missing doc comments of the API), and lint and build of the changed consumers. Before the push, the development build with the browser suites (see Testing).

Changing an existing feature

The same list applies to the parts you touch. In addition:

A change of the consumer API before 1.0 is allowed only with a section in Upgrading: what changed, why, and what consumers do. From 1.0 on, the API only grows within a major version.

The filters and actions between instances (wp_app_framework/api/{slug}, wp_app_framework/template/{slug}, wp_app_framework/init/{slug}, wp_app_framework/namespace/{namespace}) may only be extended, never changed, because instances of different framework versions use them together.

Changing behavior also changes the doc comments, the guide and the tests in the consumers in the same commit.
description: A new feature of the framework touches the same places every time: the attribute or class consumers use, the build, the manifest, the run time, the tests in two repositories, the benchmark and the documentation. This checklist goes through them in order. Architecture explains the chain behind it; src/Hook/ is the smallest complete example.

title: Architecture
content:
This page describes how the framework works inside: what happens in the build and what at run time, how instances stay apart, how the container, the editor runtime and the release build work, and where each part lives in the source. Concepts explains the same ideas from the point of view of a consumer; read it first if you haven't.

Build and run time

The framework reads PHP attributes – #[Block], #[Hook], #[RestRoute] and all the others – only in the build. The build discovers the classes of a consumer, reads their attributes with reflection, checks everything it can and writes a manifest: a plain PHP array (var_export), no generated code. At run time, the framework loads the manifest and registers blocks, hooks, routes and the rest from it, without reflection.

This split is the most important rule of the framework: compile only in the build, never at run time. It makes errors surface early – every build error names the class, file and parameter at fault – and it keeps a request in release mode free of extra work. Release mode uses no reflection, no stat checks and no composer.json, and it never writes into the consumer's directory.

The build runs in two places:

Development mode – the consumer has no generated/manifest.php – builds the manifest on the first request and caches it in wp-content/cache/{slug}/manifest/ (src/Manifest/DevCache/). On every request it compares the modification times of the source files with the cache, and only if a file changed, a hash of the signatures (attributes, signatures of constructors and public methods; no method bodies). The manifest is rebuilt only when that hash changes. A new kind of input to the build must therefore be part of the signature or of the listing hash, or changes to it would not trigger a rebuild.

The release build (wp-app-framework release) writes generated/manifest.php into a copy of the consumer, after prefixing (see below).

Manifest::FORMAT (src/Manifest/Manifest.php) versions the structure of the manifest. Every change of its structure raises it; a cached or released manifest of another format is rejected instead of misread.

From attribute to WordPress

Each feature follows the same chain. Taking hooks as the simplest example (src/Hook/):

The attribute – Hook.php, a final readonly class with public promoted properties – is what a consumer writes.

The collector – HookCollector.php – runs in the build. It finds the attribute on the discovered classes, checks it (method visibility, parameters, return type, names) and produces plain data. Every mistake is a build error with class and method name.

The definition – HookDefinition.php – describes the shape of that data for PHPStan (array shapes), shared by the collector and the registrar.

The manifest – src/Manifest/ManifestBuilder.php – calls all collectors in order and puts their data into the manifest.

The registrar – HookRegistrar.php – runs at run time. src/Instance.php boots one instance: it loads the manifest, builds the container and hands each part of the manifest to its registrar, which calls add_action(), register_block_type(), register_rest_route() and so on. Services are resolved only when a hook fires, a route is called or a block renders.

Larger areas add more classes to the same directory – stores, codecs, template functions – but keep this order. Adding a feature turns it into a checklist.

Instances

Every consumer that boots creates its own instance (Instance), and instances share nothing. All global names are derived from the consumer:

the namespace (extra.wp-app-framework.namespace, stored in the manifest) for everything content and data refer to: blocks, REST routes, WP-CLI commands, settings options, post types, taxonomies, meta keys and tables;

the slug (the directory name) for technical names: script handles, the JavaScript global wpAppFramework[slug], cache paths, the editor routes, hooks of the framework such as wp_app_framework/init/{slug}.

Instances talk to each other only through WordPress filters named after the slug: the public API (#[PublicApi], filter wp_app_framework/api/{slug}) and public template functions and filters (filter wp_app_framework/template/{slug}). Only plain PHP and WordPress types cross that boundary, because every release prefixes the framework differently: a Twig\Markup of one instance is a different class in another. The build rejects framework or dependency classes in such signatures.

In development mode, all consumers share the unprefixed framework and Twig classes – whichever autoloader runs first provides them. The boot checks that the loaded framework is the consumer's own (by real path) and that the loaded Twig version is the one it installed, so a consumer never silently runs another framework checkout.

The container

The framework has its own minimal dependency injection container (src/DependencyInjection/). It does what the consumers of earlier frameworks actually used: constructor autowiring of concrete classes, one shared instance per class, nothing else – no public get(), no aliases, no tags, no string IDs. All concrete classes of the consumer's PSR-4 directories are candidates; only those reachable from an entry point (a block, hook, route …) are built and checked. Unresolvable parameters and cycles are build errors.

A few instances are provided by the framework (Theme, Plugin, ChildTheme, TemplateRenderer, CacheStore, CronScheduler, ViewData, Assets, MediaLibrary); internal ones such as the editor's render context or the post store may only be injected into framework classes. Post and row objects (Event::get(), LogEntry::query()) are active records and no services: they reach the store of their instance through internal static registries (PostRegistry, TableRegistry), filled at boot.

The build never loads a class that builds on a class outside the project, its Composer dependencies and PHP – for example extends WP_Widget – because loading it would fail outside WordPress. src/Manifest/Discovery/ reads such classes with the tokenizer, excludes them from the candidates and lists them.

The editor runtime

Blocks are rendered on the server, also in the editor. The editor runtime (assets/runtime/, built by the consumer's webpack) sends the attributes of the blocks to a batch route of the instance, POST /wp-app-framework/v1/{slug}/render, and receives their HTML. Twig marks editable elements only in these renders: field() adds data-field, inner_blocks() adds data-inner-blocks. The runtime parses the HTML with html-react-parser and replaces the marked elements with WordPress' RichText, InnerBlocks and image controls; the markup exists only once, in Twig. Changes of inline text fields need no new render; every other attribute change re-renders, with the old HTML kept until the new one arrives.

The inspector is generated from the attribute schema in the manifest; consumers extend it with registerControl(), registerPanel(), registerSupportControl() and registerToolbarButton(). Front-end scripts (*.view.js) run in their own view runtime (assets/view/). The framework ships only JavaScript sources and the webpack helper (webpack.config.js); each consumer builds the runtime of its own instance into its build/.

The release build

A release ZIP must run next to other themes and plugins built with other framework versions. The release build (src/Release/, command wp-app-framework release) therefore copies the consumer and prefixes the framework and every dependency into the consumer's own namespace:

Copy the files Git knows (git ls-files -co --exclude-standard).

composer install --no-dev --classmap-authoritative in the copy.

Prefix with Strauss into vendor-prefixed/, including the call sites in the consumer's code; then patch Twig, whose compiler writes class names as strings into compiled templates (a fixed list of replacements with expected counts – a Twig update that changes them fails the build on purpose).

Build the manifest and compile the templates in the copy.

npm ci && npm run build, then check that every file the manifest needs at run time exists (BuildCheck).

Remove the development files (everything export-ignore) and check with the tokenizer that no unprefixed name is left.

Write dist/{slug}-{version}.zip.

The order is fixed, because the manifest needs the prefixed class names.

Source layout

src/ is organized by feature: each directory holds everything of one area – the attributes consumers use, the build-time collectors and the runtime classes.

Directory	Contents
Theme.php, ChildTheme.php, Plugin.php	Boot and paths of the active theme, child theme or of a plugin
Instance.php	Boot of one framework instance
Api/	Public API between instances (#[PublicApi], #[PluginApi], #[ThemeApi])
Asset/	Scripts next to classes, static assets, image variants, media library
Block/	Blocks, their attributes and categories; Support/ for block supports
Cache/	#[Cache], tags, variants, CacheStore and its backends
Console/	Command line entry point bin/wp-app-framework
Cron/	Cron events and tasks
DependencyInjection/	Candidates and resolver (build), container (run time)
Editor/	Editor template functions, render context, render and preview routes, editor assets
Filesystem/	Atomic file writes, removal of directory trees
Hook/	#[Hook]
Lifecycle/	Activation, deactivation, uninstallation
Manifest/	Manifest builder, generator and loader; Discovery/ (classes), DevCache/ (development mode)
Post/	Post types, meta, taxonomies, post objects
Project/	Kind, slug, namespace and settings of a consumer from its composer.json
Query/	Post queries and the field classes shared with tables
Release/	The release build
Rest/	REST controllers and routes
Setting/	Settings groups and the settings page
Style/	Loading of the consumer's stylesheet
Table/	Tables, row objects, row queries, schema sync
Twig/	Twig environment, template functions and filters, WordPress functions
Value/	Field markers, typed values, references, links, the value factory
View/	Front-end scripts of blocks and supports
WpCli/	WP-CLI commands

New areas get their own directory following the same pattern; tests/Unit/ mirrors the layout.

Next to src/:

assets/ – the JavaScript and styles of the runtimes: editor.js (editor runtime, modules in runtime/), view.js (view runtime, view/), settings.js and meta-box.js (settings page and meta boxes) with their styles, and their Vitest tests in test/ directories;

webpack.config.js – the webpack helper consumers use (@webcodingcat/wp-app-framework/webpack);

types/ – TypeScript declarations of both JavaScript imports, checked by tsc over types/check/;

tools/ – the generators of the API reference, run by the documentation build;

docs/ – this website (Rspress, docs/content/), not part of the package;

tests/ – PHPUnit tests, fixtures and the test doubles of WordPress.
description: This page describes how the framework works inside: what happens in the build and what at run time, how instances stay apart, how the container, the editor runtime and the release build work, and where each part lives in the source. Concepts explains the same ideas from the point of view of a consumer; read it first if you haven't.

title: Conventions
content:
These rules apply to the framework and to all repositories around it: the test consumers, the benchmark, the starter and the test and development environments. Each repository adds its own in its README and CLAUDE.md.

Code

PHP. The code follows the PER Coding Style, with sorted imports and no unused ones (PHP-CS-Fixer, composer lint), and passes PHPStan at level max with the WordPress stubs of szepeviktor/phpstan-wordpress. Every check passes without errors and without warnings; a warning is fixed, not suppressed. Files start with declare(strict_types=1). Classes are final unless they are meant to be extended (AbstractPost, AbstractRow), and readonly where they can be.

Properties are never public. Access goes through getters named get…, for booleans is… or has…. The exceptions, each because the property is the API:

PHP attribute classes (#[Hook], #[Block] …);

block attribute classes and the value classes inside them: readonly, with public promoted properties, because templates read them;

meta classes (#[PostMeta]): not readonly, with promoted properties, preferably private with getters and setters;

test doubles of WordPress classes, which mirror the public properties of WordPress.

JavaScript and styles follow the configurations of @wordpress/scripts (ESLint with Prettier, Stylelint; npm run lint, fixes with npm run format). The public JavaScript API is exactly what types/*.d.ts declares.

The consumer API is resolvable by IDEs. Use enums and classes instead of magic strings (BlockCategory::Text, CoreBlock::Paragraph, Event::class), first-class callables instead of method names (self::check(...)), and required attribute arguments for required information.

Language. Everything in the repositories is English: code, identifiers, comments, commit messages, documentation. Repositories link to each other by GitHub URL (https://github.com/webcodingcat/<repo>), never by relative path; pages of this website link to each other by relative .md paths.

Errors and messages

A mistake of a consumer is found as early as possible: in the build if it can be, at boot otherwise. The message says what is wrong, where, and how to fix it, with the class, file, method and parameter at fault:

Acme\Theme\Setup::init() has #[Hook] and must be public and non-static.
#[Hook] on Acme\Theme\Setup::init() has an empty hook name.

Rules for error handling at run time:

Hooks, REST routes, blocks, cron events and commands resolve their services only when they run.

With WP_DEBUG, exceptions are thrown on; without it, they are logged with error_log() and the request continues (a filter returns its original value, a block renders '', a route answers 500 without details). The error path itself must not fail.

Arguments are checked where they enter: a value out of range is an InvalidArgumentException when the method is called; a combination or state that does not fit (a call order, a missing prerequisite) is a LogicException; a failure of WordPress or the file system is a RuntimeException.

Texts for editors

Texts the framework shows to editors and administrators – the controls of the editor, the settings page and the meta boxes, notices, errors of the editor's renders – are translated with the text domain wp-app-framework; messages for developers (build errors, exceptions, console warnings) stay English and untranslated.

PHP uses WordPress' functions with the domain written out: __('Add item', 'wp-app-framework'), sprintf(/* translators: %d: ID of the post */ __('Post %d does not exist.', 'wp-app-framework'), $id).

The scripts import __ and sprintf from @wordpress/i18n: __( 'Add item', 'wp-app-framework' ), with the same translators: comments. Placeholders instead of template literals, so translators can move them.

After adding or changing such a text, run php tools/translations (in the tools image): it writes languages/wp-app-framework.pot from src/ and assets/ and compiles every languages/wp-app-framework-{locale}.po into the .l10n.php file next to it, which ships with the framework. Translate the new texts in the PO files and run it again; FrameworkTranslationsTest fails while a text is untranslated or a compiled file is out of date.

The first instance of a request loads the translation for PHP; the scripts of the editor, the settings page and the meta boxes get it as locale data of wp.i18n (I18n\FrameworkTranslations).

The public API

What consumers may rely on is the consumer API: attributes and their parameters, the boot methods, Twig functions, the JavaScript exports of its imports (@webcodingcat/wp-app-framework, /view, /settings), the webpack helper and its conventions, the documented script handles, the release command and the generator commands, the filter wp_app_framework/cache/backends/{slug} and the inputs of consumer-release.yml. The API reference lists it: classes marked @api <group> (without their @internal members), types/*.d.ts, the exports of package.json and the pages on hooks, commands and the workflow. Everything else is internal.

Every class, public member and parameter of the API has a doc comment, written for the readers of the reference. Members only the framework uses are @internal. The documentation build fails on a missing description, on references to internal classes and on @see without target.

Within a major version, the consumer API only grows: nothing is renamed, removed or changed in its behavior. Before 1.0, a minor version may still break it; every such change gets a section in Upgrading with the reason and the steps for consumers.

The filters wp_app_framework/api/{slug} and wp_app_framework/template/{slug}, the action wp_app_framework/init/{slug}, the action wp_app_framework/namespace/{namespace} and the shape of their values are a contract between framework versions, because instances of different versions use them together. They may only be extended, also across major versions.

Internals such as the manifest format may change at any time; Manifest::FORMAT is raised with every change of its structure.

Documentation

Every change of the consumer API or of observable behavior updates the Guide in the same commit. Every change of conventions, tests or pipelines updates these pages in the same commit.

The guide pages are written for people learning the framework, not as a specification:

Explanatory prose that addresses the reader ("you"), in active sentences with one idea each. A page starts with what the feature is for and why it exists, then how it works, then an example built up step by step with text between the code blocks.

WordPress internals go into a sentence of their own, not into parentheses in the middle of a rule.

Exact rules – signatures, parameters, defaults, build errors – stay complete; they are collected in a "Rules" section or a table at the end of a section. Tables and lists are for reference, not for explanations.

Shared ideas are explained once in Concepts; other pages link there.

Guides link signatures to the API reference instead of repeating every parameter. Doc comments contain no raw {, }, <, > outside backticks, because the reference is MDX.

Callouts (:::warning, :::tip) are used sparingly, for pitfalls.

The API reference is generated: tools/api-reference writes a page per @api class and per Twig function, tools/api-reference-js.mjs a page per export of types/*.d.ts. Only its overview and the pages on hooks, composer.json, commands, the webpack helper and the release workflow are written by hand.

Commits and releases

One or two commits per step of work, each one passing lint and build; a later change gets a new commit instead of a rewritten one. Commit messages are English, with a summary line and a body that says what changed and why.

Pushes come after the tests of their stage (see Testing).

Tags are v<semver>. Every GitHub release gets release notes written for the people who use it – summary, new features, changes of behavior and breaking changes with a link to Upgrading, fixes, compatibility, documentation – instead of the generated compare link alone; Pipelines and releases has the details.
description: These rules apply to the framework and to all repositories around it: the test consumers, the benchmark, the starter and the test and development environments. Each repository adds its own in its README and CLAUDE.md.

title: Design decisions
content:
The framework grew out of several earlier frameworks and themes. This page records the principles it follows, the decisions that are fixed and why, the alternatives that were considered and rejected, and the mistakes of the earlier projects that it must not repeat. Read it before you propose a larger change: many obvious ideas have been tried.

Principles

No markup in post content. Every block renders on the server. post_content holds only block comments with their attributes as JSON; block supports are attributes too. The single exception is one #[RichText(postContent: true)] field per block, stored as inline HTML between the comments, so that the text stays readable in the database and for search. Markup lives in Twig and nowhere else, so a change of a template changes every page at once and no content has to be migrated.

Inline editing in the editor canvas. Content editors type into the blocks themselves, not into forms in the sidebar.

Full site editing. Pages consist of block templates and template parts. Twig renders block markup and fragments (mails, HTML responses), never page layouts.

Twig for markup, Tailwind CSS for styles. The framework provides the build and loads the result; design tokens belong to the theme.

Plain WordPress on the server. Consumers need neither Composer nor Bedrock on the server; a release is a ZIP with everything prefixed.

Everything that is a value is configurable in the backend (colors, spacing, variants, order); new block types, roles and layout structures stay code.

The rules for working on the framework follow from these:

Verify before you rely. Behavior of WordPress, Twig, Strauss, Composer or a browser is checked in their source or official documentation, with file and line, before code depends on it. What is not verified is said to be unverified.

Fix the cause. No workaround on top of a workaround.

Explicit over implicit. No silent fallbacks, no silently failing file_exists(), no unmarked placeholders, no undocumented behavior sold as reliable. A missing prerequisite is an exception or a build error that names class, file and parameter.

Minimal. No dependency and no abstraction without a demonstrated need.

Fixed decisions

A library, not a plugin or parent theme. Consumers include the framework with Composer and ship it inside their release. A plugin could be deactivated and break the theme; a parent theme would take away the child theme that client projects need for their customizations.

No block.json. A block is a PHP class; its attribute schema is derived from the constructor of its attribute class. Schema and the object the template receives can never diverge, and IDEs resolve every name.

Compile only in the build. Attributes are read in the build; the manifest is plain data; run time uses no reflection and never writes into the consumer. A container compiled at run time into the theme directory, or file checks of all sources on every request, are what made earlier frameworks slow and fragile.

An own, minimal container. Earlier projects used Symfony's DI container or Laravel's, but only ever for constructor autowiring of concrete classes. Their run time, the prefixing patches they needed and their reflection at run time are not worth it.

Every consumer is an isolated instance, named by its namespace (content and data) and its slug (technical names); instances talk only through filters with plain types. A theme and plugins built with different framework versions run side by side.

The namespace is required. It has no default and is not derived from the directory name: the directory name is decided when a theme or plugin is installed, and content must not silently depend on it.

Prefixing is mandatory in every release, for the framework and all dependencies, Twig included (with Strauss, chosen over PHP-Scoper because it prefixes only the symbols of the dependencies and brings its own autoloader).

The server renders the editor. The editor shows the markup of the same Twig templates as the front end, through a batch render route of the instance.

Settings are stored in options of the instance, not in theme mods or global styles: those belong to the stylesheet, and a child theme without code would lose all values.

The API is resolvable by IDEs: enums and classes instead of strings, first-class callables instead of method names, required information as required arguments.

Stable WordPress APIs in the runtime, with one exception. The editor runtime uses only stable components and hooks of the block editor, except __experimentalUseBlockPreview for the previews of repeating blocks (Repeater). It is the hook core/post-template, core/comment-template and core/term-template use for the same purpose, it previews the items live while an editor types and needs no server render per change; rendering the previews on the server instead would send all inner blocks on every change. The runtime checks at start that the hook exists and fails with a message naming the repeating blocks otherwise, and the framework's CI runs against the newest WordPress, so a change shows up there first.

Rejected alternatives

Do not propose these again without new arguments:

Alternative	Why not
The framework as a plugin	Plugins can be deactivated; the theme would break.
The framework as a parent theme	It would block child themes for client customizations.
Rendering Twig in the editor with twig.js	twig.js is not compatible with Twig for PHP in all details and has no WordPress data; the server render guarantees identical markup.
PHP-only blocks with autoRegister (WordPress 7.0)	No inline editing, no inner blocks.
block.json	Only tooling comfort; PHP classes with a derived schema keep schema and object in sync.
Symfony DI or the Laravel container	Only constructor autowiring was ever used; run-time dependencies, prefixing patches and reflection at run time are not needed.
Compiling the container at run time into the theme directory	Writes into the consumer and costs every request.
Twig components looked up as services	Not needed; templates receive what they need.
Theme mods or global styles as storage of settings	They belong to the stylesheet; a child theme without code would lose everything.
A bundled copy of WordPress' DataForm for the settings page	A frozen bundle can break on private APIs after WordPress updates; the page uses stable components.
role: content as the signal for re-rendering in the editor	It describes editing modes, not rendering; the runtime decides by inline fields instead.
WordPress' /wp/v2/block-renderer route for the editor	It cannot render a batch and has no editor flag; a shared route would also be a contract between framework versions.
The Interactivity API and script modules for front-end scripts	Hardly used outside of core; modules can import almost no WordPress package, and the editor canvas does not load them.
Declarative targets and actions in the style of Stimulus	Not resolvable by IDEs.
The slug as default namespace	The directory name is decided at installation; data must not depend on it silently.
Template parts from bundles through WordPress' template filters	There is no registration API for them; bundles would deliver patterns instead.

Lessons from earlier projects

The earlier frameworks and themes made these mistakes; the framework is built so that they cannot happen again:

The editor preview depended on calling a manual re-render, so previews went stale. The runtime now re-renders automatically on every attribute change that is not an inline text field.

Each block sent its own render request after a 500 ms debounce, and a spinner replaced the content, so layouts jumped. Renders are batched, cached in the client, and the old HTML stays until the new one arrives.

Blocks had no apiVersion and a wrapper div without useBlockProps. Every block now uses API version 3, and the block props go onto the root element of the rendered markup.

React.memo had no effect because every render created new callbacks, props and contexts.

{{ title | upper | raw }} changed tags, URLs and entities. String filters do not belong on HTML.

href attributes were printed without esc_url(); Twig's escaping does not stop javascript: URLs.

The template lookup order was parent before child, so overrides of the child theme had no effect.

Twig ran without cache and with debug mode always on.

Twig was left out of prefixing, and the DI container needed patches of the prefixer.

REST routes were public by default, parameters were read by hand instead of through the args schema, output buffers stayed open on missing parameters, errors went out as HTTP 200 or with a stack trace, and services were resolved eagerly.

The error path of a hook failed itself, and exceptions were swallowed.

The container was built at run time into the theme directory, every request checked the modification time of every source file, composer.json was needed at run time, and parent and child theme registered hooks twice.

All block services were instantiated when the blocks were registered, and the WP_Block context was thrown away.

title: Developing the framework
content:
These pages are for people who work on wp-app-framework itself: who fix a bug, add a feature or prepare a release. If you build a theme or plugin with the framework, the Guide and the API reference are what you need.

The pages explain how the framework is built and why, the rules its code follows, how it is tested and how releases go out:

Architecture – build and run time, the manifest, instances, the container, the editor runtime and the release build, and where each part lives in the source.

Design decisions – the principles behind the framework, the decisions that are fixed, and the alternatives that were considered and rejected.

Conventions – code style, error messages, the public API and its compatibility, and how to write documentation.

Testing – which test goes where, what to run at which stage, and how the browser tests work.

Pipelines and releases – the GitHub workflows and the release procedure step by step.

Adding a feature – a checklist from the attribute to the documentation.

The repositories

The framework is developed together with a few repositories that test it, measure it or make it easier to use. All of them live on GitHub under webcodingcat:

Repository	What it is	Its part in the development
wp-app-framework	The framework: a Composer library with the JavaScript sources of its runtimes and the documentation website	Unit tests of everything, including every build error
theme-dev-test	Test theme with a block, hook, route, setting, post type … for every feature	Browser, render, WP-CLI and lifecycle tests against real WordPress; release gate
plugin-dev-test	Test plugin	Plugin support, the public interface between instances, two framework versions side by side; release gate
theme-dev-test-child	Test child theme with code of its own	Child theme support and overrides; release gate
theme-bench	Benchmark: a theme with the framework against the same theme without it	The cost of the framework per request, now and then on request
wp-test-env	Docker test environment: fresh WordPress instances, run in parallel, and a tools image with PHP, Composer and Node	Runs every check and test, locally and in CI
wp-dev-env	Docker development environment: one local WordPress site per project	Trying things out; never used for tests
wp-app-starter	composer create-project webcodingcat/wp-app-starter for new themes and plugins	Release gate: projects created from it must pass their own checks

wp-test-env and wp-dev-env know nothing about the framework; they are general environments for any WordPress project. Each repository has a README with its details and a CLAUDE.md with the instructions for Claude Code; these pages describe what concerns the framework and the interplay of the repositories.

Setting up

You need Git and Docker; everything else – PHP 8.5, Composer, Node 24, a browser for the tests – runs in containers. Clone the repositories next to each other. The directory that contains them is the workspace of wp-test-env:

mkdir wp-app && cd wp-app
for repo in wp-app-framework theme-dev-test plugin-dev-test theme-dev-test-child theme-bench wp-test-env wp-app-starter; do
    git clone "https://github.com/webcodingcat/${repo}.git"
done

The test consumers require the framework from Packagist. To test your checkout instead, wp-test-env replaces the installed package with a symlink to it (a package link) while it prepares the projects; their lock files stay untouched. The first checks:

cd wp-test-env
bin/build                                                   # the images, pulled or built
bin/tools -w wp-app-framework composer install
bin/tools -w wp-app-framework composer test                 # PHPUnit
bin/tools -w wp-app-framework npm ci
bin/tools -w wp-app-framework npm test                      # Vitest
bin/run ../theme-dev-test/tests/dev.pools                   # browser tests of the test theme with your checkout

Testing explains these commands and when to run which.

To try something out in a browser, use wp-dev-env: it runs a local WordPress per project, with the framework linked into the consumers the same way (WP_PACKAGE_LINKS). Its data persists, which is why tests never run there.
