title: Pipelines and releases
content:
The repositories check every push in GitHub Actions, and a release of the framework is only published if the test consumers and the starter pass with it. This page describes the workflows and the release procedure.

Workflows of the framework

Workflow	When	What
ci.yml	every push to main, every pull request; called by release.yml	PHPUnit, Vitest, PHPStan, PHP-CS-Fixer, ESLint, Stylelint in the tools image of wp-test-env; the documentation build with the generated API reference
docs.yml	every push to main	publishes the documentation as next to the gh-pages branch
release.yml	a tag v<version>	the checks, the release gates, the package ZIP and the documentation of the minor version
consumer-release.yml	called by the release workflow of a consumer, and by the gates	builds, tests and publishes the release ZIP of a theme, child theme or plugin

All of them check out wp-test-env next to the framework and run the commands in its images, the same way as locally.

The release gates

release.yml tests a tag of the framework with the consumers before anything is published. The gates run at the same time as the checks of ci.yml, so the slowest gate – the starter – sets the duration:

gate – theme-dev-test (main) built with the framework of the tag: lint, manifest, release build, its browser tests against the ZIP and its WP-CLI tests;

gate-plugin – plugin-dev-test next to an old release of theme-dev-test, so two framework versions run side by side;

gate-child-theme – theme-dev-test-child on an old release of theme-dev-test;

gate-starter – the CI of wp-app-starter: a theme, a child theme and a plugin created from it with every option, linted, built, released and tested, with the framework of the tag.

Only if the checks and all gates pass, publish attaches the package ZIP (git archive, without the export-ignore files) to the GitHub release, and docs publishes the documentation of the minor version (0.16/ …). A pre-release tag gets no documentation of its own.

The release workflow of consumers

A consumer's own release.yml calls consumer-release.yml for its tags (see Releases and CI). It reads the kind from composer.json and style.css, installs, lints and checks the manifest, builds the release ZIP (the tag must equal the version in the header), installs it into fresh instances of wp-test-env – a child theme on its parent theme release, a plugin next to a theme release or on the default theme of WordPress – runs the browser tests and, with cli: true, the WP-CLI tests, and only then attaches the ZIP. With framework-ref, the gates build with a checkout of the framework instead of the locked version.

Images, packages and documentation

wp-test-env publishes its images to the GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io/webcodingcat/wp-test-env-wordpress, -tools), tagged with a hash of their Dockerfiles, on every change and daily, so they carry the latest stable WordPress and PHP within a day. bin/build pulls the image of its checkout and builds it only if it is missing.

Packagist updates webcodingcat/wp-app-framework and webcodingcat/wp-app-starter through the GitHub integration on every push and tag.

The documentation lives in directories of the gh-pages branch: one per minor version and next for main, with a version switcher (docs/scripts/publish.mjs). Never push to gh-pages by hand.

The release procedure

A release of the framework is also a release of the test consumers, and a new minor version is followed by one of the starter. The workflows test everything a release needs, so nothing runs locally besides the checks before the push (Testing).

wp-test-env first. If the release needs changes of wp-test-env, push them first: the workflows check out its main.

Framework main. Push the framework, wait for its CI and for Packagist (a few minutes).

Consumers and framework tag at the same time. In theme-dev-test, plugin-dev-test, theme-dev-test-child and theme-bench, move the lock file to the new main (composer update webcodingcat/wp-app-framework). Raise the version in style.css or the plugin's main file of the three test consumers; plugin and child theme name the previous theme release in with-theme, so two framework versions run side by side. Commit, push and tag them (v<version>), and tag the framework (v<version>) right away: the gates of release.yml build the consumers' main with the framework of the tag and do not need their tags. Wait for all release workflows. GitHub Pages serves the new documentation a minute or two after the job docs.

Release notes for every release (see below).

Starter. After a new minor version, raise the starter's requirement ("webcodingcat/wp-app-framework": "^0.x"), tag the starter with release notes, and check composer create-project webcodingcat/wp-app-starter against Packagist (a Composer home of its own, so neither cache nor path repositories hide the published versions). There is no need to wait for the CI of the starter: gate-starter tested the same starter with the framework of the tag.

Package links. composer update replaced the links to your framework checkout in the local consumers; restore them with bin/prepare --link of wp-test-env.

A release workflow that fails publishes nothing – no ZIP, no package ZIP, no documentation – and deletes its tag: consumer-release.yml in a last step (with the GitHub release, if it created one), release.yml in the job withdraw as long as publish has not run. Fix the cause and push the same tag again; after a failure outside the release, such as a network error, push it again right away. Failed jobs cannot be rerun, because the tag is gone. Packagist may have read a framework tag in the minutes before it was deleted and drops it with its next update. Only the job docs runs after publish: if it fails, the release stays and the job is rerun. To reproduce a failed consumer release locally, run its release pools (tests/release.pools): they build the ZIP with your framework checkout and install it as the workflow does, plugin and child theme with the theme release of with-theme (tests/download-with-theme).

The benchmark is no part of a release; see The benchmark.

Release notes

release.yml creates the GitHub release with generated notes. Once the workflow has passed, replace them with notes written for the people who use the release:

a short summary;

new features, changes of behavior and breaking changes, each with the steps to upgrade and a link to Upgrading;

fixes;

compatibility: WordPress, PHP, the consumers the tag was gated with and the releases that went out with it;

links to the documentation of the version;

the compare link last.

gh release edit v0.16.0 --notes-file notes.md

A rerun of the workflow only uploads the ZIP and keeps the text. The test consumers and the starter get short notes: what they test anew, the framework version they are built with, and the compare link.
description: The repositories check every push in GitHub Actions, and a release of the framework is only published if the test consumers and the starter pass with it. This page describes the workflows and the release procedure.

title: Testing
content:
The framework is tested in two places. Its own repository tests every unit and every build error without WordPress. The test consumers test everything that needs WordPress, a browser or a complete build of a theme or plugin. All tests run in wp-test-env, locally and in CI, never against a development site of wp-dev-env.

Which test goes where

What	Where	How
A unit of PHP code, a collector, a build error	wp-app-framework, tests/Unit/ (mirrors src/), fixtures in tests/Fixtures/	PHPUnit
A module of the editor runtime, the view runtime or the webpack helper	wp-app-framework, assets/runtime/test/, assets/view/test/, assets/test/	Vitest
The JavaScript API against its declarations	assets/test/public-api.test.js, types/check/	Vitest, tsc
A successful build of a consumer, blocks on the front end and in the editor, REST, Twig in WordPress, settings, post types, tables, cron …	theme-dev-test, tests/e2e/specs/	Playwright
Rendering and escaping with fixed attribute sets, without a browser	theme-dev-test, tests/render/cases.php	tests/render/run
WP-CLI commands	theme-dev-test and plugin-dev-test, tests/cli/run	shell script against an instance
Activation, deactivation, uninstallation	theme-dev-test and plugin-dev-test, tests/lifecycle/run	shell script against an instance
Plugin support, the public interface between instances, two framework versions side by side	plugin-dev-test and the theme's plugin.spec.js	Playwright
Child theme support and overrides	theme-dev-test-child	Playwright
The cost per request	theme-bench	bin/bench, --coverage
Projects created by the starter	wp-app-starter, tests/projects	all of the above for a theme, a child theme and a plugin

Build errors are always tested in the framework: a class that is wrong on purpose cannot live in a consumer, because it would break the consumer's build. Such fixtures carry @phpstan-ignore with the reason. A successful build, and everything a consumer does at run time, is tested in theme-dev-test. Code written to check a feature stays there as a permanent test.

What a consumer does with the plugin – calling its public API, its public template functions, overriding its templates – is tested by the theme's suite; it branches explicitly on the plugin status it reads from the REST API, so the suite passes with and without the plugin.

Test doubles

WordPress is not loaded in unit tests. tests/Stubs/ holds minimal doubles of the WordPress classes and functions the framework uses, with the real signatures of WordPress 7.1, loaded only by the PHPUnit bootstrap; PHPStan checks the tests against these signatures. A double behaves like WordPress where the framework depends on it – for example, wp_delete_post() moves only posts and pages to the trash, as WordPress does – and a comment says which behavior it models. The WP-CLI double (tests/Stubs/wp-cli.php, WP-CLI 2.12.0) is also PHPStan's signature file: add a symbol there with its real signature before the framework uses it.

Browser tests

The browser tests of the consumers follow a few rules, so that they stay reliable when they run in parallel:

One WordPress instance per Playwright worker. bin/e2e of wp-test-env passes the URLs of the instances (WP_BASE_URLS); the Playwright configuration picks one per worker by TEST_PARALLEL_INDEX. Tests of different workers never share a site, and a spec never depends on another spec file.

Every test cleans up exactly what it created – posts, media, users – never "delete all".

No console noise. The fixtures in tests/e2e/fixtures.js fail a test on every console warning, console error and page error. A test that expects a message declares it with expectConsole; a warning WordPress causes with every theme goes into ALLOWED, with the reason and where WordPress causes it.

30 seconds per test. A test that needs longer sets its own timeout and says why.

The same suite runs against the release ZIP (E2E_TARGET=release); only expectations that differ between the modes branch on it.

Every spec is listed in the spec table of the consumer's README.

An unstable test is a bug: find the cause and fix it, instead of retrying. The login test of the settings page, for example, typed into the wrong field because wp-login.php moves the focus 200 ms after loading; it now waits for the focus.

When to run what

The checks are staged, so that development stays fast:

While you develop: only the tests of the change – PHPUnit with --filter, one Vitest file, one spec.

Before a commit: all linters and builds of the repositories you changed – composer lint, npm run lint, composer build-manifest and npm run build of a changed consumer, the documentation build when pages changed.

Before a push: the development build – the browser suites of the affected consumers in development mode, with your framework checkout linked into them:

cd wp-test-env
bin/run ../theme-dev-test/tests/dev.pools ../plugin-dev-test/tests/dev.pools ../theme-dev-test-child/tests/dev.pools

At a release: nothing locally. The release workflows build the consumers' ZIPs, run their suites against them and gate the framework (see Pipelines and releases). To reproduce a failed release workflow, run the release pools of the consumer:

bin/run ../theme-dev-test/tests/release.pools ../plugin-dev-test/tests/release.pools ../theme-dev-test-child/tests/release.pools

Every check passes without errors and without warnings.

Commands

All commands run in the tools image of wp-test-env, from its directory, with the repositories next to it:

bin/tools -w wp-app-framework composer test        # PHPUnit
bin/tools -w wp-app-framework composer lint        # PHPStan and PHP-CS-Fixer; fix: composer fix
bin/tools -w wp-app-framework npm test             # Vitest
bin/tools -w wp-app-framework npm run lint         # ESLint, Stylelint, tsc over types/; fix: npm run format
bin/tools -w wp-app-framework/docs npm run build   # documentation; fails on broken links and anchors
docker run --rm -v "$PWD/../wp-app-framework:/repo" -w /repo rhysd/actionlint:1.7.12   # after changing workflows

npm run lint includes the scripts and styles in docs/, so install docs/ first (npm ci there).

For the browser tests, wp-test-env starts instances, runs the suites and removes the instances again:

bin/run ../theme-dev-test/tests/dev.pools                      # all pools of one consumer
bin/up tdt --theme theme-dev-test --activate theme-dev-test     # one instance, kept running
bin/e2e --instances tdt --project theme-dev-test --results tdt -- specs/blocks.spec.js
bin/down tdt

A pool file (tests/dev.pools, tests/release.pools of each consumer) describes the instances of a run: which projects are prepared and linked, which themes and plugins (or ZIPs) each pool installs, and whether it runs the browser tests or a script. The package links (link webcodingcat/wp-app-framework=wp-app-framework) replace the framework the consumer installed with your checkout, so the consumers test it without a release. Plugins can run without a theme; then the default theme of WordPress is active. The README of wp-test-env describes the format.

The benchmark

theme-bench measures the cost of the framework per request: a theme built with the framework against the same theme without it, in release mode, in an instance of wp-test-env of its own. It is no part of a release: run it now and then, on request, to make sure the framework does not cost too much, and compare it with the last report – a new database query on the base load or a cost nobody can explain is fixed in the next release. Never run other tests at the same time. Every area of the framework that runs on requests has a scenario there; a new feature gets one (bin/bench --coverage checks it), and existing scenarios stay so reports remain comparable.
description: The framework is tested in two places. Its own repository tests every unit and every build error without WordPress. The test consumers test everything that needs WordPress, a browser or a complete build of a theme or plugin. All tests run in wp-test-env, locally and in CI, never against a development site of wp-dev-env.

title: Getting started
description: In this walkthrough you set up a block theme called my-theme and give it a first block: a teaser with a title and a text that content editors type directly into the editor canvas, and a switch in the inspector that highlights it. Along the way you see every file a consumer of the framework needs and why it is there. Plugins and child themes with code of their own are set up the same way. Boot and modes, Plugins and Child themes describe what differs.

title: Static assets

toc.text: Overrides and the child theme's own files

description: A theme ships more than code: a logo, icons, placeholder images, a font, a PDF to download. These files live in the assets/ directory of the theme or plugin, next to src/. The framework gives each a URL that changes with its content, prints images with their size and in smaller versions and modern formats, inlines SVG icons, preloads fonts, imports files into the media library and lets a child theme replace a file without code.

title: Blocks
content:
Blocks are the heart of a framework theme. Every block is rendered on the server from a Twig template, and content editors edit it inline in the editor canvas. This page shows how to write a block, which attributes it can have and how its values reach the markup. How blocks are stored A WordPress block usually stores its HTML in the post content. Once saved, that HTML stays as it is: changing the block's markup later means either migrating old posts or leaving them with the old markup. Framework blocks store no markup. The post content holds only the block comment with the attributes as JSON: When the page is displayed, the framework renders the block from its Twig template. A change to the template therefore shows up in every post at once. Block supports such as alignment or an anchor are attributes as well. There is one exception: the value of a #[RichText(postContent: true)] field is stored as inline HTML without a wrapping element, e.g. Summer party. That keeps the text of paragraphs and headings in the post content, where search and other plugins expect it (see Text in the post content). Anatomy of a block A block is made of three parts: a service class with #[Block] and a render() method, a typed attribute class, and a Twig template. There is no block.json. The build derives the attribute schema from the attribute class, and WordPress passes it to the editor on its own (through get_block_editor_server_block_settings()). The schema and the PHP object you work with therefore always match. Here is a hero block with a topline, a headline, an image, a gradient and a list of buttons. The block class use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Block\Align; use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Block\Block; use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Block\BlockCategory; use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Block\Supports; use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Twig\TemplateRenderer; #[Block('hero', title: 'Hero', category: BlockCategory::Design, icon: 'cover-image')] #[Supports(anchor: true, align: [Align::Wide, Align::Full])] final class Hero { public function __construct(private readonly TemplateRenderer $renderer) { } public function render(HeroAttributes $attrs, string $content, WP_Block $block): string { return $this->renderer->render('Block/Hero/Hero.twig', ['attrs' => $attrs, 'content' => $content]); } } #[Block] names the block and describes it for the inserter. #[Supports] switches on WordPress features: here an HTML anchor and the wide and full alignments. render() receives what it asks for. HeroAttributes is the attribute object, string $content the rendered inner blocks, and WP_Block $block WordPress' block instance. A block that asks for $content can contain inner blocks (see Container blocks). The attribute class use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\Content; use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\Image; use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\Label; use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\PlainText; use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\RichText; use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\ListOf; use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\Url; final readonly class HeroAttributes { public function __construct( #[PlainText] public string $topline = '', #[RichText(allowedFormats: ['core/bold', 'core/italic'])] public string $headline = '', #[Image] #[Label('Image')] public ?int $imageId = null, public Gradient $gradient = Gradient::Black, #[ListOf(Button::class)] public array $buttons = [], ) { } } final readonly class Button { public function __construct( #[PlainText] public string $label, #[Content] #[Url] public string $url = '', ) { } } Each constructor parameter becomes an attribute, and its type decides how it is edited: $topline and $headline are edited in the canvas: plain text, and rich text with bold and italic. $imageId is an image chosen from the media library in the canvas. Only the attachment ID is stored. $gradient is a backed enum. The editor shows a select with its cases in the inspector. $buttons is a list of Button value objects. The inspector shows a list editor, and each button's label is edited in the canvas. The template
{% if attrs.topline or is_editor() %} {{ attrs.topline }}

{% endif %} {{ attrs.headline|raw }} {{ wp_attachment_image(attrs.imageId, 'large') }} {% for button in attrs.buttons %} {{ button.label }} {% endfor %} {{ content|raw }}
The template is ordinary Twig with a few helpers: block_wrapper_attributes() goes on the root element. It adds the classes and the anchor of the block's supports, and the marker of its front-end scripts. field('topline') marks the element that shows a field, so the editor can turn it into an editor. inner_blocks() marks where inner blocks go. is_editor() keeps the empty topline in the editor, so content editors can fill it in, while the front end leaves it out. On the front end field(), inner_blocks() and is_editor() print nothing; they only matter in the editor (see Editor). The headline is printed with |raw because it holds HTML; everything else is escaped by Twig (see Escaping). #[Block] #[Block(name, title, category, icon: '', description: '', keywords: [], usesContext: [], excerptWrapper: false, parent: null, ancestor: null)] goes on a service class. The name is the name of the block without namespace, in lowercase letters, digits and -, for example hero. The framework registers it in the namespace of your theme or plugin (extra.wp-app-framework.namespace in composer.json, see Concepts): with the namespace sections, hero becomes sections/hero. That full name is what WordPress stores in posts and what you write in templates, patterns and filters. A name with / and duplicate names are build errors. The framework itself declares no blocks. The category is a BlockCategory case for the categories of WordPress, or a case of an enum of your own (see Categories); an enum instead of a string lets your IDE complete it. usesContext lists the context values of other blocks the block reads from WP_Block::$context. The typical case is postId in a query loop, where a block shows data of the current post. Values of your own containers are read with #[Context] instead. parent and ancestor limit where the block can be inserted: directly into one of the named blocks, or anywhere inside them (see Container blocks). Which blocks a container accepts, its template and its lock are declared with #[InnerBlocks]. excerptWrapper adds a container to WordPress' excerpt_allowed_wrapper_blocks (see Excerpts). It also requires string $content. The framework registers blocks on init with api_version 3. #[Supports] #[Supports] switches on the block supports of WordPress. Its arguments and their defaults are WordPress' own: #[Supports(contentRole: false, anchor: false, align: [], customClassName: true, multiple: true, reusable: true, inserter: true, lock: true, renaming: true, customCSS: true)] Only values that differ from WordPress' defaults are registered. html is always disabled, because a framework block has no stored HTML to edit. contentRole: true is for container blocks without content of their own. WordPress 7 opens patterns and template parts in contentOnly mode, where editors may only insert blocks into containers that count as content. A block counts as content if it has a content attribute (see Fields) or contentRole: true. A section that only holds inner blocks needs contentRole: true, so that blocks can be inserted into it in contentOnly mode. The build reports a container without it in your patterns and template parts. customCSS, enabled by default in WordPress 7, lets users with edit_css store free CSS for each block instance. Whether to allow that is the theme's decision: per block with customCSS: false, or for all blocks with a register_block_type_args hook of its own. Settings of your own that several blocks share, such as a color scheme, are block supports of the theme or plugin, added with #[UseSupport]. render() render() is public, non-static and returns string. Its parameters are matched by type, each at most once and in any order: the attribute class, string – the rendered inner blocks, Repeater – instead of string, renders the inner blocks once per item (see Repeating inner blocks), WP_Block – WordPress' block instance, parameters marked with #[Context] – values an enclosing block passes on, parameters marked with #[Item] – the post, term, comment, user or row a repeater shows the block for. Services come through the constructor. The block service is created when the block renders for the first time, not when WordPress registers it. Attribute class The attribute class is a value class (see Values). Every parameter needs a default value, because any attribute can be missing in the content: the block was inserted before the attribute existed, or the editor never set it. Some names are taken. WordPress adds the attributes lock, metadata, className, anchor, align and style itself (style comes with the customCSS support, enabled by default in WordPress 7). The attributes of the block's own block supports are taken as well. None of these can be a parameter of the attribute class. From the class, the build creates the attribute schema with type, enum, properties/items, default and role: content (see below). Fields Most blocks hold text and images that content editors should change directly where they see them. Mark these parameters, and the editor makes them editable in the canvas: #[PlainText] – inline text, on strings only. #[RichText(allowedFormats: null)] – inline HTML, on strings only. allowedFormats lists the formats the editor offers, e.g. ['core/bold']; null allows all, [] none. #[Image] – an attachment ID, on ?int only. Some values are not visible in the markup, or are better edited in a form. With inspector: true – #[RichText(inspector: true)], also on #[PlainText] and #[Image] – a field is edited in the block inspector instead of the canvas. An address or a short poem needs line breaks. #[PlainText(multiline: true)] allows them: in the canvas, Enter and Shift+Enter insert a line break, and with inspector: true the inspector shows a text area. The value contains \n; print it with |nl2br, which escapes the text before it adds
:

{{ attrs.address|nl2br }}

The canvas shows a line break at the very end of the text as an empty line, the front end does not. A Link is a link to a post, term or media file, or a free URL. It has its own control in the inspector and counts as content. #[Content] marks other content, such as the URL of a link. It is edited in the inspector like any other value, but it counts as content: its control appears in the inspector's "Content" group, and WordPress keeps it editable in contentOnly mode (see below). References to posts, terms and users (#[PostReference], #[TermReference], #[UserReference]) are edited with a search in the inspector, and they count as content too. Content in contentOnly mode In WordPress 7, template parts and inserted patterns open in contentOnly mode. Content editors can change the content of blocks there, but not their design. A pattern becomes such a section only if it has a single top-level block, such as a group around its content; WordPress inserts a pattern with several top-level blocks as ordinary blocks. A block without content attributes is still shown, but it cannot be selected. WordPress decides by the attribute's role: content. The build sets it for you: an attribute gets role: content if it, or a field nested in it, carries #[PlainText], #[RichText], #[Image] or #[Content], or is a reference or a Link. In the example, buttons is content because each button has a label and a URL. The marks have no effect on REST arguments. Editor labels The editor needs a label for each value. #[Label('…')] sets the label in the inspector and the placeholder of an inline field. Without it, the label is derived from the parameter name: imageId becomes "Image id". A backed enum labels its cases by implementing Value\Labeled with a method label(): string. The build evaluates it, so it may not depend on run-time state. Without it, the editor shows the case values. #[Hidden] keeps a value out of the generated inspector. It is not allowed on inline fields. Text in the post content Text blocks such as paragraphs and headings are a special case. Search, SEO plugins and exports read the raw post content, and for most blocks they find only JSON there. For a block whose whole purpose is text, it is better to keep the text in the post content. #[RichText(postContent: true)] does that. The value is stored as the block's inner HTML instead of in the block comment: inline HTML without a wrapping element. The markup around it still comes from Twig. final readonly class ParagraphAttributes { public function __construct( #[RichText(postContent: true)] public string $text = '', ) {} }

{{ attrs.text|raw }}

As the example shows, the root element of the template may be the field itself. For your code nothing changes: the template prints the value like any other. Under the hood, the attribute is a sourced attribute (source: html without selector), and the editor saves it with RawHTML. WordPress never parses sourced attributes on the server, so the framework takes the value from the block content before it creates the attribute object. The following are build errors, each for a reason: The field is not a parameter of the attribute class itself (but of a value class or a list item): only top-level values can map to the inner HTML. A block has more than one such field: there is only one inner HTML. The block has inner blocks: inner blocks and the field would share the block content. The default is not '': the editor stores an empty value as empty block content. Excerpts WordPress creates automatic excerpts from the post content – for archives, core/post-excerpt, feeds and REST – when a post has no manual excerpt (get_the_excerpt()). To do that, it renders only blocks that it knows contain text. Framework blocks tell WordPress which of their texts belong in an excerpt. excerpt: true on #[PlainText] or #[RichText] includes the value in automatic excerpts. It also works in list items, in value classes and with inspector: true. Blocks with such fields are added to excerpt_allowed_blocks. When WordPress renders a block for an excerpt, the block renders only its excerpt fields, one paragraph each: rich text as stored, plain text escaped. Neither render() nor the template runs. wp_trim_excerpt() then strips the tags. WordPress renders blocks for an excerpt while the get_the_excerpt filter runs, and offers no other signal. If other code renders blocks inside a get_the_excerpt filter, framework blocks render as excerpts there, too. WordPress never renders blocks with inner blocks for excerpts, so excerpt: true in such a block is a build error. For a container, use #[Block(excerptWrapper: true)] instead. It includes the excerpts of the container's allowed inner blocks, like core/group. Search Search is unchanged. WordPress searches the raw post content, and it finds single words of values in the block comment JSON, which stores non-ASCII characters as they are. It does not find phrases across formatting, nor values with &, <, > or " (stored as & etc.). Attribute names and enum values match, too. Categories The inserter groups blocks by category. WordPress brings six (BlockCategory: text, media, design, widgets, theme, embed). A theme with many blocks of its own usually wants its own categories, so editors find them at once. Declare them as a string backed enum that implements CustomBlockCategory. Each case is a category; label() is its title in the inserter and icon() the name of a dashicon shown next to it, or null: enum Category: string implements CustomBlockCategory { case Sections = 'sections'; case Teasers = 'teasers'; public function label(): string { return match ($this) { self::Sections => 'Sections', self::Teasers => 'Teasers', }; } public function icon(): ?string { return $this === self::Sections ? 'layout' : null; } } #[Block('hero', title: 'Hero', category: Category::Sections)] The framework registers every case of each enum a block uses, before the categories of WordPress: enums in the order of their class names, the cases in their order. The slug of a category is {namespace}-{value}, here sections-sections for the namespace sections. The build reports a value other than lowercase letters, digits and -, an empty label and an empty icon (return null instead). Inserter preview When an editor hovers a block in the inserter, WordPress shows a preview of it. The preview renders the block like the canvas does. Without further declarations the preview shows the block with its default attributes, and a container with the template of its #[InnerBlocks]. #[Example] sets the values instead: #[Block('hero', title: 'Hero', category: Category::Sections)] #[Example(attributes: ['headline' => 'Spring sale', 'tone' => Tone::Dark], viewportWidth: 1200)] #[Example(attributes: [], innerBlocks: [], viewportWidth: null)] takes the attribute values (a backed enum stands for its value), the inner blocks as TemplateBlock and the width in pixels the preview is rendered at (WordPress uses 500). #[Example(false)] shows no preview. The build checks the attribute values against the attribute class and reports inner blocks for a block without inner blocks. Variations Some blocks come in a few typical setups: a dark hero, tabs with three tabs. A variation offers such a setup in the editor under a title of its own, without a block of its own. The post stores the block with the preset attributes, so the variation is just a starting point. #[Block('hero', title: 'Hero', category: Category::Sections)] #[Variation('dark', 'Dark hero', attributes: ['tone' => Tone::Dark], isActive: ['tone'])] #[Variation] is repeatable. Its arguments are WordPress' own: Argument Meaning name unique within the block; lowercase letters, digits and - title, icon, description, keywords how the inserter shows the variation (in the order of #[Block]) attributes preset attribute values; a backed enum stands for its value innerBlocks preset inner blocks as TemplateBlock, for containers scope where the editor offers it: VariationScope::Inserter (an item of its own), VariationScope::Block (the placeholder, like the layouts of core/columns), VariationScope::Transform (a switch in the toolbar); default inserter and block isDefault replaces the block itself in the inserter isActive the attributes by which the editor recognizes the variation of a block, to show its title and icon in the block card and the list view; each must be preset in attributes The build checks the attribute values against the attribute class and the inner blocks against the container, and reports invalid or duplicate names and an empty title. Attributes at render time WordPress validates the attributes against the schema before rendering: an invalid value falls back to the default. It checks each attribute as a whole, so a list with one invalid item or a value object with one invalid field falls back to its default completely. It does not sanitize them, though. The framework's value factory therefore sanitizes each attribute against its schema (rest_sanitize_value_from_schema()) and only then creates the attribute object. Attributes of block supports, WordPress' and your own, are not part of the attribute object. Caching A block that queries data can keep its output with #[Cache]: it renders once per attribute set and is read from the cache until a tag is invalidated or its lifetime ends. See Cache. Errors An exception in render() or while the attribute object is created is rethrown if WP_DEBUG is enabled. Otherwise it is logged with error_log(), and the block renders nothing. The rest of the page still renders. Core blocks The framework disables no core blocks. Which ones a theme offers is the theme's decision. A hook on allowed_block_types_all limits them: final class AllowedBlocks { /** * @param bool|list $allowed * @return bool|list */ #[Hook('allowed_block_types_all')] public function filter(bool|array $allowed): bool|array { return ['core/post-content', 'core/template-part', 'sections/hero' /* … */]; } } Escaping Twig escapes every value unless you say otherwise. This table shows how each kind of value gets into the markup: Value Output #[PlainText] and other strings {{ attrs.topline }} – Twig's autoescaping #[PlainText(multiline: true)] {{ attrs.address|nl2br }} – escaped, then line breaks as
#[RichText] {{ attrs.headline|raw }} – exactly as stored; WordPress filters it with wp_kses when a user without unfiltered_html saves #[Url] strings {{ button.url }} – the schema has format: uri, so the value is sanitized with sanitize_url() (disallowed protocols such as javascript: become empty) and then autoescaped Images #[Image] attachment ID with {{ wp_attachment_image(attrs.imageId, size = 'full', attributes = {}) }} (wp_get_attachment_image(); empty for null; more in WordPress functions) Links – href with esc_url(), plus target and rel for a new tab; empty without URL (see Links) References IDs; {{ wp_post_title(attrs.target) }}, {{ wp_post_url(attrs.target) }}, wp_term_name(), wp_term_url(), wp_user_name() and more WordPress functions (see References) Inner blocks {{ content|raw }} Root element {{ block_wrapper_attributes(extra = {}) }} (get_block_wrapper_attributes(): classes and anchor of the supports, plus the classes of block supports and the marker of front-end scripts) Don't apply string filters such as upper to HTML: they change tags, URLs and entities too. Use CSS for uppercase text.
description: Blocks are the heart of a framework theme. Every block is rendered on the server from a Twig template, and content editors edit it inline in the editor canvas. This page shows how to write a block, which attributes it can have and how its values reach the markup.

title: Boot and modes
content:
Before the framework can register anything, your theme or plugin has to start it. That takes one call in the file WordPress loads first: functions.php for a theme, the main plugin file for a plugin. This page shows that call for each kind of project. It then explains the two modes the framework runs in: development mode for your checkout and release mode for production.

Boot

Themes

A theme loads Composer's autoloader and boots the framework in its functions.php:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// Release builds ship prefixed dependencies in vendor-prefixed/; source checkouts use Composer's vendor/.
require is_file(__DIR__ . '/vendor-prefixed/autoload.php')
    ? __DIR__ . '/vendor-prefixed/autoload.php'
    : __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php';

WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Theme::boot();

The autoloader lines choose between two directories. In your Git checkout, Composer installs everything into vendor/. A release ZIP contains vendor-prefixed/ instead, with every dependency renamed into the theme's own namespace (see Release). If neither exists, require fails with a fatal error that names the missing path.

Plugins

A plugin does the same in its main file. The main file must be named after the plugin's directory, for example my-plugin/my-plugin.php, and it passes its own path to the boot:

<?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: My Plugin
 * Version: 1.0.0
 * Requires PHP: 8.5
 */

declare(strict_types=1);

require is_file(__DIR__ . '/vendor-prefixed/autoload.php')
    ? __DIR__ . '/vendor-prefixed/autoload.php'
    : __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php';

WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Plugin::boot(__FILE__);

The framework needs the file to find the plugin's directory and its URL; asset URLs of a plugin come from plugin_dir_url().

Child themes

A child theme without code needs neither a boot nor a build. It overrides templates of its parent theme and adjusts theme.json like any child theme.

A child theme with code of its own – blocks, hooks, REST routes – boots its own framework instance in its functions.php. It uses the same autoloader lines and WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\ChildTheme::boot();. Child themes explains how it works next to its parent theme.

Slug, namespace and init action

Each instance is identified by a slug. For a theme it is get_template(), for a child theme get_stylesheet() and for a plugin its directory name. The framework derives the technical global names of the instance from it: script handles, the JavaScript global, the cache directory and the init action. Blocks, REST routes, WP-CLI commands and settings options use the namespace from composer.json instead (see Concepts).

A slug can boot only once. A second boot with the same slug is an error, whether it comes from the same project or from a theme and a plugin that happen to share a directory name. The same holds for the namespace: when an instance boots, the framework fires the action wp_app_framework/namespace/{namespace}, and a second instance with the same namespace stops with an error.

At the end of the boot the framework fires the action wp_app_framework/init/{slug}, without arguments.

The kind of project

The framework's build reads the kind of project from the type in its composer.json, which must be wordpress-theme or wordpress-plugin. A theme needs a style.css. If that file names a parent theme in its Template: header, the project is a child theme.

Modes

The framework reads your attributes in a build step and writes the result into a manifest (see Concepts). Where that manifest comes from depends on the mode, and the framework chooses the mode by itself. You never set a constant or a flag.

Release mode

A theme or plugin is in release mode when it contains generated/manifest.php. Only the release build creates that file, so release mode is what runs on a live site.

In release mode the framework loads the manifest as it is: no reflection, no file checks, and no writes into the theme or plugin directory. Compiled Twig templates go to a cache directory named after the template version of the release (see Twig templates).

Development mode

Without generated/manifest.php the framework is in development mode. This is the mode of your checkout. You change a class, reload the page, and the change is there.

The framework builds the manifest by reflection and caches it in wp-content/cache/{slug}/manifest/, never in the project itself. To avoid rebuilding on every request, it works like Symfony's container cache in debug mode. A meta file records the files the build depended on, with relative paths only. On each request the framework compares modification times. Only for files that are newer does it recompute the class signature or the file content. The signature covers attributes, parents, interfaces, traits and the signatures of the constructor and public methods; it does not cover method bodies. Only a difference triggers a rebuild, so editing the body of a method costs nothing.

Several consumers in development mode

In development mode the framework and its dependencies are not prefixed. All consumers therefore share the same classes, and whichever autoloader runs first provides them. A plugin built against one framework checkout would silently run with the framework of the theme.

To rule that out, the boot checks two things and fails if either does not hold:

the loaded framework is the consumer's own vendor/webcodingcat/wp-app-framework, compared by real path;

the loaded Twig version is the one recorded in the consumer's vendor/composer/installed.php.

In practice, link the same framework checkout into every consumer. The option WP_PACKAGE_LINKS of wp-dev-env does exactly that. Twig may also come from somewhere else: in a Bedrock site, the root vendor/ of the site can load it before any consumer. The error names the directory the loaded Twig comes from, so you know which installation to align.

It then explains the two modes the framework runs in: development mode for your checkout and release mode for production.

title: Cache
content:
Some work is too expensive to repeat on every request: a block that queries the latest posts, a REST route that adds up statistics, a service that calls an external API. The framework can keep the result and use it again until something changes. You decide what is cached and what a result depends on; the framework stores it, finds it again and throws it away when it is outdated.

This page explains how the cache works, how you cache a block, a REST route and data of your own, and how entries are invalidated.

How it works

Every theme or plugin has a cache of its own, named after its slug. An entry is stored under a key. The framework builds the key from four things:

The inputs. For a block, its attributes, its inner content and the values of the context it uses (usesContext, such as postId). For a REST route, the arguments of the request. For your own data, the key you choose.

The variants. The circumstances you declare the result depends on, such as the logged-in user or a parameter of the URL. Each variant adds its current value to the key, so every value gets an entry of its own.

The tags. Each tag has a version; invalidating a tag gives it a new version, so the entries with that tag are never read again.

The code. New code never reads entries of old code. In release mode the framework uses the version of your PHP code and templates from the release build. In development mode it looks at the modification times of your files, so a changed template or class takes effect on the next request.

An entry also has a lifetime, the ttl in seconds. It expires after that time, even if no tag is invalidated.

Nothing depends on the request unless you say so. If a block shows something different for logged-in users and you declare no variant for it, the first visitor decides what everybody sees until the entry expires. Declare every circumstance the result depends on.

A block, step by step

A block that shows the latest posts queries the database each time it renders. With #[Cache] it renders once and is then read from the cache:

// src/Block/LatestPosts/LatestPosts.php
use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Cache\Cache;
use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Cache\Tag\PostTypeTag;

#[Block('latest-posts', title: 'Latest posts', category: BlockCategory::Widgets)]
#[Cache(ttl: 3600, tags: [new PostTypeTag('post')])]
final class LatestPosts
{
    public function __construct(private readonly TemplateRenderer $templates) {}

    public function render(LatestPostsAttributes $attrs): string
    {
        $posts = get_posts(['numberposts' => $attrs->count]);

        return $this->templates->render('Block/LatestPosts/LatestPosts.twig', ['attrs' => $attrs, 'posts' => $posts]);
    }
}

The block now renders once per combination of attributes and stays cached for an hour. The PostTypeTag invalidates it as soon as a post is published, changed, trashed or deleted, so a new post shows up right away.

If the block shows a page of the list depending on a URL parameter, declare that parameter as a variant:

#[Cache(ttl: 3600, tags: [new PostTypeTag('post')], vary: [new QueryParamVary('page')])]

Now ?page=2 gets an entry of its own.

The cache is used only on the front end. Renders for the block editor and its preview always run render(), so editors see their changes at once. Excerpts are never cached either.

What a cached block keeps

A block read from the cache skips its template and render(). Everything that ends up in the HTML is kept. Beyond that, the framework keeps one more thing: the scripts, styles and script modules render() enqueues are recorded with the entry and enqueued again when the block comes from the cache. The block's view scripts are enqueued as usual. Register the scripts and styles you enqueue before blocks render, for example on init: when the block comes from the cache, a handle that is not registered is an error.

Other side effects of render() do not happen when the block comes from the cache. Decisions WordPress makes per request are kept as they were, too: WordPress decides loading="lazy" and fetchpriority of images by their order on the page, so a cached block keeps the attributes of the render that stored it. A block with inner blocks caches only its own output; the inner blocks render before it, as always, and their output is part of its input.

Template functions that depend on the request

Some WordPress functions in Twig depend on the request. In a cached block, the framework checks them:

wp_is_user_logged_in() needs the variant LoggedInVary, RoleVary or UserVary.

wp_logout_url() contains a nonce of the user's session and cannot be used in cached blocks.

wp_date() without a timestamp and wp_human_time_diff() without a second timestamp depend on the current time and cannot be used in cached blocks.

A call that breaks these rules throws an error that names the block and the missing variant. Your own PHP code is not checked: if render() asks for the current user, declare UserVary yourself.

A REST route

A route that only reads data can be cached the same way. Put #[Cache] on the method:

#[RestRoute('/stats', HttpMethod::Get, new Capability('edit_posts'))]
#[Cache(ttl: 300, tags: [new TaxonomyTag('category')], vary: [new UserVary()])]
public function stats(int $limit = 10): array
{
    // …
}

The arguments of the request are part of the key: ?limit=5 and ?limit=20 get entries of their own. The permission check runs on every request, also when the response comes from the cache. Errors – a RestException or any other exception – are answered as usual and never stored.

A route may return a WP_REST_Response as well. The cache keeps its data, status and headers, but only for a status below 400: a deliberate 404 is answered every time, like an error.

A route may also take the WP_REST_Request. Only the arguments of the method are part of the key, though: whatever the route reads from the request beyond them – a header, a parameter it does not declare – must be declared as a variant, such as new HeaderVary('Accept-Language').

A cached route answers only GET.

Data of your own

For anything else, inject CacheStore and call remember(). It returns the cached value or calls your function, stores its result and returns it:

use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Cache\CacheStore;

final readonly class Weather
{
    public function __construct(private CacheStore $cache, private WeatherClient $client) {}

    /**
     * @return array<string, mixed>
     */
    public function current(string $city): array
    {
        return $this->cache->remember(
            'weather-' . $city,
            fn(): array => $this->client->fetch($city),
            ttl: 600,
            tags: [Feed::Weather],
        );
    }
}

The key identifies the entry within your theme or plugin; include everything the value depends on, or declare it as a variant. Values must be plain data: null, booleans, numbers, strings and arrays of them. If your function throws, nothing is stored and the exception reaches you.

Queries of posts have a shortcut: Event::query()->…->cache(ttl: 600) caches their result with the tags of the post type and of the taxonomies they use (see Queries).

Rows of tables have no tag of the framework. To cache a value computed from a table, give it a tag of your own and invalidate that tag where your code saves or deletes rows, right after save().

Invalidating entries

Three tags are invalidated by the framework itself:

PostTypeTag('product') when a post of that type is created, changed, trashed, deleted, changes its status or its post meta. The edit lock the block editor sets while somebody edits a post does not count. Name your own post types by their post class: new PostTypeTag(Event::class).

TaxonomyTag('category') or TaxonomyTag(Category::class) when a term of that taxonomy is created, changed or deleted, changes its term meta, or is assigned to or removed from a post or another object, such as a user in a taxonomy for users.

SettingsTag(SiteSettings::class) when the settings group is saved, or when its option is deleted, which resets the group to its defaults.

For everything else, define tags of your own. A tag is a case of a string-backed enum that implements CacheTag:

use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Cache\CacheTag;

enum Feed: string implements CacheTag
{
    case Weather = 'weather';
}

Invalidate it with CacheStore::invalidate(), for example in a hook that runs when the external data changes:

$this->cache->invalidate(Feed::Weather);

Invalidating a tag does not delete anything. It gives the tag a new version, so the entries with the old version are no longer found and expire after their ttl. The versions are stored as options of your theme or plugin.

Where entries are stored

The framework stores entries in the first available backend of a list:

object: the persistent object cache, if the site has one (an object-cache.php drop-in such as Redis).

file: PHP files below wp-content/cache/{slug}/data, written atomically and read through OPcache. A daily WP-Cron event deletes expired files.

transient: transients in the database.

The site can change the list with the filter wp_app_framework/cache/backends/{slug}, for example in a must-use plugin. The values are plain strings, so the filter works without the theme's classes. An empty list turns the cache off:

add_filter('wp_app_framework/cache/backends/my-theme', fn(): array => ['transient']);
add_filter('wp_app_framework/cache/backends/my-plugin', fn(): array => []);

CacheStore::getBackendName() tells you which backend is used in the current request.

Variants

Variant	Value in the key
new UserVary()	ID of the current user, 0 for visitors who are not logged in
new LoggedInVary()	Whether the visitor is logged in
new RoleVary()	The roles of the current user
new UrlVary()	Path of the requested URL, without the query string
new QueryParamVary('page')	A parameter of the query string; a missing parameter differs from an empty one
new HeaderVary('Accept-Language')	A request header; a missing header differs from an empty one
new CookieVary('region')	A cookie; a missing cookie differs from an empty one
new ServiceVary(Region::class)	The value of a service of yours implementing VaryProvider (value(): string|int|float|bool|null)

Data sent with a POST request is no variant. A block that shows the result of a form submission must not be cached.

Rules

#[Cache(ttl, tags: [], vary: [])]:

Parameter	Type	Rule
ttl	int	Required; lifetime in seconds, at least 1.
tags	list<CacheTag>	PostTypeTag (a name of 1–20 characters or a post class), TaxonomyTag (a name of 1–32 characters or a taxonomy class), SettingsTag with a class that has #[SettingsGroup] in the same theme or plugin, or a case of a string-backed enum implementing CacheTag. No tag twice.
vary	list<CacheVary>	The variants above. QueryParamVary, HeaderVary and CookieVary need a name; the class of a ServiceVary must be a service implementing VaryProvider. No variant twice.

Build errors:

#[Cache] on a class without #[Block] or on a method without #[RestRoute].

A ttl below 1, an invalid tag or variant, a tag or variant listed twice.

A cached route that answers another method than GET, or declares a return type other than array, string, int, float, bool, null, WP_REST_Response or a union of them (void, other objects and mixed are errors).

At run time:

CacheStore::remember(string $key, Closure $compute, int $ttl, array $tags = [], array $vary = []) checks its arguments like the build; an empty key, an invalid ttl, tag or variant throws an InvalidArgumentException. A value that is not plain data throws a LogicException. A cached REST route whose data or headers are not plain data answers with status 500, like any other exception.

CacheStore::invalidate(CacheTag ...$tags) invalidates the tags of this theme or plugin.

The filter wp_app_framework/cache/backends/{slug} returns a list of 'object', 'file' and 'transient'; another value throws a LogicException.

A block with a Repeater has its inner blocks in the key, since they do not render into $content (see Repeating inner blocks).

Blocks are never cached in renders for the block editor, its preview or excerpts. Errors and REST responses with a status of 400 or more are never cached.

toc.text: Template functions that depend on the request

description: Some work is too expensive to repeat on every request: a block that queries the latest posts, a REST route that adds up statistics, a service that calls an external API. The framework can keep the result and use it again until something changes. You decide what is cached and what a result depends on; the framework stores it, finds it again and throws it away when it is outdated. This page explains how the cache works, how you cache a block, a REST route and data of your own, and how entries are invalidated.

title: Child themes
description: Child themes are where customer projects adapt a theme: different markup for a block, adjusted colors, an extra block or two. The framework supports two kinds of child theme, and you pick the one that fits the job.

title: WP-CLI commands
description: Some tasks don't belong in a web request: importing a feed with thousands of entries, cleaning up old data, migrating content after a change of its structure. WP-CLI runs such tasks from the command line, without a time limit and without a browser. A plain WP-CLI command is a class or closure that you register with WP_CLI::add_command(). It receives its arguments as an array of strings, and its help text and the rules for its arguments live in a doc comment that WP-CLI parses. WP-CLI only checks the form of the arguments: --limit=many reaches your code as the string "many". With the framework, a command is a method with #[CliSubcommand]. The build derives the command line from the method signature, and the framework converts every value to the declared type before your method runs. Like a hook or a REST route, the class is a service: it gets its dependencies injected and is created only when the command runs.

title: Container blocks
content:
Many blocks hold other blocks: a section holds teasers, tabs hold one panel per tab, a slider holds slides. In WordPress these are blocks with inner blocks. A container decides which blocks may go inside, which ones a new container starts with, and how editors may change them. The blocks inside often depend on their container, too: a tab only makes sense inside tabs, and it needs to know which tab is active. This page shows how to build such a pair of blocks. The basics of a block – attribute class, template, render() – are explained in Blocks. A container and its children A block becomes a container when its render() accepts string $content, the rendered inner blocks. Its template marks the element that holds them with inner_blocks(): #[Block('tabs', title: 'Tabs', category: BlockCategory::Design)] final class Tabs { public function __construct(private TemplateRenderer $twig) {} public function render(TabsAttributes $attributes, string $content): string { return $this->twig->render('Block/Tabs/Tabs.twig', ['attrs' => $attributes, 'content' => $content]); } }
{{ content|raw }}
Without further declarations every block may be inserted into it, and the editor behaves as for core/group. #[InnerBlocks] changes that. Inner blocks #[InnerBlocks] on the block class describes the inner blocks: #[Block('tabs', title: 'Tabs', category: BlockCategory::Design)] #[InnerBlocks( allowed: [Tab::class], template: [new TemplateBlock(Tab::class, ['title' => 'Tab 1']), new TemplateBlock(Tab::class, ['title' => 'Tab 2'])], templateLock: TemplateLock::Insert, orientation: Orientation::Horizontal, )] final class Tabs { /* … */ } allowed limits the blocks that can be inserted. Here only tabs. template is what a newly inserted container starts with: two tabs with their titles. templateLock restricts changes. TemplateLock::Insert lets editors reorder the tabs, but not add or remove them; TemplateLock::All allows no changes to the structure, TemplateLock::ContentOnly only changes of the content. Without it the container inherits the lock of its parent, and TemplateLock::Unlocked lifts a lock of the parent. orientation tells the editor that the tabs sit side by side. The movers then show arrows to the left and right. Three more options control how blocks are added. defaultBlock is the block the editor suggests, and with directInsert: true the "+" at the end of the container inserts it right away. prioritized lists blocks that the quick inserter of the container – the small "+" – and the slash command offer first. appender chooses that "+" at the end: Appender::Default lets WordPress decide (an empty paragraph to type into, or the "+" button if paragraphs are not allowed), Appender::Button always shows the button, and Appender::None shows nothing, so blocks are added through the toolbar or the list view only. With TemplateLock::All or TemplateLock::ContentOnly, the editor brings the inner blocks of every container in line with the template whenever it opens one. Inner blocks that differ – in a post, a template or a pattern – are replaced. The build reports templates, template parts and patterns whose inner blocks differ from a locked template. Referring to blocks allowed and the other options name blocks in three ways, so that your IDE can resolve them wherever possible: blocks of your theme or plugin by their class, Tab::class; core blocks by a case of CoreBlock, CoreBlock::Paragraph; other blocks by their full name, 'acme/slider'. A TemplateBlock takes the block in the same way, its attribute values and, for a container, its inner blocks: new TemplateBlock(Tab::class, ['title' => 'Tab 1'], [new TemplateBlock(CoreBlock::Paragraph)]). Attribute values of your own blocks are checked in the build against their attribute class; a backed enum stands for its value. Restricting where a block goes A tab outside of tabs makes no sense. parent on the child limits it to the containers it may be inserted into directly; the inserter then offers it only there: #[Block('tab', title: 'Tab', category: BlockCategory::Design, parent: [Tabs::class])] final class Tab { /* … */ } ancestor is the looser variant: the block may be inserted anywhere inside the named blocks, also deeper down. Both take the same values as allowed. The build checks that each container of your own in parent allows the child, and it reports your blocks placed elsewhere in templates, template parts and patterns. Passing values to inner blocks The tabs know which tab is active; each tab needs that value to render itself open or closed. WordPress passes such values as block context: a container provides values of its attributes, and the blocks inside read them, at any depth, without storing them themselves. The container marks the attributes it passes on with #[ProvidesContext] in its attribute class: final readonly class TabsAttributes { public function __construct( #[ProvidesContext] public int $active = 0, public TabStyle $style = TabStyle::Line, ) {} } A block inside reads the value with a parameter of render() marked #[Context]. It names the container class and its attribute: final class Tab { public function render( TabAttributes $attributes, string $content, #[Context(Tabs::class, 'active')] int $active = 0, ): string { // … } } The parameter receives the value with its type, created like an attribute: an enum as its case, a value class as an object. Outside of tabs there is no value, and the parameter keeps its default; that's why it needs a default or a nullable type. In the editor the value reaches the block as well: when an editor changes the active tab, the tabs inside render again. The attribute name is the only string here, and the build checks it: the container must be a block of your theme or plugin, its attribute class must have the attribute, the attribute must be marked with #[ProvidesContext], and the parameter must have the attribute's type. WordPress itself names context values; the framework derives the names, {namespace}/{block}/{attribute} – here sections/tabs/active. Values of other blocks, such as postId in a query loop, are read as before with usesContext and WP_Block (see Blocks). Repeating inner blocks A list of events, the terms of a taxonomy, the comments of a post: some containers show their inner blocks once for every item, like core/post-template in a query loop. Editors design one item from blocks, and the container repeats it. Such a container asks for a Repeater in render() instead of string $content, decides which items there are, and renders the inner blocks for each: use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Block\Repeater; #[Block('event-list', title: 'Event list', category: BlockCategory::Design)] #[InnerBlocks(allowed: [EventCard::class, CoreBlock::PostTitle])] final readonly class EventList { public function __construct(private TemplateRenderer $renderer) {} public function render(EventListAttributes $attrs, Repeater $repeater): string { $items = array_map($repeater->post(...), Event::query()->limit($attrs->count)->get()); return $this->renderer->render('Block/EventList/EventList.twig', ['items' => $items]); } } The template marks the element of each item with repeater_item() and prints the item's inner blocks in it:
    {% for item in items %} {{ item.content|raw }} {% endfor %}
Kinds of items Each method of the repeater renders the inner blocks once and returns a RepeaterItem. The inner blocks get the item as block context: Method Item Block context post($post) an ID, a WP_Post or a post object postId, postType; the post is the global post while the item renders term($term) an ID or a WP_Term termId, taxonomy comment($comment) an ID or a WP_Comment commentId user($user) an ID or a WP_User userId row($row) a saved row object of a table {namespace}/{table}, e.g. sections/log Posts, terms and comments use the context of WordPress' own loop blocks, so core blocks such as core/post-title, core/term-name or core/comment-content show the item. One repeater may mix kinds: a list can show a post, then a term. The context of the ancestors stays available to the inner blocks, and the container's own #[ProvidesContext] values reach them as well. An item that does not exist – a deleted post, a row without primary key – throws an InvalidArgumentException. The current item A block of your theme or plugin reads the item it is shown for with #[Item] on a parameter of render(): public function render(EventCardAttributes $attrs, #[Item] ?Event $event): string The type says which item: a post class of the theme or plugin or WP_Post, WP_Term, WP_Comment, WP_User or a row class. The parameter is nullable; it is null outside an item of its kind. A block can take several of them and show whichever is there. The framework adds the context names to the block's usesContext itself. A post comes from the postId context, which WordPress also sets for the post being shown, so outside a repeater a #[Item] ?WP_Post is that post, as for core/post-title; a post class gets only posts of its own type. In the editor The editor shows the inner blocks of the first item to edit and the other items as live previews of the same blocks in their own context, like core/post-template. A click on a preview edits that item instead. Everything typed shows up in all items at once; the blocks are stored once, as inner blocks of the container. In renders for the editor, item.content is empty: the runtime fills the element of each item. The previews render each framework block for its item with the item's context. For a post that the editor may not edit, such as the published post of another author, the render route allows the render if the post is public; drafts of others stay closed. Core blocks in a preview load their data themselves; core/post-title asks for the post with context=edit, which WordPress refuses an author for posts of others, as in a query loop of WordPress. A container without items shows no inner blocks in the editor. Render something else in that case, for example {% else %}
  • No events yet
    • . Caching #[Cache] works on a repeating container: its key contains the inner blocks, so a changed item design renders anew. The items themselves are data like any other – invalidate them with tags, such as new PostTypeTag(Event::class). Inner blocks with a cache of their own are cached per item, because their key contains their context. Rules #[InnerBlocks(allowed: null, template: null, templateLock: null, orientation: null, defaultBlock: null, directInsert: false, prioritized: [], appender: Appender::Default)]: Argument Type WordPress allowed list of block references, null for all allowed_blocks of the block type template list of TemplateBlock template of useInnerBlocksProps() templateLock TemplateLock (All, Insert, ContentOnly, Unlocked = false), null to inherit templateLock orientation Orientation (Horizontal, Vertical) orientation defaultBlock TemplateBlock without inner blocks defaultBlock directInsert bool; needs defaultBlock directInsert prioritized list of block references, each in allowed prioritizedInserterBlocks appender Appender (Default, Button, None) renderAppender A block reference is a block class of the same theme or plugin, a CoreBlock case or the full name of another block. The build reports: #[InnerBlocks] on a block whose render() takes no string $content; a class that is no block of the theme or plugin, a name without /, a name in your own namespace (name those blocks by class) and a core block named as string although CoreBlock has a case for it – strings are only for core blocks newer than the framework; template blocks, a default block or prioritized blocks that the container does not allow, inner blocks in a template block of a block without inner blocks, a default block with inner blocks, and directInsert without defaultBlock; unknown or invalid attribute values of your own blocks in a TemplateBlock; parent naming a container of your own that does not allow the block. #[Block(parent: null, ancestor: null)] takes lists of block references. Context: #[ProvidesContext] marks parameters of a block attribute class only, not of value classes or settings groups. The value is passed as context {namespace}/{block}/{attribute}. #[Context(Block::class, 'attribute')] marks parameters of render() only. The block must be a block of the same theme or plugin, the attribute marked with #[ProvidesContext], the parameter type that of the attribute (it may be nullable where the attribute is not), and the parameter needs a default or a nullable type. usesContext must not name context of your own blocks; use #[Context] instead. Repeaters: render() takes either string $content or a Repeater, not both; #[InnerBlocks] works the same for both. A repeating block cannot be an excerptWrapper, nor have a #[RichText(postContent: true)] field, and its template marks items with repeater_item(), not inner_blocks() – in every render, inner_blocks() throws there, and repeater_item() throws in other blocks. #[Item] goes on a nullable parameter of render() whose type is a post class of the theme or plugin, WP_Post, WP_Term, WP_Comment, WP_User or a row class of the theme or plugin, and not together with #[Context].
