The basics of a block – attribute class, template, render() – are explained in Blocks.

title: Cron events and tasks
content:
Some work does not belong to a page view. A feed is synchronized every hour, old data is cleaned up every night, a report goes out on Monday morning, a reminder is sent an hour after someone saved a post. WordPress runs such work with WP-Cron. Using it by hand takes a fair amount of code: you add an action, check with wp_next_scheduled() whether the event exists, schedule it, register custom intervals, and unschedule everything when the theme or plugin goes away. Small mistakes leave orphaned events behind, keep an old interval forever or let a nightly run drift by an hour twice a year.

The framework does this for you. You put #[CronEvent] on a method that should run regularly, and #[CronTask] on a method that handles a one-time task, which you plan with the CronScheduler service.

How WP-Cron works

WP-Cron is no real scheduler: nothing runs at the exact time of an event. Instead, WordPress checks on every page view whether an event is due. If one is, it sends a request to its own wp-cron.php in the background, and that request runs the due events. On a site with few visitors, an event therefore runs late; on a site without any visitors, it does not run at all.

Busy sites often turn this off with define('DISABLE_WP_CRON', true); in wp-config.php and call wp-cron.php from a system cron job instead, for example every minute. Everything on this page works the same way then.

WordPress stores all scheduled events, with their arguments, in the option cron. The option is loaded on every request.

Recurring events

A recurring event is a public method of a service with #[CronEvent]. It names the event and its interval:

use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Cron\CronEvent;
use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Cron\CronInterval;

final readonly class FeedSync
{
    #[CronEvent('sync-feed', CronInterval::Hourly)]
    public function sync(FeedClient $client, FeedStore $store): void
    {
        $store->replace($client->fetch());
    }
}

The method returns void. Its parameters are services, which the framework passes in when the event runs. WP-Cron passes no arguments to recurring events, so every parameter must be a service.

On the first request after the build, the framework schedules the event. It is due at once, runs with the next WP-Cron request and then every hour. Like hooks (see Hooks), the service is created only when the event runs.

The interval is one of the four intervals of WordPress – CronInterval::Hourly, CronInterval::TwiceDaily, CronInterval::Daily and CronInterval::Weekly – or a number of seconds:

#[CronEvent('poll-status', 15 * 60)]
public function poll(): void { /* … */ }

Write the number itself. Attribute arguments are evaluated in the build, where the constants WordPress defines, such as MINUTE_IN_SECONDS, do not exist. An interval in seconds must be at least 60.

Fixed start times

A nightly report should run at night, not at whatever time the first request after the deployment came in. at fixes the start time, in the time zone of the site (Settings → General):

#[CronEvent('nightly-report', CronInterval::Daily, at: '03:00')]
public function nightly(): void { /* … */ }

#[CronEvent('digest', CronInterval::TwiceDaily, at: '06:30')]   // 06:30 and 18:30
public function digest(): void { /* … */ }

#[CronEvent('weekly-summary', CronInterval::Weekly, at: '08:00', weekday: Weekday::Monday)]
public function weekly(): void { /* … */ }

The event is scheduled for the next occurrence of that time. A twice daily event runs at at and twelve hours later; a weekly event runs on its weekday.

WP-Cron keeps the rhythm of an event in UTC, so after a change to or from daylight saving time a 03:00 event would run at 04:00 or 02:00. The framework checks on every request whether an event with a start time still runs at its local time. If it does not – after a change of daylight saving time, after someone changed the time zone of the site, or after you changed at or weekday – it moves the event to the nearest occurrence. When that occurrence has already passed, the event runs once on the next request and then keeps its local time again. That way a change of daylight saving time never skips a run.

A start time that does not exist on a day, such as 02:30 when the clocks go forward, moves forward by the gap (03:30). In the hour that repeats when the clocks go back, the first of the two times counts.

If you remove at from an event and keep its interval, the event keeps the time of day it ran at so far. It goes on running in its interval, but it is no longer moved back to its local time, so after the next change of daylight saving time it runs an hour earlier or later. The comparison described below does not give it a new start time; only a change of the interval schedules it anew, due at once.

One-time tasks

A one-time task carries data: the post a reminder is about, the kind of reminder. You describe that data as a value class and write one handler for it:

final readonly class SendReminder
{
    public function __construct(
        public int $postId,
        public ReminderKind $kind = ReminderKind::Mail,
    ) {}
}

use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Cron\CronTask;

final readonly class Reminders
{
    #[CronTask('send-reminder')]
    public function send(SendReminder $task, Mailer $mailer): void
    {
        $post = get_post($task->postId);
        // …
    }
}

The first parameter of the handler is the task; further parameters are services. Each task class has exactly one handler. The name, here send-reminder, identifies the task in WordPress: keep it when you rename the class or the method.

To plan a task, inject CronScheduler and pass it a task object and a time:

use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Cron\CronScheduler;
use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Hook\Hook;

final readonly class ReminderPlanner
{
    public function __construct(private CronScheduler $cron) {}

    #[Hook('save_post_event')]
    public function plan(int $postId): void
    {
        $this->cron->schedule(new SendReminder($postId), new DateTimeImmutable('+1 hour'));
    }
}

When the task is due, WP-Cron runs the handler with a new SendReminder object that has the same values. isScheduled() tells you whether a task is waiting, and unschedule() removes it again:

$this->cron->isScheduled(new SendReminder($postId));   // bool
$this->cron->unschedule(new SendReminder($postId));    // number of tasks removed

Equal tasks

Two task objects are the same task if their values are equal. WordPress compares events by their arguments, and the framework passes the values of the task as plain data: enums as their value, nested value objects as arrays, defaults included. So new SendReminder(5) and new SendReminder(postId: 5, kind: ReminderKind::Mail) are the same task, and unschedule() finds a task you planned elsewhere as long as you build an equal object.

WordPress refuses a task that equals one already planned within ten minutes of the same time; schedule() then returns false. For a time in the past or in the next ten minutes, every earlier equal task that has not run yet counts as well.

What a task may contain

A task class is a value class with int, float, string and bool fields (also nullable), backed enums, nested value classes and #[ListOf] lists of them. References are not allowed, neither #[PostReference], #[TermReference] and #[UserReference] nor post classes. The value factory resolves references with the rules of the front end, so a reference to a draft would become null when the task runs in the background. Store the ID as int and load the object in the handler.

The task class is data, not a service: it cannot be injected into a constructor.

WordPress keeps every planned task, with its values, in the option cron, which is loaded on every request. Store IDs, not content, and do not plan thousands of tasks at once: a task per post of a large import would slow down every page.

Keeping WP-Cron in line with the code

On every request (on init), the framework compares the events of your code with what WP-Cron has scheduled and fixes the differences:

A new event is scheduled.

An event whose interval changed is rescheduled.

An event with a start time that runs off its local time moves to the nearest occurrence (see above).

An event or task you removed from the code is unscheduled. Planned tasks of a removed task class are lost.

The framework remembers the events and tasks of your theme or plugin in an autoloaded option ({slug}_cron, with underscores instead of hyphens). When nothing changed, the comparison costs no database query and writes nothing.

When a plugin is deactivated, or the site switches to another theme, the framework removes all events and tasks of that plugin or theme and its option. Switching from a theme to its own child theme keeps them, because the theme stays active as parent theme. Activating the plugin or switching back to the theme schedules them again on the next request. See Activation, deactivation and uninstallation for what else happens at these moments.

The daily clean-up of the file cache and of compiled templates of older releases is an event of the same kind.

Hook names

Each event and task has a WordPress hook, which you see in tools like WP-CLI:

What	Hook
Recurring event	wp_app_framework/cron/{slug}/{name}
Task	wp_app_framework/cron/{slug}/task/{name}
Interval in seconds	schedule wp_app_framework/cron/{slug}/every-{seconds}

The name of a task is the name in its #[CronTask].

The name of a task is part of what WordPress stores. If you change the name in #[CronTask], the tasks planned under the old name are unscheduled on the next request and never run. Renaming the class or the method is safe.

With WP-CLI you can list the events and run one by hand:

wp cron event list
wp cron event run wp_app_framework/cron/my-theme/sync-feed

When things go wrong

If an event or task throws an exception, the outcome depends on WP_DEBUG, as with hooks. Without it, the exception is logged with error_log() and the other due events still run. The log names the hook, the handler and, for tasks, the task class, but not the values of the task, which may be personal data.

WordPress removes a task before it runs it, so a task that fails is not tried again. With WP_DEBUG, the exception also ends the WP-Cron request: the remaining due events run only with a later request.

A task whose stored values no longer match its class – for example because you changed a field type while tasks were planned – fails the same way, with an InvalidArgumentException that names the field.

Rules

#[CronEvent(name, interval, at: null, weekday: null)]:

Parameter	Type	Rule
name	string	Required; lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter; unique among the events of the theme or plugin.
interval	CronInterval|int	Required; an interval of WordPress or seconds, at least 60.
at	?string	Start time HH:MM (00:00 to 23:59) in the time zone of the site; only with Daily, TwiceDaily and Weekly.
weekday	?Weekday	Required for Weekly with at; only there.

#[CronTask(name)]:

Parameter	Type	Rule
name	string	Required; lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter; unique among the tasks of the theme or plugin.

Build errors for both:

The class is no service, or the method is not public, is static or does not return void.

A method has #[CronEvent] and #[CronTask].

The arguments of the attribute cannot be evaluated, for example because they use a constant of WordPress.

Build errors for #[CronEvent]:

An invalid or duplicate name, an interval below 60 seconds.

An invalid at, at with Hourly or seconds, Weekly with at but without weekday, weekday without Weekly and at.

A parameter that is no service.

Build errors for #[CronTask]:

No first parameter, or one that is not typed with a value class: no type, a scalar, nullable, a union, a post class, variadic or by reference.

A task class that is no valid value class, or that contains a reference at any depth (the error names the path, such as task.author.user).

A further parameter that is no service.

Two handlers for one task class; an invalid or duplicate name.

A task class injected into a constructor.

At run time:

CronScheduler::schedule(object $task, DateTimeInterface $at): bool returns true if the task was planned and false if an equal task is already planned within ten minutes. Any other refusal of WordPress, such as a time before 1970 or a plugin that blocks the event, throws a RuntimeException.

CronScheduler::unschedule(object $task): int returns the number of tasks removed; it throws a RuntimeException if WordPress cannot save the events.

CronScheduler::isScheduled(object $task): bool.

All three throw a LogicException for an object whose class has no #[CronTask] handler in this theme or plugin. $task is typed object; static analysis does not catch a wrong class.

When WordPress cannot save the events while the framework brings them in line, the error is thrown as LogicException with WP_DEBUG and logged otherwise; the next request tries again.

toc.text: Keeping WP-Cron in line with the code

description: Some work does not belong to a page view. A feed is synchronized every hour, old data is cleaned up every night, a report goes out on Monday morning, a reminder is sent an hour after someone saved a post. WordPress runs such work with WP-Cron. Using it by hand takes a fair amount of code: you add an action, check with wp_next_scheduled() whether the event exists, schedule it, register custom intervals, and unschedule everything when the theme or plugin goes away. Small mistakes leave orphaned events behind, keep an old interval forever or let a nightly run drift by an hour twice a year. The framework does this for you. You put #[CronEvent] on a method that should run regularly, and #[CronTask] on a method that handles a one-time task, which you plan with the CronScheduler service.

title: Editor
content:
Content editors should see a block in the editor exactly as it appears on the page, and type straight into it. Core blocks achieve that with an edit component in JavaScript, which duplicates the block's markup. A framework block has no such duplicate. Its markup exists only once, in the Twig template. This page explains how the editor runtime makes that work, how you mark editable elements in a template, what the generated inspector offers, and how to extend and build the editor scripts. How it works The framework ships an editor runtime, a script that your theme or plugin builds and the block editor loads. For each framework block in the editor it does three things: It asks the server to render the block, from the same Twig template the front end uses. It parses the returned HTML and finds the elements the template marked as editable. It replaces those elements with editors – rich text, an image picker, inner blocks – and keeps the rest of the markup as it is. The result looks like the front end because it is the front end's markup. When an editor changes a value in the inspector, the runtime renders the block again; when they type into a text field in the canvas, it doesn't, because the text is edited in place. Marking editable elements When the editor renders a block, the template functions field() and inner_blocks() mark the editable elements. On the front end they print nothing. Fields field(path) goes on the element that shows a field: {{ attrs.topline }}

{{ attrs.caption.text }} {% for button in attrs.buttons %} {{ button.label }} {% endfor %} The path names a #[PlainText], #[RichText] or #[Image] field of the block: a name, a dotted path into a value class, or a list with indexes for list items. Anything else throws an exception when the block renders in the editor, so a typo shows up as soon as you insert the block. On the front end field() returns an empty string at once and checks nothing, so it costs nothing there. Text fields become WordPress' RichText with the element's tag. An image field keeps the server markup and adds buttons to select, replace and reset the image. Put field() on an element around the image, such as a

title: Front-end scripts
description: Some blocks need JavaScript on the page: an FAQ that opens its answers, a slider, a counter. The framework gives every such script the same shape. It is a class next to the block, which the framework loads only on pages that show the block, starts once per block and stops again when needed. In the editor, content editors can switch a block to a preview and try its behavior right there. Other scripts belong to no block: a mobile menu, a cookie notice, smooth scrolling. They run on every page as document views, in the same shape. This page explains how a front-end script – a view script – is written, when it runs and how the preview in the editor works. It then covers scripts for the whole page, data from PHP, external scripts and modules shared between scripts.

title: Hooks
content:
Hooks are how your code talks to WordPress. In a plain theme you would call add_filter() in functions.php, create the objects your callback needs, and count the arguments it accepts. With the framework, you put #[Hook] on a method instead. The build finds the method, and the framework registers the hook and creates the class only when WordPress actually fires it. For work that runs regularly or later, without a page view, see Cron events and tasks.

A first hook

This filter changes post titles with the help of a Formatter service:

use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Hook\Hook;

final class TitleFilter
{
    #[Hook('the_title', priority: 20)]
    public function filter(string $title, Formatter $formatter, int $postId = 0): string
    {
        return $formatter->format($title, $postId);
    }
}

Several things happen here without extra code:

Action or filter? The method returns a string, so the framework registers a filter. A method that returns void becomes an action.

Services in the signature. Formatter is a service (see Services), so the framework passes it in. You can ask for services in the constructor too; in the method signature they are handy when only this hook needs them.

WordPress arguments. All other parameters receive the arguments WordPress passes to the hook, in their order: $title gets the first, $postId the second. The framework derives accepted_args from them, so you never count by hand.

Optional arguments. If WordPress passes fewer arguments than the method declares, the missing ones use their default value. That is why $postId has = 0.

Several hooks on one method

#[Hook] is repeatable. The same method can listen to several hooks, each with its own priority:

#[Hook('the_title')]
#[Hook('single_post_title', priority: 5)]
public function filter(string $title): string { /* … */ }

When things go wrong

The class is created only when the hook fires for the first time, so a theme with many hooks loads only what a request uses.

If the method throws an exception, the outcome depends on WP_DEBUG. With WP_DEBUG enabled, the exception is rethrown and you see it right away. Without it, the exception is logged with error_log() and the site keeps running. A filter then returns the value it received, as if it had not run.

Rules

The method is public and non-static and declares a return type: void for an action, any other type for a filter.

Parameters typed with a service candidate are injected. All other parameters receive the WordPress arguments in their order; accepted_args is derived from them.

#[Hook(name, priority: 10)] is repeatable.

Services are created when the hook fires. Exceptions are rethrown with WP_DEBUG; otherwise they are logged with error_log(), and filters return their original value.

title: Activation, deactivation and uninstallation
content:
A plugin or theme leaves traces in WordPress: cron events, options, tables, posts. Some work belongs to the moments when it starts and stops: a plugin creates a default page when it is activated, pauses a connection to a service when it is deactivated, and removes everything it stored when it is deleted. Without help, every plugin repeats the same code: activation and deactivation hooks, an uninstall.php that needs to know the names of every option and table, a loop over the sites of a network.

The framework does the part that follows from your declarations by itself. It removes the cron events of a deactivated plugin or a theme the site switched away from, and when a plugin is deleted, it removes the data the plugin declared. For everything else you mark methods with #[OnActivation], #[OnDeactivation] and #[OnUninstall].

When WordPress activates and deactivates

Plugins and themes start and stop in different ways.

A plugin is activated and deactivated on the plugins screen or with wp plugin activate and wp plugin deactivate. WordPress fires an action for this in the same request. A plugin is deleted only while it is inactive; WordPress then runs its uninstallation and removes its files.

A theme is never activated on its own: the site switches from one theme to another. WordPress fires switch_theme in the request that switches, while the old theme is still loaded, and after_switch_theme on the next request, with the new theme. The framework treats the first as the deactivation of the old theme and the second as the activation of the new one. A theme and its own child theme count as one: switching from a theme to its child theme, or back, neither deactivates nor activates the parent theme, because it stays loaded. A child theme with code of its own is an instance of its own (see Child themes): switching from the parent theme to it activates it, switching back deactivates it.

Themes cannot be uninstalled. WordPress loads no code of a theme it deletes, so nothing can clean up after a theme. This is often what you want: when someone switches back to the theme, its settings and tables are still there.

What the framework does by itself

Moment	Plugin	Theme and child theme
Activation	The rewrite rules are flushed on the next request. Cron events are scheduled on the next request, tables are created on the next request or the first access.	The same.
Deactivation	All cron events and tasks of the plugin are removed.	All cron events and tasks of the theme are removed.
Uninstallation	All data of the plugin is removed (see below).	–

Methods of your own

A lifecycle method is a public method of a service that returns void. Its parameters are services; WordPress passes nothing the method could use. Take a plugin that keeps a page with its overview:

use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Lifecycle\OnActivation;

final readonly class OverviewPage
{
    public function __construct(private PageStore $pages) {}

    #[OnActivation]
    public function create(): void
    {
        $this->pages->ensureOverview();
    }
}

When the plugin is activated, create() runs. The methods of the plugin's post types and tables work already: the framework registers the post types of the plugin first, and a table is created on its first access.

#[OnDeactivation] works the same way. It runs before the framework removes the cron events, so the method can still look at them:

#[OnDeactivation]
public function pause(SyncClient $client): void
{
    $client->unsubscribe();
}

#[OnUninstall] runs when the plugin is deleted, before the framework removes its data. Use it for what the framework does not know about, such as an option you write with update_option() yourself or a file in the uploads directory:

#[OnUninstall]
public function removeExports(ExportDirectory $exports): void
{
    $exports->deleteAll();
}

A class may have any number of lifecycle methods, and one method may have several of the attributes. The methods of one moment run in the order of their class and method names.

If a method throws, the framework rethrows the exception when WP_DEBUG is on. Activating a plugin then fails with the error, as WordPress shows it for any plugin. Without WP_DEBUG, the error is logged and the next method runs, like a failing hook.

What the uninstallation removes

When a plugin is deleted, the framework first runs the #[OnUninstall] methods, then removes on each site:

every post of the plugin's post types, in any status, with its meta, comments and revisions,

every term of the plugin's taxonomies,

the meta keys of its meta classes, also from posts of other types, such as Post and Page,

the options of its settings groups,

its cron events and tasks,

its tables, with the tables an earlier namespace of the plugin left, and the state of their sync,

its technical options: the versions of cache tags, cache entries stored as transients, the rewrite hash, notices of the meta box.

Then it deletes the plugin's cache directory wp-content/cache/{slug} and lets WordPress rebuild its rewrite rules, which still contain the plugin's post types.

The framework removes only names it knows exactly: names from the build, or options in the exact form it writes them. It never deletes "everything that starts with the plugin's prefix", because another plugin whose namespace starts the same way (shop and shop-extras) would lose its data.

Some things stay:

Attachments uploaded to the deleted posts. They stay in the media library; WordPress does not delete them with a post.

Blocks of the plugin in other posts. They render nothing without the plugin.

Entries of a persistent object cache. They are never read again, because the versions of their tags are gone, and expire with their lifetime.

Everything the plugin stored without the framework: options, user meta, files. Remove it in an #[OnUninstall] method.

WordPress runs an uninstall.php of a plugin instead of the uninstall hook the framework registers. A plugin with this file would keep all its data, so the file is a build error. Move its code into a method with #[OnUninstall].

WordPress needs a static callback for the uninstall hook and stores it in the option uninstall_plugins. The framework registers it when the plugin is activated and again when it is deactivated, since a plugin is always deactivated before it is deleted. When WordPress uninstalls the plugin, it loads the plugin's main file first, so the plugin boots; this happens after init, and the framework registers the plugin's post types and taxonomies itself before the uninstallation runs.

Multisite

Every site of a network has its own options, cron events and tables. The framework therefore runs everything site by site:

Activating a plugin network-wide activates it on every site of the network; deactivating it network-wide deactivates it on every site. The lifecycle methods run once per site, with that site as the current one.

A site created while the plugin is active network-wide is activated as soon as WordPress has set it up.

Deleting a site drops the tables of the plugin on that site, together with the tables of WordPress.

Deleting the plugin uninstalls it on every site of every network.

On a large network, activating, deactivating and deleting a plugin takes a while, since each site is handled in turn.

Rules

Attribute	Runs	Allowed in
#[OnActivation]	Plugin: when it is activated (activate_{plugin}), per site when network-wide, and for new sites of a network where it is active network-wide. Theme: on the first request after the switch to it (after_switch_theme), unless the previous theme was the theme itself or its child theme.	Plugins, themes, child themes
#[OnDeactivation]	Plugin: when it is deactivated (deactivate_{plugin}), per site when network-wide. Theme: in the request that switches away from it (switch_theme), unless the new theme is the theme itself or its child theme.	Plugins, themes, child themes
#[OnUninstall]	When the plugin is deleted, on every site, before the framework removes its data.	Plugins only

Build errors:

The method is not public, is static or does not return void.

A parameter is not a service, or is variadic or passed by reference.

The class is not a service (for example #[NoService]).

#[OnUninstall] in a theme or child theme.

A plugin has an uninstall.php. In development mode, the boot reports the file as well, since the cached manifest does not notice a new file.

title: Plugins
description: A plugin uses the framework just like a theme. It boots its own instance with Plugin::boot(__FILE__) (see Boot and modes) and has its own blocks, hooks, REST routes, templates and settings. Everything in the guides applies to plugins as well. What is special about plugins is that they often work together with a theme. A plugin may provide data the theme displays, or helpers the theme's templates call. This page explains how a plugin – or a theme, towards its child theme – offers such an interface, and how the theme changes the plugin's markup.

title: Posts
description: Many sites need content of their own kind besides posts and pages: events, team members, venues, products. WordPress calls these post types, and their extra values post meta. Registering them by hand means a long list of arguments for register_post_type(), a meta key per value with a schema for the REST API, a form in the editor and code that reads the stored strings back into typed values. The framework lets you declare all of this with classes, as you do with blocks and settings: a post class declares a post type and is at the same time the object of a post of that type: you load, change and save posts through it;a meta class declares typed fields that belong to posts of one or more post types;a taxonomy class declares a taxonomy for post types. The build checks the declarations, and the framework registers everything on init, adds the forms to the editor and keeps the URLs working.

title: Queries
content:
A page often shows a list of posts: the next five events, the events of a genre, a page of news. In plain WordPress you describe such a list as an array of arguments for WP_Query, with the names of post types, meta keys and taxonomies as strings. A typo finds nothing, and your editor cannot help you. The framework lets you write the same query with the classes you already have. You start at the post class, add conditions on meta fields and terms, sort, and get post objects back: $events = Event::query() ->where(EventDetailsFields::capacity()->greaterThan(10)) ->where(Terms::in(Genre::class, [$jazz])) ->orderBy(EventDetailsFields::start()) ->limit(5) ->get(); Every name in this query is a class or a method, so your editor completes it and PHPStan checks it. The framework turns the query into arguments of WP_Query and runs it there. Plugins that filter queries, for example translation plugins, keep working. How it works Event::query() returns a PostQuery for posts of the type. A query never changes: every method returns a changed copy. You can therefore keep a query, pass it to other code and vary it without side effects: $upcoming = Event::query()->where(EventDetailsFields::start()->greaterOrEqual($today)); $teaser = $upcoming->limit(3)->get(); $total = $upcoming->count(); // counts all upcoming events, not 3 The flip side is that a call whose result you do not keep does nothing. To make that mistake visible, every method that returns a query carries PHP's #[\NoDiscard]. PHP warns when you drop the result, and PHPStan reports the line: $query->limit(3); // warning: the result is discarded $query = $query->limit(3); // right Without further methods, a query finds all published posts of the type, sorted the way WordPress sorts them (newest first). The methods get(), first(), count() and paginate() run the query. Meta fields in queries To filter or sort by a meta field, the query needs the field as an object. A field object knows its meta class, its name and its type. The type decides which comparisons it offers: an IntField takes integers, an EnumField takes the cases of EventKind. The field objects come from a class of their own next to the meta class, marked with #[MetaFields]. This keeps the meta class as it is, and you decide for each meta class whether its fields can be queried at all. Generating the class The quickest way is to let the framework write it. Run this in your theme or plugin: vendor/bin/wp-app-framework meta-fields 'Sections\Post\EventDetails' The command writes EventDetailsFields.php into the directory of EventDetails, with one method per field that can be queried: #[MetaFields(EventDetails::class)] final class EventDetailsFields { public static function capacity(): IntField { return new IntField(EventDetails::class, 'capacity'); } /** * @return EnumField */ public static function kind(): EnumField { return new EnumField(EventDetails::class, 'kind', EventKind::class); } /** * @return PostField */ public static function venue(): PostField { return new PostField(EventDetails::class, 'venue', Venue::class); } } The file is ordinary source code of your project. Commit it, remove methods you do not need, or add a method later. The command does not replace an existing file unless you pass --force. Together with table-fields for tables, it is the only command of the framework that writes source code, and it does so only when you run it. Writing it by hand You can also write the class yourself, for example with just the one field you query. The build checks it either way: it calls every public static method that returns a field and reports a field of another meta class, a field name that does not exist, a field class that does not fit the type, and a field that cannot be queried. Fields that hold a list or a value class cannot be queried. WordPress stores them serialized in one meta value, and SQL cannot look inside. Missing values A post that was never saved with a field has no meta value for it. When you load the meta object, such a field has the default of its constructor parameter. Queries follow the same rule. If the default meets a condition, the condition also finds posts without a stored value: capacity()->lessThan(5) finds events without a stored capacity, because the default is 0. Sorting follows it too: a post without a value sorts like the default. WordPress' own sorting by meta values cannot do this reliably, so the framework adds the sort order to the SQL of the query itself. It uses a filter of WordPress that it adds only while the query runs. A date without value is '', its default: it sorts before every date, and greaterOrEqual() with a date does not find it. Conditions where() takes conditions; all of them must be met. Conditions come from field objects, from Terms for taxonomies, and from the groups Any and All: $events = Event::query() ->where( Any::of( EventDetailsFields::kind()->equals(EventKind::Jazz), EventDetailsFields::venue()->equals($venue), ), Terms::notIn(Genre::class, [$children]), ) ->get(); Any::of() is met if one of its conditions is met, All::of() if all of them are; groups can contain groups. WordPress keeps conditions on meta fields and on terms in two separate parts of a query and always joins the two with AND. A group therefore contains either meta conditions or term conditions; mixing them throws an exception. The same field classes and groups work for the columns of tables of your own, in LogEntry::query(). A query of posts takes no conditions on columns, and a query of rows none on meta fields or terms. The data of the post has methods of its own, described in the next section. Posts and pages Queries work the same for the post types of WordPress: Post::query() returns posts, Page::query() pages. The fields every post has – slug, title, dates, parent, template, format, password, comments – have methods of their own, because they are columns of the posts table or data WordPress keeps in a fixed place, not fields of a meta class: $news = Post::query() ->where(Terms::in(Category::class, [$news]), Terms::notIn(Tag::class, [$internal])) ->format(PostFormat::Standard, PostFormat::Video) ->sticky(false) ->modifiedAfter(new DateTimeImmutable('-7 days')) ->search('concert', columns: [SearchColumn::Title]) ->get(); $imprint = Page::query()->slug('imprint')->first(); $wide = Page::query()->parentIn($about, $team)->template('page-wide')->orderBy(PostOrder::MenuOrder)->get(); WordPress' categories and tags are named by the framework classes Category and Tag, like its post types by Post and Page. They register nothing and work wherever a taxonomy class is accepted: in Terms, getTerms(), TaxonomyTag and #[TermReference]. A few fields need a word of explanation: Template: WordPress stores the template of a post in the protected meta key _wp_page_template, as the slug of the file in templates/. template('page-wide') finds posts with that template, defaultTemplate() posts without one. Format: post formats are terms of the taxonomy post_format. Since you know them as a fixed list, format() takes the enum PostFormat; PostFormat::Standard is a post without format. Sticky: WordPress keeps the IDs of sticky posts in the option sticky_posts. sticky() reads it when the query runs, so a cached query notices a change. Only posts of the type post can be sticky. Search: without further arguments, search() looks in the title, excerpt and content, like the search of WordPress. columns limits it, exact requires the text to be the whole value of a column, and sentence searches the words as one phrase. Sorting and pages orderBy() sorts by post data (PostOrder::Title, PostOrder::Date, …) or a field, ascending unless you pass Direction::Desc. Each further call sorts the posts that are still equal. limit() and offset() restrict get(). For pages, use paginate(), which also counts all matching posts: $page = Event::query()->orderBy(PostOrder::Date, Direction::Desc)->paginate(perPage: 10, page: $number); foreach ($page->getPosts() as $event) { /* … */ } $pages = $page->getPageCount(); Caching cache() stores the result in the cache of your theme or plugin. The framework stores the IDs of the posts and the number of matching posts, and loads the post objects from them on each call: $events = Event::query()->where(Terms::in(Genre::class, [$jazz]))->cache(ttl: 600)->get(); You do not need to name tags for the posts. The framework adds the tag of the post type and of every taxonomy in the conditions, so a changed event, meta value or term assignment invalidates the entry. Further tags and variants work as with remember(). A random order cannot be cached. WordPress caches the IDs of queries in the object cache as well, but only with a persistent object cache, and every change of any post invalidates all of them. cache() also works with the file backend and is invalidated per post type. Using results in templates Queries belong in PHP, not in templates. A block runs its query in render() and passes the post objects to its template, where their getters work as with post(): public function render(EventListAttributes $attrs): string { return $this->renderer->render('Block/EventList/EventList.twig', [ 'events' => Event::query()->limit($attrs->limit)->get(), ]); } {% for event in events %} {{ event.title }} {% endfor %} Rules AbstractPost::query() returns a PostQuery of the post class; it works once the theme or plugin has booted. Every method that returns a query is marked #[\NoDiscard]. Method Effect where(Condition ...$conditions) All conditions must be met; adds to earlier calls. status(PostStatus ...) These statuses instead of Publish. The capabilities of the current user are not checked. ids(AbstractPost|int ...) Only these posts; without arguments no posts at all. exclude(AbstractPost|int ...) Not these posts; adds to earlier calls. Next to ids() the posts are taken out of the IDs, because WordPress ignores its own exclusion when IDs are given. author(int ...) Posts of these authors. parent(AbstractPost|int|null) Children of the post (an object or its ID), or top-level posts with null; hierarchical post types only. search(string, list $columns = [], bool $exact = false, bool $sentence = false) The search of WordPress; the text must not be empty. Without columns: title, excerpt and content. slug(string ...) Posts with one of the slugs (post_name). title(string) Posts with exactly this title. parentIn(AbstractPost|int ...), parentNotIn(…) Children of one of the posts, or no children of them; hierarchical post types only. modifiedAfter(DateTimeInterface), modifiedBefore(…) Date of the last change, the time itself excluded. template(string ...), defaultTemplate() Posts with one of the templates (slug), or without template. format(PostFormat ...) Posts with one of the formats; Standard is a post without format. sticky(bool = true) Sticky posts only, or no sticky posts; Post::query() only. hasPassword(bool = true) Posts with a password, or without one. menuOrder(int) Posts with this menu order (at least 0). commentCount(int, Comparison = Equal) Posts whose number of approved comments compares to the number. commentStatus(DiscussionStatus), pingStatus(DiscussionStatus) Posts whose comments or pings are open or closed. publishedAfter(DateTimeInterface), publishedBefore(…) Publication date, the time itself excluded. orderBy(PostOrder|Field, Direction = Asc) Sorts; further calls sort what is still equal. Without it: newest first. limit(int), offset(int) At most this many posts (at least 1), skipping some (with limit()). Without limit(), all posts. cache(int $ttl, array $tags = [], array $vary = []) Caches the result; tags of the post type and the taxonomies are added. get() The posts, as objects of the post class. first() The first post or null. count() The number of all matching posts, regardless of limit() and offset(). paginate(int $perPage, int $page) A PostPage with getPosts(), getTotal(), getPage(), getPerPage() and getPageCount(); not with limit() or offset(). A value outside the allowed range, such as limit(0), throws an InvalidArgumentException when you call the method. A combination that does not fit, such as offset() without limit() or paginate() after limit(), throws a LogicException when the query runs. Fields and their conditions: Field of the meta class Field class Conditions string (also #[PlainText], #[RichText], #[Url]) StringField equals, notEquals, in, notIn, greaterThan, greaterOrEqual, lessThan, lessOrEqual, between, contains int IntField as StringField, without contains float FloatField as IntField bool BoolField equals backed enum EnumField equals, notEquals, in, notIn post class (?Venue) PostField

equals, in, notIn, isNull, isNotNull #[Image], #[PostReference], #[TermReference], #[UserReference] on ?int IdField equals, in, notIn, isNull, isNotNull Strings are compared without regard to case, like the default collations of the database. contains() matches % and _ literally. A meta value that is not stored counts as the default in conditions and in the sort order. Terms::in(), notIn() and all() take the taxonomy class, a non-empty list of WP_Term objects or term IDs and includeChildren (default true); Terms::exists() and notExists() take the taxonomy class. Any::of() and All::of() need at least one condition, all on meta fields, all on terms or all on the columns of a table. DateTimeField and the Nullable… field classes are for tables only. #[MetaFields(metaClass)] on a class of your own: metaClass is a meta class (#[PostMeta]) of the theme or plugin; one class per meta class. Every public static method that returns a field has no parameters and returns a field of metaClass with an existing field name and the field class of its type (with the enum or post class of the field). Other methods are ignored. The class is no service. In development mode the build runs again when signatures change, not when only a method body changes; a query checks its fields again when it runs. wp-app-framework meta-fields [--force] writes {MetaClass}Fields.php next to the meta class. An existing file is replaced only with --force.
description: A page often shows a list of posts: the next five events, the events of a genre, a page of news. In plain WordPress you describe such a list as an array of arguments for WP_Query, with the names of post types, meta keys and taxonomies as strings. A typo finds nothing, and your editor cannot help you. The framework lets you write the same query with the classes you already have. You start at the post class, add conditions on meta fields and terms, sort, and get post objects back: Every name in this query is a class or a method, so your editor completes it and PHPStan checks it. The framework turns the query into arguments of WP_Query and runs it there. Plugins that filter queries, for example translation plugins, keep working.

title: REST routes
content:
A REST route in WordPress needs more code than it seems. You call register_rest_route(), write an args schema for validation, add a permission callback, read and convert the parameters, and turn errors into WP_Error objects with the right status code. Forgetting the permission callback makes the route public.

With the framework, a route is a method with #[RestRoute]. The framework derives the argument schema from the method signature, so WordPress validates and sanitizes the arguments before your code runs. The permission is a required argument of the attribute, so your IDE and the build report a route without one.

Controller and routes

Routes live in a controller class. #[RestController] on the class sets the REST namespace and an optional base path for all its routes:

use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Rest\HttpMethod;
use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Rest\Permission\PublicAccess;
use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Rest\RestController;
use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Rest\RestException;
use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Rest\RestRoute;

#[RestController('v1', base: '/items')]
final class ItemController
{
    #[RestRoute('/{id}', HttpMethod::Get, new PublicAccess())]
    public function show(int $id, ItemRepository $items, Variant $variant = Variant::Short): array
    {
        return $items->find($id) ?? throw new RestException('sections_item_not_found', 'Item not found.', 404);
    }
}

With the namespace sections (extra.wp-app-framework.namespace in composer.json), this registers GET /wp-json/sections/v1/items/{id}. Read the method signature from left to right:

int $id matches the placeholder {id} in the path. Because it is an int, the route only matches digits.

ItemRepository $items is a service, so the framework injects it.

Variant $variant = Variant::Short is a backed enum with a default, so it becomes an optional request argument (?variant=long). WordPress accepts only the enum's values, and the method receives the enum case.

The method returns an array, which becomes a JSON response with status 200. If the item does not exist, it throws a RestException with status 404.

#[RestController(version, base: '')] takes the version without leading or trailing slash, for example v1; the value may be a class constant. The routes are registered under {namespace}/{version}, where the namespace is the one of your theme or plugin (see Concepts). A #[RestRoute] in a class without #[RestController] is a build error.

#[RestRoute(path, methods, permission)] is repeatable, and all three arguments are required, so the IDE and the build both report a missing permission. path is empty or starts with /. methods is an HttpMethod case or a list of them.

Permission

Every route says who may call it. There are three kinds of permission, all in the namespace WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Rest\Permission:

new PublicAccess()                      // everybody
new Capability('delete_posts')          // current_user_can('delete_posts')
new Callback(self::canEdit(...))        // your own check

A callback decides with your own logic. It is a first-class callable of a public static method that returns bool. It must be static because PHP allows first-class callables in attribute arguments only for static methods.

#[RestRoute('/{id}', [HttpMethod::Put, HttpMethod::Patch], new Callback(self::canEdit(...)))]
public function update(int $id, string $title): WP_REST_Response { /* … */ }

public static function canEdit(int $id, ItemRepository $items): bool
{
    return current_user_can('edit_post', $items->getPostId($id));
}

The callback's parameters follow the same rules as those of the route: services are injected, and request arguments must exist in the route with the same name and type. Before calling it, the framework validates and sanitizes these arguments against the route's own schema and denies access if one is invalid. That matters because WordPress also calls permission callbacks to build the Allow header, with a request validated for a different route handler.

Path placeholders

{name} in the path matches the parameter with the same name. That parameter must be required and of type int (matches \d+), string ([^/]+) or a backed enum (its values). Its value always comes from the URL, never from a query argument with the same name.

Route paths may only contain letters, digits, ., _, ~, -, / and placeholders.

Parameters

The framework looks at each parameter of the method and decides where its value comes from:

A service candidate is injected.

WP_REST_Request receives the request itself.

Everything else is a request argument with the parameter's name: int, float, string, bool, a backed enum, or an array with #[ListOf(Enum::class)] or #[ListOf(ValueClass::class)] (see Values). Each may be nullable and have a default value.

A single value class without #[ListOf] is not supported as a request argument, because a parameter with a class type is treated as a service.

From the request arguments the framework builds the route's argument schema (type, enum, items, required, default, and minItems and maxItems from the limits of lists). WordPress then does the work it always does with a schema: it validates and sanitizes the arguments, answers with 400 if one is invalid, and shows the schema on an OPTIONS request. Missing optional arguments get the parameter's default. Enums, value objects and lists are converted by the value factory, so your method receives typed values.

#[Param] (WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Rest\Param) adds further constraints to the schema:

public function update(
    int $id,
    #[Param(maxLength: 200)] string $title,
    #[Param(format: Format::Email)] ?string $contact = null,
): WP_REST_Response

Its arguments are description, minimum, maximum, minLength, maxLength, pattern and format (a case of WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Rest\Format). The build checks that each one applies to the parameter's type.

Responses and errors

What the method returns decides the response:

A void method responds with 204 No Content.

Any other value goes through rest_ensure_response() and responds with 200.

For another status code or extra headers, return a WP_REST_Response, e.g. new WP_REST_Response($data, 201).

#[RestRoute('/{id}', HttpMethod::Delete, new Capability('delete_posts'))]
public function delete(int $id): void
{
    // … responds with 204 No Content
}

For an error response, throw RestException(code, message, status, data) with a status between 400 and 599. The response adds the status to the data, so data must not have a key status of its own; that is an InvalidArgumentException. Any other exception is an unexpected error. It is logged with error_log() and answered with status 500 and the code wp_app_framework_internal_error. Class, message, file, line and stack trace of the exception are included in the response only if WP_DEBUG is enabled, so a live site never shows its internals.

Like hooks, the controller and its services are created only when the route is called.

Caching

A GET route can keep its response with #[Cache], plain data or a WP_REST_Response with a status below 400: the arguments of the method are part of the key, the permission check still runs on every request, and errors are never stored. See Cache.

title: Services

toc.text: Only what is used is built

description: Most classes in a theme or plugin need other classes: a hook needs a formatter, a block needs the template renderer, a REST route needs a repository. You don't create these objects yourself, and you don't register them anywhere. You ask for them in the constructor, and the framework's container passes them in. TitleFilter asks for a Formatter, so the container creates one and passes it in. Formatter needs no registration: it is a class in the theme's src/, which makes it a service.

title: Settings
content:
Settings are values for the whole site that a theme or plugin makes configurable in the backend: a tagline, the logo, the page with the privacy policy, the default density of lists. You describe them as typed classes, as you do with block attributes. The framework takes care of the rest: it stores each group of settings in a WordPress option, it adds a settings page with a form for all groups, it passes the values to your services and templates as typed objects. Settings that several blocks share but that are stored per block, such as a color scheme for each block, are block supports, not settings. Declaring a group Settings come in groups. A group is a readonly class with #[SettingsGroup], and each setting is a public promoted constructor parameter with a default: use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\Image; use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\Label; use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Setting\SettingsGroup; use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\ListOf; use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\Url; #[SettingsGroup('general', title: 'General', description: 'Shown on every page.')] final readonly class GeneralSettings { /** * @param list $links */ public function __construct( #[Label('Tagline')] public string $tagline = '', public Density $density = Density::Normal, #[Url] public string $contactUrl = '', #[ListOf(SocialLink::class)] public array $links = [], #[Image] public ?int $logo = null, ) {} } The settings page shows this group as a form: a text field for the tagline, a select for the density, a URL field, a list editor for the social links, and an image picker for the logo. #[SettingsGroup(name, title, description: '', position: 10)] takes these arguments: name consists of lowercase letters, digits and _ and starts with a letter. It is unique within the theme or plugin, and it names the option and the key in templates. title is the title of the group on the settings page. description is an optional text above its form. position orders the groups: lower values first, then by name. Every setting needs a default, because a setting is missing until the group has been saved for the first time. Types of settings Settings follow the rules of values: int, float, string, bool, backed enums, value classes and #[ListOf] lists, each optionally nullable. Enum cases are labeled with Labeled. #[Url] and #[Label] work as for block attributes, and #[Hidden] keeps a setting off the settings page. Some markers from blocks have a meaning in settings too: #[Image] on a ?int stores the ID of an attachment, chosen from the media library. It also works in value classes and list items. Print the image with wp_attachment_image(). A value class used both by a block and by a settings group edits its image in the block canvas there and in the form here. #[PlainText] is a text field; with multiline: true a text area. Print multiline text with |nl2br. Link is a link to a post or a free URL, with "Open in new tab": a search of published posts and a URL field. Print it with link_attributes(). #[RichText(allowedFormats: null)] is edited with WordPress' classic editor, because the rich text of the block editor works only inside a block. allowedFormats may contain core/bold, core/italic, core/link, core/strikethrough, core/subscript and core/superscript; other formats are build errors. The editor keeps only these elements and line breaks, without paragraphs. Print rich text with |raw. When a user without unfiltered_html saves (for example on multisite), it is filtered with wp_kses_post(). References (#[PostReference], #[TermReference], #[UserReference]) are chosen with a search, one or as a list. #[Identifier] in a list item gives each item an identifier that blocks and other settings can refer to. The settings page generates it when an item is added and never shows it. Other markers do not fit: inspector and excerpt have no effect in settings. postContent is a build error. #[Content] marks the content of blocks and means nothing in settings. It is a build error, also in value classes that a group uses. A group class is not a service. It is created from the stored values, never autowired, and #[Hook] or other entry points on it are build errors. Storage Each group is stored in its own option, named {namespace}_{name}, where {namespace} is the namespace of the theme or plugin (extra.wp-app-framework.namespace) with _ instead of -. A theme with the namespace my-theme stores the group general in my_theme_general. The option holds an object with every setting of the group; settings missing from a saved object get their default, and list items with #[Identifier] get missing, invalid and duplicate identifiers filled in. The framework registers the option with register_setting() on init, with its schema and show_in_rest. That makes it readable and writable through /wp/v2/settings under the same name. WordPress validates and sanitizes saved values against the schema there, and requires the capability manage_options for reading and saving. The option belongs to the theme's namespace, not to its directory name or the active stylesheet. A child theme without code therefore uses the settings of its parent theme, and switching to a child theme keeps them. A child theme with code and each plugin have their own groups and options. Deleting a plugin deletes the options of its groups (see Activation, deactivation and uninstallation); the options of a theme stay when the site switches to another theme. Using settings A service receives a group through its constructor: final class Footer { public function __construct(private readonly GeneralSettings $settings) {} #[Hook('wp_footer')] public function print(): void { printf('

%s

', esc_html($this->settings->tagline)); } } The group object is created from the stored values when it is first needed, and kept until the option changes. Groups can be injected into the constructors of services only, not as parameters of hooks, REST routes or template functions. Templates read the groups of their own theme or plugin through the global settings:

{{ settings.general.tagline }}

{{ wp_attachment_image(settings.general.logo, 'medium') }} settings exists only if the theme or plugin declares settings groups. An unknown group name is an error. Invalid stored values A stored value can stop matching its setting, for example when a case is removed from its enum. The framework replaces such a value with the setting's default and logs it (wp-app-framework: settings: … in the PHP error log). The other settings of the group keep their stored values, so one outdated value never resets the whole group. Settings page A theme or plugin with settings groups gets one settings page. Its title is the name of the theme or plugin: the Theme Name: header of style.css, or the Plugin Name: header of the plugin's main file. A missing name is a build error. Themes and child themes find the page under "Appearance", plugins under "Settings". Only users with manage_options can open it. Each group is a form built from the same controls as the block inspector: text, number, toggle, select, rich text, image from the media library, color, reference search, nested values and the list editor. The settings of a group are titled like headings, the values inside them like the inspector. Several groups appear as tabs; a tab with unsaved changes is marked with "•". A list item is titled with its first text, a #[PlainText] or #[RichText] value, else with the item label and its number (see Lists). One "Save" button saves all groups in a single request through /wp/v2/settings. If a value is invalid, WordPress rejects the whole request, the page names the group and the setting, and nothing is saved. The page script is built by the theme's or plugin's build, like the editor runtime (see Editor), to build/vendor/wp-app-framework/settings.js. Without it, the settings page fails with an exception naming the missing file. Controls of your own The generated form fits most settings. Some need more: a list of color schemes is easier to set up when each scheme shows a preview and the contrast of its colors. A settings script next to the group class replaces the control of a value with a component of your own – for src/Setting/Design.php that is src/Setting/Design.settings.js: registerSettingsControl( 'design', [ 'schemes', '*' ], ( { value, path, DefaultControl } ) => ( <> ) ); registerSettingsControl( group, path, component ) takes the name of the group and the path of the value: a setting ('schemes'), a field of a value class in it ([ 'contact', 'email' ]) or, with *, every item of a list ([ 'schemes', '*' ]). The component receives SettingsControlProps: value and onChange, the value and how to change it; path, where the value is, with the index of each list item, e.g. [ 'schemes', 0 ]; groupValue, the value of the whole group with the changes not saved yet; DefaultControl, the control the page would show without yours. Render it to add to the generated control instead of rebuilding it; the example keeps the color pickers of a scheme and adds the preview below them. The settings page loads the script after its own and before it renders, so its controls are registered in time. It warns in the console about an unknown group and about a path that names no value with a control: a #[Hidden] setting, a field the value class does not have, * after a value that is no list. The import @webcodingcat/wp-app-framework/settings is mapped to the settings page of your theme or plugin (window.wpAppFramework[slug].settingsApi), like the editor API (see Editor). The API of the editor and of the front end is not loaded there: a settings script that imports @webcodingcat/wp-app-framework or @webcodingcat/wp-app-framework/view, also through a shared module, fails the build, and so does an editor or view script that imports @webcodingcat/wp-app-framework/settings. A settings script next to a class without #[SettingsGroup] is a build error, because it would never be loaded.

title: Styles
description: Block markup is styled with Tailwind CSS 4. The work is split between the framework and the theme. The framework compiles the stylesheet and loads it on the front end and in the editor. The design – which Tailwind tokens exist and which WordPress values they point to – belongs to the theme. The framework ships no stylesheet for the front end of its own, because design tokens differ from theme to theme.

title: Block supports
content:
Some settings belong to many blocks at once. A color scheme is the typical example: a card, a section and a teaser should all offer the same choice, look the same in the inspector and produce the same class names. Copying an enum into every attribute class and a class into every template would work, but every new block would have to repeat it, and nothing would keep the copies in line.

A block support declares such a setting once. Every block that uses it gets an attribute, a control in the inspector and class names on its root element; the framework derives all of that in the build. WordPress uses the same idea for its own supports such as alignment, which you switch on with #[Supports].

Block supports apply only to the blocks of the same theme or plugin, not to core blocks or blocks of other instances. Values for the whole site rather than for a single block are settings.

Declaring a support

A support is a service class with #[BlockSupport] and a public method className(). The method receives the value of the attribute and returns the class names for it:

use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Block\Support\BlockSupport;

#[BlockSupport('surface', label: 'Surface')]
final class Surface
{
    public function className(SurfaceTone $value = SurfaceTone::Light): ?string
    {
        return 'surface-' . $value->value;
    }
}

The signature of className() describes the whole support. Its parameter type sets the attribute's schema and the control in the inspector, and its default is the attribute's default. Here SurfaceTone is a backed enum, so the inspector shows a select, and blocks start with SurfaceTone::Light.

#[BlockSupport(attribute, label, group: SupportGroup::Styles)] takes three arguments:

attribute is the name of the block attribute, in camelCase (colorScheme). The names WordPress reserves (lock, metadata, className, anchor, align, style) and a name that another support of the same theme or plugin uses are build errors.

label labels the control.

group places the control in the "Styles" tab (SupportGroup::Styles) or in the block's "Settings" panel (SupportGroup::Settings).

className() has exactly one parameter, with a default. Its type is one of these, each optionally nullable:

Type	Control
backed enum	select; label the cases with Labeled
bool	toggle
int, float	number
string	text

Value classes and lists are not supported, and the parameter takes no attributes such as #[Label]. The method returns string or ?string: the class names for the value, several separated by spaces, or null or '' for none.

The class is a service. It can depend on other services through its constructor – for example to read the available color schemes from the settings – and it is created when a block with the support renders for the first time. A support that no block uses is not built.

Using a support

A block adds a support with #[UseSupport]. It is repeatable, one per support:

#[Block('card', title: 'Card', category: BlockCategory::Design)]
#[UseSupport(Surface::class, default: SurfaceTone::Dark)]
final class Card
{
    public function render(CardAttributes $attrs): string { /* … */ }
}

The block now has the attribute surface. Its default comes from the parameter of className(); default overrides it for this block and must have the type of the value – a case of the enum, a bool, and so on.

The template doesn't need to know about the support. It prints the root element with block_wrapper_attributes(), as every block template does, and that adds the class names of all supports to the classes of WordPress' supports:

<article {{ block_wrapper_attributes({class: 'card'}) }}>…</article>

A block with supports that renders without calling block_wrapper_attributes() fails. That way a support never stays without effect unnoticed.

Like every attribute, the value is stored in the block comment, e.g. <!-- wp:sections/card {"surface":"light"} /-->. The attribute object passed to render() does not contain it; the support handles it.

The following are build errors: an attribute of a support with the name of a parameter of the block's attribute class, the same support used twice, and a class without #[BlockSupport] in #[UseSupport].

At render time

Before the block renders, the framework sanitizes the value against its schema, converts it to its PHP type (an enum case, for example) and calls className().

Each returned class name must consist of letters, digits, - and _, so it must equal its sanitize_html_class(). Anything else is an error, because a class name built from user data could otherwise break the markup. Errors are handled like the render errors of blocks: rethrown with WP_DEBUG, otherwise logged, and the block renders nothing.

Blocks rendered for an excerpt evaluate no supports.

In the editor

The control appears in the support's group, only in the default editing mode. In contentOnly mode – in patterns and template parts – it is hidden, as WordPress hides its own design settings there. Changing the value renders the block again, so the class names in the canvas come from the server, just like on the front end.

A script next to the support class can replace the generated control in every block that uses the support. For src/Support/Surface.php that is src/Support/Surface.editor.js; it is loaded with the runtime if a block uses the support:

registerSupportControl( 'surface', ( { value, onChange } ) => <SurfacePicker value={ value } onChange={ onChange } /> );

The component receives { value, onChange, attributes, setAttributes, clientId, isPreview }. A control that a block registers with registerControl() for the same attribute wins over the support's control.

On the front end

When a support needs JavaScript on the page – an element that fades in while it scrolls into view, for example – put a view script next to its class: src/Support/Reveal.view.js. It runs in every block that uses the support and receives the support's value. See Front-end scripts.

Styling

className() builds class names at run time, so Tailwind does not find them in the templates. Style them with CSS of the theme, or list them with @source inline(…) in assets/styles.css (see Styles).
