title: Tables
content:
Some data does not fit into posts: a log of imports, counters, assignments between objects, the state of a background job. Each of them has many rows with the same few columns, is rarely edited by hand and does not need revisions, URLs or the block editor. Stored as posts with meta fields, every row would cost a post and one meta row per field, and a query would join the meta table once per condition. A table of its own is faster and simpler.

In plain WordPress you would write the CREATE TABLE yourself, keep it up to date with dbDelta() and read rows as arrays of strings with $wpdb. The framework lets you declare a table as a class instead. It creates the table, changes it when the class changes, and loads and saves rows as objects – the same way post classes work for posts.

$entry = new LogEntry(level: Level::Error, message: 'Import failed');
$entry->save();

$errors = LogEntry::query()
    ->where(LogEntryFields::level()->equals(Level::Error))
    ->orderBy(LogEntryFields::created(), Direction::Desc)
    ->limit(20)
    ->get();

Use posts for content that people edit, link to or translate; use a table for data your code writes and reads.

The row class

A row class extends AbstractRow and carries #[Table] with the name of the table. Its promoted constructor parameters are the columns:

use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Table\{AbstractRow, Table, PrimaryKey, Indexed, Length, Text};

#[Table('log')]
final class LogEntry extends AbstractRow
{
    public function __construct(
        #[PrimaryKey]
        private ?int $id = null,
        #[Indexed(group: 'level_created', position: 1)]
        private Level $level = Level::Info,
        #[Length(500)]
        private string $message = '',
        #[Text]
        private string $context = '',
        #[Indexed]
        private ?int $postId = null,
        #[Indexed(group: 'level_created', position: 2)]
        private DateTimeImmutable $created = new DateTimeImmutable(),
    ) {}

    public function getId(): ?int
    {
        return $this->id;
    }

    public function setLevel(Level $level): void
    {
        $this->level = $level;
    }

    // further getters and setters …
}

The table is called {prefix}{namespace}_{name}: with the table prefix wp_ and the namespace dev-test of your composer.json, wp_dev_test_log. A theme and a plugin therefore never share a table, even if both name it log.

Each column is named after its parameter in snake case: $postId becomes the column post_id. The parameters are private or protected; you decide with getters and setters what the rest of your code may read and change.

Types

The type of a parameter decides the type of its column. A nullable type (?int) allows NULL; otherwise the column is NOT NULL.

PHP	Column
int	bigint(20)
float	double
bool	tinyint(1)
string	varchar(191); with #[Length(n)] varchar(n); with #[Text] longtext
backed enum	the value of the case: varchar(191) for string enums, bigint(20) for int enums
DateTimeImmutable	datetime, in UTC
#[PrimaryKey] ?int	bigint(20) unsigned with auto increment

A constant default of the parameter – a number, a string, null or an enum case – is the default of the column, too. Long text and times have no default in the table; new DateTimeImmutable() is evaluated by PHP when you create the object.

Floats are written with every digit, so a float you save is the float you load. Times are stored in UTC to the second; a time of another time zone is converted when it is saved.

Indexes

#[Indexed] gives the column an index of its own, named after the column. Add unique: true for a unique index. An index over several columns is a group: give each column the group name and its position.

#[Indexed(group: 'level_created', position: 1)]
private Level $level = Level::Info,
// …
#[Indexed(group: 'level_created', position: 2)]
private DateTimeImmutable $created = new DateTimeImmutable(),

The primary key has its index already. Long text and strings longer than 191 characters cannot be indexed: MariaDB and MySQL limit an index to 3072 bytes, and a character takes up to four.

Loading, saving and deleting

A new row is an object you create with new. save() inserts it and sets its primary key:

$entry = new LogEntry(level: Level::Error, message: 'Import failed', postId: $post->getId());
$entry->save();
$id = $entry->getId();

get() loads a row by its primary key and throws an exception if there is none; find() returns null instead. After a change, save() writes only the columns that changed. Without a change, it writes nothing.

$entry = LogEntry::get($id);
$entry->setLevel(Level::Info);
$entry->save();

$entry->delete();   // its primary key is null afterwards

You can also create a row object with a primary key of your own, for example to restore a row you exported. save() writes it like a loaded row: it updates the row with that key, and if there is none, it inserts the row with that key and all columns.

new LogEntry(id: 42, level: Level::Error, message: 'Restored')->save();

The same happens when the row of a loaded object was deleted in the meantime and you change and save the object: the row comes back with its old primary key. Finding out whether the row exists costs a query of its own, but only when the update changed nothing. MariaDB and MySQL count only the rows an UPDATE really changed, so an update of a row that already has these values looks the same as an update of a missing row.

Every get(), find() and query returns new objects. When two of them change the same row, each save() writes its changed columns; for a column changed by both, the last one wins. save() and delete() check no capabilities.

If the database refuses a row – a string longer than its column, for example – save() throws a RuntimeException with the error of the database. A stored value that no longer fits the class, such as the value of a removed enum case, makes loading the row throw an exception; the framework does not quietly use the default instead.

Queries

LogEntry::query() starts a query of rows. It works like a query of posts: it never changes, so keep the result of each method, and it takes conditions from field objects and the groups Any and All.

$rows = LogEntry::query()
    ->where(LogEntryFields::created()->greaterThan(new DateTimeImmutable('-1 day')))
    ->where(Any::of(
        LogEntryFields::level()->equals(Level::Error),
        All::of(LogEntryFields::attempts()->greaterThan(3), LogEntryFields::postId()->isNotNull()),
    ))
    ->orderBy(LogEntryFields::created(), Direction::Desc)
    ->limit(20)
    ->get();

The framework writes the SQL of the query itself, with every value passed through $wpdb->prepare(). Groups can contain groups to any depth. Without orderBy(), rows come in the order of their primary key.

count() counts all matching rows. delete() deletes them and returns how many – with limit() only the first ones in the order of the query:

$removed = LogEntry::query()->where(LogEntryFields::created()->lessThan($cutoff))->delete();

Field classes

As with meta fields, the field objects come from a class of their own, marked #[TableFields]. Let the framework write it:

vendor/bin/wp-app-framework table-fields 'Sections\Table\LogEntry'

The command writes LogEntryFields.php next to the row class, with one method per column:

#[TableFields(LogEntry::class)]
final class LogEntryFields
{
    /**
     * @return EnumField<Level>
     */
    public static function level(): EnumField
    {
        return new EnumField(LogEntry::class, 'level', Level::class);
    }

    public static function postId(): NullableIntField
    {
        return new NullableIntField(LogEntry::class, 'postId');
    }

    // …
}

The file is ordinary source code, like the one of meta-fields: commit it, shorten it, or write it by hand. The build checks every method that returns a field. A column that allows NULL needs the Nullable… variant of its field class, which adds isNull() and isNotNull(); any other column needs the plain class.

Null

A nullable column without a value holds NULL. Conditions on it behave like comparisons in PHP: equals(5) does not find a row without value, and notEquals(5) and notIn(…) do find it, because null !== 5. Plain SQL would leave such rows out of both; the framework adds OR … IS NULL for you. Use isNull() and isNotNull() to ask for the missing value itself.

When you sort by a nullable column, rows without value come first in ascending order and last in descending order.

Strings are compared without regard to case, like the collation of WordPress' tables.

SQL of your own

For anything a query cannot express – joins, sums, groups – write SQL yourself. LogEntry::tableName() returns the full name of the table on the current site:

global $wpdb;
$counts = $wpdb->get_results($wpdb->prepare(
    'SELECT level, COUNT(*) AS count FROM %i GROUP BY level',
    LogEntry::tableName(),
));

Rows you change this way bypass the row objects; objects loaded before keep their values.

Keeping tables up to date

The framework creates and changes the tables itself; you never write CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE. The build stores the structure of all tables of your theme or plugin in its manifest, together with a hash of it. On init, the framework compares that hash with the one stored after the last change of the tables. This comparison reads an option WordPress loads anyway, so a request whose tables are current costs no database query.

When the hashes differ, the framework syncs the tables of the current site:

It creates every table that does not exist.

It compares each table with its class and changes it in one ALTER TABLE: it adds missing columns and indexes, changes columns whose type, NULL or default differ, renames columns, and drops columns and indexes the class does not declare.

It reads the table again; a remaining difference is an error.

It drops the tables of row classes you removed.

Every change goes to the error log with the prefix wp-app-framework: tables:.

The sync makes the tables match your classes, also when that loses data, and also in development mode – switching to a branch with fewer columns drops them:

A removed parameter drops its column; a removed row class drops its table.

A renamed parameter is a new column; the old one and its data are dropped. Rename with #[RenamedFrom], a table with renamedFrom of #[Table].

A shorter #[Length] cuts longer values. A column that becomes NOT NULL gets 0, an empty string or the zero date where it held NULL; the log says how many values changed.

Keep #[RenamedFrom] as long as an installation may still have the old column.

Renaming

#[RenamedFrom('text')] names an earlier name of the parameter. If the table has a column of that name and none of the new name, the sync renames it, and the data stays. For a parameter renamed several times, add one attribute per earlier name, newest first.

#[RenamedFrom('text')]
private string $message = '',

If both columns exist – after a manual change, for example – the sync leaves the old one alone and logs it, so you can merge them by hand.

A table is renamed the same way: #[Table('entries', renamedFrom: ['log'])] renames wp_dev_test_log if wp_dev_test_entries does not exist yet.

The sync drops only tables it created itself, and only in the current namespace. If you change the namespace of your theme or plugin, the tables of the old namespace stay and the log names them.

When the sync does not run

A sync changes tables that other requests use at the same time, so it takes a lock first. A request that finds the tables locked leaves them to the request that holds the lock.

During a deployment, an older version of your code may still run next to the new one. That code must not undo the changes of the new one. The framework therefore stores the version of your theme or plugin (the Version: header) with the tables and does not sync them for code with a lower version. If you roll back to an older version on purpose, the tables stay as the newer version left them.

If a sync fails, the framework writes the error to the log and tries again after five minutes. With WP_DEBUG, a failure on init is thrown.

Code that uses a table while its sync cannot run – locked, failed or blocked by the version – gets a RuntimeException that names the reason. Code that runs before init, or after switch_to_blog() on another site, syncs the tables before it uses them. While WordPress installs, nothing is synced.

Multisite

Each site has its own tables, with the table prefix of the site. The sync runs for a site on the first request to it, or when code switches to it with switch_to_blog() and uses a table. There are no tables shared by the network. When a site is deleted, its tables of your plugin are dropped with it.

Removing tables

The tables of a theme stay when the site switches to another theme, so they are there again when it switches back. When a plugin is deleted, the framework drops its tables on every site – also tables an earlier namespace of the plugin left – and deletes the state of their sync. See Activation, deactivation and uninstallation.

Rules

#[Table(name, renamedFrom: [])] on a class that extends AbstractRow:

name and each earlier name: lowercase letters, digits and _, starting with a letter; unique among the tables of the theme or plugin. {namespace}_{name} has at most 50 characters.

The class is concrete and has a public constructor of its own. Every constructor parameter is a promoted property, private or protected; the class declares no other properties.

Exactly one parameter has #[PrimaryKey]: ?int with the default null, not readonly.

Types: int, float, bool, string, backed enums and DateTimeImmutable, each also nullable. Not: arrays, other objects, DateTime, DateTimeInterface, union types, mixed.

Parameters take #[PrimaryKey], #[Indexed], #[RenamedFrom], #[Length] and #[Text] only. Column names are unique and have at most 64 characters.

#[Length(n)]: string columns, 1 to 16383; a default must fit. #[Text]: string columns, not together with #[Length]. Values of string enums have at most 191 characters.

#[Indexed(group, position, unique)]: not on the primary key, long text or strings longer than 191 characters. A group needs a position and vice versa; positions are 1 to n without gaps; unique is the same for every column of a group. Group names follow the rules of table names (not primary), have at most 64 characters and differ from the columns with an index of their own. Two indexes with the same columns are an error, and so is an index of more than 3072 bytes.

A row has at most 65535 bytes without long text, as MariaDB and MySQL count them.

#[RenamedFrom(column)]: an earlier parameter name; not the current one, not the name of another column, not twice in the class.

A class that extends AbstractRow without #[Table] is an error. Row classes are no services and cannot be injected or passed to hooks or routes.

AbstractRow:

Method	Effect
static get(int $id)	The row; InvalidArgumentException if there is none.
static find(int $id)	The row or null.
static query()	A RowQuery of the class.
static tableName()	The full table name on the current site.
save()	Inserts the row and sets the primary key, or writes the changed columns; without changes, nothing. With a primary key whose row does not exist, inserts the row with that key and all columns. RuntimeException if the database refuses it, e.g. a duplicate key when another request inserted the row first.
delete()	Deletes the row; the primary key becomes null. LogicException for a row that was never saved.

All of them work once the theme or plugin has booted; before, they throw a LogicException.

RowQuery (every method that returns a query is #[\NoDiscard]):

Method	Effect
where(Condition ...$conditions)	All conditions must be met; adds to earlier calls. Conditions on columns of the class only.
orderBy(Field $field, Direction = Asc)	Sorts; further calls sort what is still equal. Without it: by primary key.
limit(int), offset(int)	At most this many rows (at least 1), skipping some (with limit()).
get()	The rows, as objects of the row class.
first()	The first row or null.
count()	The number of all matching rows, regardless of limit() and offset().
delete()	Deletes the matching rows (with limit() the first ones) and returns their number; not with offset().

As in post queries, a value outside the allowed range, such as limit(0), throws an InvalidArgumentException when you call the method. A combination that does not fit, offset() without limit() in get() or offset() in delete(), throws a LogicException when the query runs.

Columns and their field classes:

Column	Field class	Conditions
string	StringField	equals, notEquals, in, notIn, greaterThan, greaterOrEqual, lessThan, lessOrEqual, between, contains
int, primary key	IntField	as StringField, without contains
float	FloatField	as IntField
bool	BoolField	equals
backed enum	EnumField<E>	equals, notEquals, in, notIn
DateTimeImmutable	DateTimeField	as IntField, with DateTimeInterface
nullable (?string, …)	NullableStringField, NullableIntField, NullableFloatField, NullableBoolField, NullableEnumField<E>, NullableDateTimeField	as above, and isNull, isNotNull

#[TableFields(rowClass)] on a class of your own: one class per row class; every public static method that returns a field has no parameters and returns a field of rowClass with an existing column and its field class (with the enum of the column). The class is no service. In development mode the build runs again when signatures change, not when only a method body changes; a query checks its fields again when it runs.

wp-app-framework table-fields <row class> [--force] writes {RowClass}Fields.php next to the row class. An existing file is replaced only with --force.

description: Some data does not fit into posts: a log of imports, counters, assignments between objects, the state of a background job. Each of them has many rows with the same few columns, is rarely edited by hand and does not need revisions, URLs or the block editor. Stored as posts with meta fields, every row would cost a post and one meta row per field, and a query would join the meta table once per condition. A table of its own is faster and simpler. In plain WordPress you would write the CREATE TABLE yourself, keep it up to date with dbDelta() and read rows as arrays of strings with $wpdb. The framework lets you declare a table as a class instead. It creates the table, changes it when the class changes, and loads and saves rows as objects – the same way post classes work for posts. Use posts for content that people edit, link to or translate; use a table for data your code writes and reads.

title: Translations
content:
A theme or plugin is written in English, and its editors may work in German, French or any other language of WordPress. The framework translates what editors and visitors read with the text domain of your theme or plugin – the Text Domain header of style.css or of the main file of the plugin – like WordPress translates any theme or plugin. There are three kinds of texts: Texts in attributes: the title of a block, the labels of a post type, the #[Label] of a value, the label of an enum case. You write them in English; the framework translates them when it hands them to WordPress or the editor. Texts in templates: {{ __('Load map') }} in Twig. Texts in PHP and JavaScript: WordPress' own functions, __('Load map', 'my-plugin'), as in any plugin. The translations themselves are PO files in languages/, which the framework compiles and loads. The text domain The text domain is the Text Domain header, usually the slug of the theme or plugin: /** * Plugin Name: Datebook * Text Domain: datebook */ The header is required: a project without it is a build error. Use the same domain in your own calls of __(), so that all texts of the project end up in one translation. Texts in attributes You write the texts of attributes in English, as before. The build keeps them as they are, and the framework translates each one with your text domain where it reaches WordPress or the editor: Text Translated #[Block] and #[Variation]: title, description, keywords when the block is registered block categories (CustomBlockCategory::label()) when the categories are added #[PostType] and #[Taxonomy]: labels (also the derived ones, such as "Add New Event") and description when the type is registered #[PostMeta]: title in meta boxes and meta panels #[SettingsGroup]: title, description; the name of the theme or plugin as title of the settings page on the settings page #[Label], labels derived from parameter names, Labeled::label() of enums, itemLabel of #[ListOf], label of #[BlockSupport] in the inspector, meta boxes, meta panels and the settings page The labels the framework derives for a post type are whole sentences – "Add New Event", "No events found." – and are translated as such. That suits languages in which the words change with the type: "Neue Veranstaltung hinzufügen", but "Neuen Ort hinzufügen". Texts in the attributes and the content of #[Example] and #[InnerBlocks] templates are content, not labels, and are not translated. Texts in templates Templates translate with __(), _x(), _n() and _nx(), which take the arguments of WordPress' functions without the text domain: {{ _x('May', 'month') }}

{{ _n('%d event', '%d events', events|length)|format(events|length) }}

The result is text; Twig escapes it like any other value. Fill placeholders with Twig's format filter. The template of the translations Translators start from a template that lists every text of the project, a POT file. The framework writes it: vendor/bin/wp-app-framework pot It writes languages/{text domain}.pot with: the name and the description of the theme or plugin from its header; the texts of attributes (see above), each with the file of the class that declares it; the texts of templates: every call of __(), _x(), _n() and _nx() in src/ whose texts are literal strings – a text built at run time cannot be translated ahead, and the command names such calls; the texts of PHP files: every call of WordPress' translation functions (__(), _e(), _x(), _n(), esc_html__(), esc_attr__() and their siblings) with the text domain of the project and literal strings, in the PSR-4 directories and the boot file (functions.php or the main file of the plugin). A comment starting with translators: before a call becomes the comment of its text, as with WordPress' own tools. The command needs no WordPress and no WP-CLI. Run it after changing texts; it replaces the template each time. Create a translation from it with a PO editor such as Poedit (languages/datebook-de_DE.po), and update an existing translation with the editor's "Update from POT file": new texts are added, texts that are gone are marked obsolete. Texts in JavaScript of your editor scripts are not part of the template. Translation files The translations are PO files in the directory languages/ of your theme or plugin, named after the text domain and the locale: languages/ └── datebook-de_DE.po The framework loads the translation for the locale of the request (determine_locale(), the language of the user in the backend) on init, before blocks and post types are registered: In development mode, it compiles the PO file into the cache directory of the instance (wp-content/cache/{slug}/languages/) whenever the PO file changed, so an edited translation shows on the next request. The release build compiles every PO file into generated/languages/{domain}-{locale}.l10n.php, the translation format of WordPress since 6.5, and the release loads it without looking at the file system. Fuzzy and untranslated entries of a PO file are left out, as gettext's msgfmt does. Translations WordPress has for the text domain in wp-content/languages/ – from translate.wordpress.org or a translation plugin – are loaded as well; an entry of your PO file wins. Texts of the framework The controls of the editor, the settings page and the meta boxes – "Add item", "Remove", "No date" – are texts of the framework, with the text domain wp-app-framework. The framework brings their translations along, German so far (also for de_DE_formal, de_AT and de_CH), and loads them by itself. Rules The Text Domain header is required; without it the build fails. A PO file in languages/ is named {text domain}-{locale}.po, for example datebook-de_DE.po or datebook-de_DE_formal.po; any other name of a PO file is a build error. Texts in attributes are English source texts; they are translated at run time with the text domain of the instance that declares them, also when another theme or plugin renders its templates. The Twig functions __(), _x(), _n() and _nx() use the text domain of the instance whose template calls them.

The framework translates what editors and visitors read with the text domain of your theme or plugin – the Text Domain header of style.css or of the main file of the plugin – like WordPress translates any theme or plugin. There are three kinds of texts: Texts in attributes: the title of a block, the labels of a post type, the #[Label] of a value, the label of an enum case. You write them in English; the framework translates them when it hands them to WordPress or the editor.Texts in templates: {{ __('Load map') }} in Twig.Texts in PHP and JavaScript: WordPress' own functions, __('Load map', 'my-plugin'), as in any plugin. The translations themselves are PO files in languages/, which the framework compiles and loads.

title: Twig templates
content: Markup in the framework lives in Twig templates, not in PHP strings. Twig escapes every value by default, so you don't have to remember esc_html() for each one; only |raw and functions marked HTML print a value unescaped. It also keeps markup readable, and it lets child themes and themes override the markup of a block without touching its code. Twig renders the markup of blocks and fragments your code produces, such as the body of a mail or an HTML response. Page layouts are not Twig; they are block templates and template parts, as in any block theme. Where templates live Templates sit in the src/ directory of the theme or plugin, next to the code that uses them (src/Hook/Mail.twig, src/Block/Hero/Hero.twig), or in shared directories (src/Component/Button.twig). There is no separate views/ directory. A template name is always the full path relative to src/, including the extension: 'Component/Button.twig'. That holds in PHP and in templates alike. There are no relative names, so a name means the same thing wherever it appears. Rendering a template A service renders a template through the TemplateRenderer, which it asks for in its constructor. render(name, context) returns the HTML as a string: use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Hook\Hook; use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Twig\TemplateRenderer; final class Mail { public function __construct(private readonly TemplateRenderer $renderer) { } #[Hook('sections_mail_body')] public function body(string $body, string $name): string { return $this->renderer->render('Hook/Mail.twig', ['body' => $body, 'name' => $name]); } } The Twig environment is created when the first template renders, so a request without templates pays nothing for it. Blocks render their templates the same way (see Blocks). Lookup A template name without a namespace is searched in several layers. The first layer that has the file wins: overrides/{theme-slug}/ of the active child theme, if it has that directory, the theme's src/, the framework's src/. A higher layer overrides a template by providing a file with the same path. For example, a child theme of my-theme changes the markup of the theme's hero block, src/Block/Hero/Hero.twig, with its own overrides/my-theme/Block/Hero/Hero.twig. The theme's PHP code stays as it is. Sometimes you need exactly one layer, for example when an override extends the original template it replaces. @theme/… and @framework/… address exactly that layer and cannot be overridden: {% include 'Component/Button.twig' %} {# child overrides → theme → framework #} {% include '@framework/Component/Button.twig' %} {# exactly this layer #} wp-app-framework build lists the project's templates that override framework templates. Child themes and plugins The src/ of a child theme belongs to its own framework instance, if it boots one. Its templates are searched in its own src/, then in the framework's, and they never override templates of the theme. To override the theme, a child theme uses overrides/{theme-slug}/. A plugin's templates are searched in this order: overrides/{plugin-slug}/ of the child theme, overrides/{plugin-slug}/ of the theme, the plugin's src/, the framework's src/. A theme overrides src/Block/Note/Note.twig of the plugin my-plugin with overrides/my-plugin/Block/Note/Note.twig. Because overrides live in their own directory, the theme's templates in src/ never collide with the plugin's. @plugin/… addresses the plugin's own templates exactly. The plugin's Twig environment renders the override. The override therefore sees the plugin's template functions and filters and the context the plugin passes, not those of the theme. Compiled templates are named after the slug of their instance, so a theme and a plugin never share compiled code of templates with the same path. Their names also include a hash of the template functions and filters of the instance – name, class and method: when a function moves to another class or method, the templates are compiled anew. Environment Twig runs with settings that catch mistakes early: Autoescaping (html) is always on. strict_variables is always on, so an undefined variable is an error instead of an empty string. In development mode, debug, auto reload and dump() are enabled; in release mode they are off. A theme or plugin with settings groups has the global settings (see Settings). The framework provides the template functions of blocks (block_wrapper_attributes(), see Blocks), of the editor (field(), list_item(), inner_blocks(), is_editor(), see Editor), has_plugin() (see Plugins), post() for post objects (see Posts), link_attributes() for links, asset_url(), asset_image() and asset_svg() for the files in assets/ (see Static assets), __(), _x(), _n() and _nx() for texts in the language of the site (see Translations) and the WordPress functions below. Twig exceptions reach the code that rendered the template, so the error handling of hooks and REST routes applies to them. Cache Compiled templates are cached in wp-content/cache/{slug}/twig/. Release mode compiles without auto reload: Twig never checks whether a template changed. Each release therefore uses its own directory, wp-content/cache/{slug}/twig/{templateVersion}/. The template version is a hash over the names and contents of all templates of the project and the framework; build --output writes it into the release manifest. Overrides add one more level. If the active theme or child theme overrides templates of another instance – a plugin, or the theme overridden by its child theme – that instance's cache directory gets a further level named after the versions of theme and child theme. A changed override therefore needs a new version of the theme or child theme. Directories of older releases are removed by a daily WP-Cron event, the same event that cleans up the file cache. It keeps the directory of the current template version and, below it, the directory of the current theme and child theme versions. On multisite, all sites share the cache directory but may run other themes, so the event keeps the override directories of the current release; they go with the next release. Template functions and filters Your own Twig functions and filters are methods of services with #[TemplateFunction] or #[TemplateFilter]: use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Twig\TemplateFilter; use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Twig\TemplateFunction; final class Formatting { #[TemplateFunction('price')] public function price(int $cents): string { return number_format($cents / 100, 2, ',', '.') . ' €'; } #[TemplateFilter('highlight', html: true)] public function highlight(string $value): string { return '' . $value . ''; } } {{ price(total) }} {{ name|highlight }} The service is created when a template calls one of its functions for the first time. Like other services, it gets its dependencies through its constructor. Escaping By default Twig escapes the result of a function or filter. A method that returns HTML sets html: true; its result is printed as it is, and it must return string. An HTML filter receives the filtered value already HTML-escaped, unless the value is safe already (for example after |raw). Twig's nl2br works the same way. In the example, highlight can wrap $value in without escaping it first. Other arguments are passed unescaped: an HTML function or filter must escape every argument it puts into its result. Rules #[TemplateFunction(name, html: false, public: false)] and #[TemplateFilter(name, html: false, public: false)] go on public, non-static methods of services. Names are valid identifiers and unique per kind. They must not reuse a function or filter Twig provides, because Twig would silently replace it. Parameters must not be services (inject them through the constructor), variadic or by reference. A filter receives the filtered value as its first parameter. Callables offered to other consumers (public: true) are described in Plugins. WordPress functions Templates often need data from WordPress: an image for an attachment ID, the title and URL of a linked post, the site name. The framework provides these as template functions. Each is a thin wrapper around a WordPress function, and the wp_ prefix tells you so at a glance. {{ wp_post_title(attrs.target) }} {{ wp_attachment_image(attrs.imageId, 'large', { class: 'rounded' }) }} {{ wp_post_date(attrs.target, 'j. F Y') }} The names follow one rule: wp_ + object + property, without get_ or the_. A WordPress function that already starts with wp_ keeps its name (wp_date, not wp_wp_date). The prefix is not reserved for the framework, but a name the framework already uses is a build error. The functions handle missing data for you: IDs may be null, for example an empty #[Image] or reference. null and objects that do not exist give '', so a template does not need to check first. Posts that are not publicly viewable count as missing, except when the block editor renders the block: a draft, or a post of a type that is not public. Attachments are not checked for visibility. post() checks only the status, so it also returns posts of your data types (see Posts). Text is escaped by Twig. Some values come from WordPress already escaped: term and user names, the site name and description, and the logout URL. The framework decodes them first, so they are not escaped twice. Functions marked HTML below print their result unescaped. Function WordPress Result wp_attachment_image(id, size = 'full', attributes = {}) wp_get_attachment_image() HTML wp_attachment_image_url(id, size = 'full') wp_get_attachment_image_url() URL wp_attachment_url(id) wp_get_attachment_url() URL wp_attachment_caption(id) wp_get_attachment_caption() HTML as stored (filtered with kses when saved without unfiltered_html) wp_attachment_alt(id) meta _wp_attachment_image_alt text wp_post_url(id) get_permalink() URL wp_post_title(id) post_title text wp_post_excerpt(id) get_the_excerpt() plain text: tags removed, entities decoded wp_post_date(id, format = '') get_the_date() text; '' uses the date format of the site wp_post_thumbnail(id, size = 'post-thumbnail', attributes = {}) get_the_post_thumbnail() HTML wp_term_url(id) get_term_link() URL wp_term_name(id) name of the term text wp_user_name(id) display_name of the user text wp_user_url(id) get_author_posts_url() URL of the author archive wp_avatar(id, size = 96) get_avatar() HTML; '' if avatars are turned off wp_home_url(path = '') home_url() URL wp_site_name() get_bloginfo('name') text wp_site_description() get_bloginfo('description') text wp_login_url(redirect = '') wp_login_url() URL wp_logout_url(redirect = '') wp_logout_url() URL with a nonce wp_is_user_logged_in() is_user_logged_in() true/false wp_date(format, timestamp = null) wp_date() text in the site's time zone and language; null for now wp_human_time_diff(from, to = 0) human_time_diff() text, e.g. "5 minutes"; 0 for now wp_number_format(number, decimals = 0) number_format_i18n() text wp_size_format(bytes, decimals = 0) size_format() text, e.g. "2 KB" The output of wp_logout_url() (a nonce), wp_is_user_logged_in() (the login state), wp_date() without a timestamp and wp_human_time_diff() without a second timestamp (the current time) depends on the request, not only on the attributes of a block. In cached blocks the framework checks them. Links link_attributes(link) prints the attributes of an element for a Link, like block_wrapper_attributes() prints those of the root element: {% if attrs.cta.url %} More {% endif %} The result is href="https://example.org/about/", escaped with esc_url(), plus target="_blank" rel="noopener" if the link opens in a new tab. For a link without URL – also a link to content that no longer exists or is not public – it prints nothing, so check link.url before you print the element. The function takes no further attributes; write classes and other attributes next to it.
description: Markup in the framework lives in Twig templates, not in PHP strings. Twig escapes every value by default, so you don't have to remember esc_html() for each one; only |raw and functions marked HTML print a value unescaped. It also keeps markup readable, and it lets child themes and themes override the markup of a block without touching its code. Twig renders the markup of blocks and fragments your code produces, such as the body of a mail or an HTML response. Page layouts are not Twig; they are block templates and template parts, as in any block theme.

title: Values
content:
Blocks, REST routes and settings all deal with structured values: a headline, a choice among variants, a list of buttons, a link to another page. In WordPress these arrive as untyped arrays, either from the block comment, the request or an option. The framework lets you describe them once, as typed PHP classes, and uses that description in two places: In the build, it derives a JSON schema from the class. WordPress uses the schema to validate block attributes, REST arguments and settings. At run time, the value factory turns the stored array into an instance of your class, with enums as enum cases and nested objects as objects. It does this without reflection. Block attribute classes, settings groups, nested value classes and #[ListOf] REST arguments all work this way, so what you learn here applies to all of them. The data of a one-time cron task is a value class too, without references. Value classes A value class is a readonly class whose values are all public promoted constructor parameters: final readonly class Button { public function __construct( #[PlainText] public string $label, #[Url] public string $url = '', public ButtonStyle $style = ButtonStyle::Primary, ) {} } It declares no other properties. Elsewhere in the framework, class properties are never public; value classes are the exception, because they are plain data. Types A value can have one of these types, each optionally nullable: PHP type Schema int, float, string, bool integer, number, string, boolean backed enum the type of its values, with enum listing the case values value class object with properties array with #[ListOf(Enum::class)] or #[ListOf(ValueClass::class)] array with items; see Lists A nullable type adds null to the schema type (type: [..., 'null']). PHP has no generic types, so a list says what it contains with #[ListOf]. Lists of scalars exist only for references. Enums and value classes must be in the scanned PSR-4 directories. A value class that contains itself, directly or indirectly, is a build error. The columns of tables use the same value factory with one more type: DateTimeImmutable, read from the database as a UTC time Y-m-d H:i:s. Anything else in such a column, including the zero date 0000-00-00 00:00:00, is an error. Blocks, REST routes and settings have no time type; a date there is a string marked with #[DateTime]. Defaults and missing values The default value of a parameter becomes the schema's default: enums as their value, value objects as arrays. A missing value uses the constructor's default. Inside a nested value class, a parameter without a default is required in the schema. Unknown keys in nested objects are ignored, just as WordPress ignores unknown block attributes. Wrong values The value factory never coerces silently. A value that does not match its type throws an InvalidArgumentException that names the path to the value, for example buttons[1].url. Blocks, REST routes and settings each decide what happens next; see their pages. Lists A list holds items of one backed enum or one value class, declared with #[ListOf(class, min: 0, max: null, itemLabel: null, appender: false)]. Many lists have a natural size: a hero shows at most three buttons, a comparison needs at least two columns. min and max set these limits: #[ListOf(Button::class, max: 3)] public array $buttons = [], #[ListOf(Column::class, min: 2, max: 4)] public array $columns = [new Column(), new Column()], The limits apply where people edit the list. In the block inspector, on the settings page and in meta boxes, "Add item" is disabled when the list has max items, and "Remove" when it has min items. A list of post objects (#[ListOf(Venue::class)]) hides its search at max instead. A stored list can still be outside the limits, for example after you lowered max in an update of your theme. The framework keeps such a list as it is, so changing a limit never loses content: Your template receives only the first max items. It can rely on the limit. The editor shows all stored items, marks the ones beyond max as unused and says how many to remove. Nothing changes until an editor removes them. A list shorter than min reaches your template as it is; the editor asks for the missing items. This is why the limits are not part of the JSON schema of stored values. WordPress would treat a list with too many items as invalid and replace the whole list with its default. REST arguments are different: a request is not stored content, so their schema contains minItems and maxItems, also for lists inside value classes, and WordPress answers a request outside the limits with 400. Editors see each item as a card that shows only its title, so a list stays clear even when its items have many values. A click on the title expands the item's controls; several items can be expanded at once, and a new item starts expanded. Items are sorted by dragging them at their handle, or with "Move up" and "Move down" in their menu, which also work with the keyboard. The title is the first text of the item, such as the text of a badge, or the label of an enum case. An item without text is titled with itemLabel and its number, "Badge 2". Without itemLabel, the framework uses the short name of the item class in words: Badge becomes "Badge", SocialLink becomes "Social link". Set itemLabel when the class name does not fit, for example for a German editor interface: #[ListOf(Badge::class, max: 3, itemLabel: 'Auszeichnung')] public array $badges = [], With appender: true, editors also add items in the canvas of the block editor, through a faded new item at the end of the list; see New list items in the canvas. Rules Rule itemLabel not empty; null (default) for the short name of the class in words appender block attributes only, also in value classes, but not in list items; not on #[Hidden] lists and lists of posts min 0 or more; default 0 max 1 or more and at least min; null (default) for no limit Default value must have between min and max items, because a new block or setting starts with it; null for a nullable list is allowed Stored values not validated against the limits; the value factory creates the first max items REST arguments validated with minItems and maxItems A min below 0, a max below 1, a min greater than max, a default outside the limits, an empty itemLabel and appender where it is not allowed (settings groups, meta classes, REST arguments, list items, hidden lists, lists of posts) are build errors. Lists of references without #[ListOf] have no limits. URLs #[Url] on a string adds format: uri to the schema, so the value is sanitized with sanitize_url(). Disallowed protocols such as javascript: become an empty string. Colors A background, an accent, the color of a banner: some values are colors that editors choose freely. Mark such a string with #[Color] (namespace WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\): use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\Color; final readonly class BannerAttributes { public function __construct( #[Color] public string $background = '', #[Color] public string $overlay = '#00000080', ) {} } The value is a hex color – #rgb, #rgba, #rrggbb or #rrggbbaa, the last two digits being the transparency – or an empty string for no color. Editors see a compact button with a swatch and the hex value, like the color controls of the block editor; it opens the colors of the theme's palette, a picker for any color with transparency, and "Clear" for no color. The palette is the one of the block editor: the colors changed in the site editor if there are any, else those of theme.json. Only its hex colors can be chosen, because a color is stored as hex value, not as the slug of the palette entry. A color picked from the palette therefore stays as it is when the palette changes later. The schema of a color has a pattern, so WordPress rejects any other value, and the value factory checks it again – also values that were stored without the schema, such as an option changed with update_option(). A template can therefore print the color into a style attribute:
Rules Rule Type string, never nullable; '' means no color Allowed in block attributes, value classes, lists, settings groups, meta classes, REST arguments Schema string with a pattern that allows the four hex formats and the empty string Control a button with swatch and value that opens the color palette of the theme and a color picker with transparency The following are build errors: #[Color] on another type than string, or on ?string; #[Color] together with #[PlainText], #[RichText], #[Image] or #[Url]; a default that is no hex color, such as 'red'; #[Color] together with #[Param(pattern:)] on a REST argument. A stored value that is no color is a wrong value. The build checks colors in templates and patterns against the pattern. Dates The start of an event, the day a sale ends, the date of a notice: some values are dates that editors choose. Mark such a string with #[DateTime] (namespace WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\), or with #[DateTime(time: false)] for a date without time of day: use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\DateTime; final class EventDetails { public function __construct( #[DateTime] private string $start = '', #[DateTime(time: false)] private string $saleEnds = '', ) {} } The value is the local time of the site, as the editor chose it, without time zone: 2026-11-14T20:00, or 2026-11-14 without time of day. An empty string means no date. A concert at eight in the evening stays at eight when the time zone of the site changes or the clocks change for summer time; that is what an event, an opening hour or a deadline usually means. Editors see a compact button with the date in the date and time formats of the site's settings; it opens the date picker of WordPress, with the time of day unless time: false, and "Clear" for no date. The schema of a date has a pattern, so WordPress rejects any other format. The pattern cannot tell whether a date exists, so the value factory checks every value again and rejects 2026-02-30 or 2026-11-14T24:00 as well – also values that were stored without the schema, such as meta changed with update_post_meta(). Dates in this format sort and compare as text. A query therefore compares and sorts them with the methods of a string field, which wp-app-framework meta-fields generates for a date: $upcoming = Event::query() ->where(EventDetailsFields::start()->greaterOrEqual(wp_date('Y-m-d\TH:i'))) ->orderBy(EventDetailsFields::start()) ->get(); wp_date() gives the current time in the time zone of the site, the time the values are stored in. To show a date, turn it into a time with that time zone: $start = DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat('Y-m-d\TH:i', $details->getStart(), wp_timezone()); In a file that uses the marker, PHP's own DateTime class needs its leading backslash, \DateTime, or an alias; DateTimeImmutable is not affected. Rules Rule Type string, never nullable; '' means no date Allowed in block attributes, value classes, lists, settings groups, meta classes, REST arguments Format Y-m-d\TH:i (2026-11-14T20:00); with time: false Y-m-d (2026-11-14); the local time of the site Schema string with a pattern that allows the format and the empty string Control a button with the date in the site's formats that opens the date picker of WordPress The following are build errors: #[DateTime] on another type than string, or on ?string; #[DateTime] together with #[PlainText], #[RichText], #[Image], #[Url] or #[Color]; a default that is no date in the format, or a date that does not exist, such as '2026-02-30'; #[DateTime] together with #[Param(pattern:)] on a REST argument. A stored value that is no date in the format, or a date that does not exist, is a wrong value. The build checks dates in templates and patterns against the pattern. Identifiers Some list items are referred to from elsewhere: a block picks one of the color schemes listed in the settings, a tab is opened by a link. The position of the item is no good reference, because editors reorder lists, and neither is its name, because they rename items. Mark a string of the item class with #[Identifier] (namespace WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\), and each item gets an identifier that never changes: use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\Color; use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\Identifier; use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\PlainText; final readonly class ColorScheme { public function __construct( #[Identifier] public string $id = '', #[PlainText] public string $name = '', #[Color] public string $background = '#ffffff', ) {} } An identifier is eight lowercase hex digits, such as 3f9a1c2e. The list editors generate it when an item is added – in the block inspector, in the canvas of the block editor, on the settings page and in meta boxes – unique within the list. Editors never see or change it; it has no control. Store it wherever you refer to the item, and look the item up by it: {% set scheme = settings.design.schemes|filter(s => s.id == attrs.scheme)|first %} An item that was stored before its class had an identifier has the empty string. When a settings group or post meta is saved, the framework fills in such missing identifiers and gives a duplicate a new one; the first item with an identifier keeps it. Block attributes are saved by the block editor without the framework, so an old item of a block keeps '' until it is removed and added again. Items in the default of a list have no identifier either, unless you give them one. Write a fixed identifier into an item the theme refers to itself, for example the first color scheme: #[ListOf(ColorScheme::class, min: 1)] public array $schemes = [new ColorScheme('a1b2c3d4', 'Page')], Rules Rule Type string, never nullable; default '' Allowed in value classes that are items of #[ListOf], in block attributes, settings groups, meta classes and REST arguments; one identifier per item class Schema string with a pattern that allows eight lowercase hex digits and the empty string Control none; generated when an item is added Filled in when a settings group or post meta is saved: missing, invalid and duplicate identifiers The following are build errors: #[Identifier] on another type than string, or on ?string; a default other than ''; #[Identifier] together with #[PlainText], #[RichText], #[Image], #[Content], #[Url], #[Color], #[Hidden] or a reference; #[Identifier] on a parameter of a class that is no list item – a block attribute class, a settings group, a meta class, a value class used as a single value, a REST argument; two identifiers in one item class; an item in the default of a list whose identifier is invalid or appears twice. A stored value that is no identifier is a wrong value. The build checks identifiers in templates and patterns against the pattern. Links A call to action, a link in a footer setting, a registration link of an event: a link points either to content of the site or to any address. #[Url] stores the address as text, so a link to a page breaks when someone changes the page's slug. A Link (namespace WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\) stores the ID of the page instead, and the framework looks up its current URL when it renders – the same idea as references, plus a URL entered freely and "Open in new tab". use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\Label; use WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\Link; final readonly class TeaserAttributes { public function __construct( #[Label('Call to action')] public Link $cta = new Link(), ) {} } A link is never null. A new Link() has an empty URL, and an empty URL means "no link". Print it with link_attributes(), which writes href and, for a new tab, target and rel: {% if attrs.cta.url %} More {% endif %} Linked content and free URLs Editors choose the target in the block inspector with the link control of the block editor. It searches posts, terms and media files. A chosen result stays synced: the link stores its kind and ID, and the input field is locked until the editor chooses "Unsync and edit". An address typed into the field is a free URL: it is stored as it is, without ID. A link is stored as four values: {"url":"https://example.org/about/","opensInNewTab":true,"kind":"post","id":42} {"url":"https://example.com/","opensInNewTab":false,"kind":"url","id":0} kind is a LinkKind: Url for a free URL, Post, Term or Attachment for linked content. For linked content, the stored URL is only what the editor showed when the target was chosen; templates never see it. Resolution When the value is created, a linked post, term or media file gets its current URL: the permalink of a post, the archive of a term, the file of a media item. A link becomes empty – an empty url, while kind and id stay – if its target: no longer exists, is of a post type or taxonomy that is not viewable, is a post or media file that is not publicly viewable, such as a draft or the attachment of a draft. Renders for the block editor keep posts and media files that are not public, so editors still see what they chose. Free URLs stay as they are; like #[Url], they are sanitized with sanitize_url(). Resolving costs about as much as a reference: one lookup of the object, usually from the object cache, and one call for its URL. A cached block keeps the resolved URL until its cache entry is invalidated. If the URLs of linked pages matter, tag the block with the types it links to, for example PostTypeTag(Page::class), as you would for references. In templates and patterns of your theme, use free URLs only. IDs of pages, terms and media files differ from site to site, and the build does not check them. Outside the block editor The settings page and meta boxes on the classic edit screen do not load the block editor. There a link is edited with a form of its own: a search of published posts, which links the chosen post with its ID, a field for a free URL and the toggle "Open in new tab". A linked post shows its title and can be unlinked, which keeps its current URL as a free URL. Links to terms and media files are chosen in the block editor only. Rules Rule Type Link, never nullable; default new Link() Allowed in block attributes, value classes, lists (#[ListOf(Link::class)]), settings groups, meta classes Schema object with url (format: uri), opensInNewTab, kind (enum url, post, term, attachment) and id Blocks counts as content (role: content), editable in contentOnly mode Kind and ID kind: url with id: 0; any other kind with a positive ID The following are build errors: ?Link: a link is never null; an empty URL means no link; #[Content], #[Url], #[PlainText], #[RichText], #[Image] or a reference on a Link: a link is content with its own control. A stored link whose kind and ID do not match is a wrong value. The build checks links in templates and patterns against the schema, so a wrong kind or a string as opensInNewTab is an error there; it does not check whether an ID exists. References A block that links to another page, a setting that names the privacy policy page, a teaser that shows a category: these are references to WordPress objects. Storing the URL or the title would break as soon as someone renames the page. References store the ID instead, and the framework looks up the current data when it renders. #[PostReference(postTypes: null)], #[TermReference(taxonomies: null)] and #[UserReference] (namespace WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\Value\) mark such IDs in block attributes, value classes and settings groups: #[PostReference(postTypes: ['page'])] public ?int $target = null, // one page, null without #[PostReference] public array $featured = [], // a list of post IDs, in order (list) #[TermReference(taxonomies: ['category'])] public ?int $topic = null, #[UserReference] public ?int $author = null, On ?int the parameter holds one reference, or null if nothing is chosen. On array it holds a list of IDs in the chosen order; there is no #[ListOf] for it. The schema is integer or ["integer", "null"], or an array of integers. postTypes and taxonomies limit the choice to these keys; null allows all viewable post types or taxonomies. The build does not check the keys against the registered types, because types are registered at run time. The search in the editor accepts only searchable post types and taxonomies. In blocks, a reference counts as content (role: content), like #[Image]. Post objects A parameter typed as a post class – a class with #[PostType], or the framework's Post and Page – is a reference too, without an attribute: it stores the ID and gives you the post object. public ?Event $event = null, // the event, null without #[ListOf(Venue::class)] public array $venues = [], // a list of venues (list) The single reference must be nullable. It resolves if the post has the type of the class and is published, also for post types that are not public, such as data types. The search in the editor uses the REST collection of the post type, so it finds posts of these types too. postTypes and taxonomies also take post and taxonomy classes instead of names: #[PostReference(postTypes: [Event::class, 'page'])], #[TermReference(taxonomies: [Genre::class, Category::class])]. WordPress' own types and taxonomies are the framework classes Post, Page, Category and Tag. Editing References are edited with a search, in the block inspector and on the settings page. Posts and terms are searched through /wp/v2/search, which finds published posts only. Users are searched through /wp/v2/users; users without the capability list_users see only authors of published posts. A list shows its entries as cards that can be dragged, moved up, moved down and removed. Resolution Content changes after a reference was stored. A page is deleted, or put back into draft. The framework checks this when it creates the value. A reference becomes null, or is left out of a list, if its target: no longer exists, is of another type, or not of a viewable type, is a post that is not publicly viewable. A deleted page therefore simply disappears from the output; nothing is logged. Renders for the block editor keep posts that are not public, such as drafts, so editors still see what they chose. Output The WordPress functions take the IDs: wp_post_title(id), wp_post_url(id), wp_term_name(id), wp_term_url(id), wp_user_name(id) and more. They return '' for null and missing objects. Posts that are not publicly viewable count as missing outside the editor. {% if attrs.target %} {{ wp_post_title(attrs.target) }} {% endif %} Rules The following are build errors: a reference on a type other than ?int or array, or together with #[ListOf]; a reference combined with #[PlainText], #[RichText], #[Image], #[Content] or #[Url]; several references on one parameter; empty or invalid postTypes or taxonomies; a reference on a REST argument. Declare the ID as int there. Where values are used Blocks, REST routes and Settings describe what each of them adds to these rules; Tables list the types of columns.

title: wp-app-framework
description: wp-app-framework is a PHP and JavaScript framework for building standalone full site editing themes, child themes and plugins for WordPress 7 on PHP 8.5. You write blocks, hooks, REST routes and settings as plain PHP classes with attributes. The framework turns them into everything WordPress expects: registered blocks with an attribute schema, an editor with inline editing, REST routes with validation, and a settings page. The framework is a library, not a theme or a plugin. Your theme, child theme or plugin includes it through Composer; the documentation calls these projects consumers. The framework registers no blocks itself; the blocks, hooks and routes you see in WordPress come from your code. Each consumer runs its own copy of the framework, called an instance. Its blocks, REST routes and settings are named after the consumer's namespace from composer.json; technical names – script handles, the JavaScript global, the cache directory, the init action – after its slug (its directory name). That is why a theme and several plugins can run side by side, even with different framework versions. Concepts explains this and the other ideas the guides build on.

title: Upgrading
content:
From 1.0 on, the consumer API only grows within a major version: nothing is renamed, removed or changed in behavior, and a theme built against 1.0 keeps working with 1.9. Before 1.0, a minor version may still break the API. This page lists every such change, why it was made, and what you need to change in your theme or plugin.

The documentation is published for each minor version. The version switcher in the navigation bar shows the documentation of other versions, so you can compare the old and the new state.

0.20

The framework is published by Web Coding Cat. The repositories moved from the personal account saijsaij to the organization webcodingcat, and every name with the vendor saij follows: the Composer package is webcodingcat/wp-app-framework, the PHP namespace WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework, the npm package @webcodingcat/wp-app-framework. saij/wp-app-framework is abandoned on Packagist and gets no release after 0.19. Nothing changes at run time: the global wpAppFramework, the hooks between instances, and the names of blocks, options, tables and REST routes derive from your namespace and slug as before, so stored content and settings stay valid. In your theme or plugin:

In composer.json, replace "saij/wp-app-framework": "^0.19" with "webcodingcat/wp-app-framework": "^0.20" and run composer update saij/wp-app-framework webcodingcat/wp-app-framework, which removes the old package and installs the new one.

In package.json, replace the dependency with "@webcodingcat/wp-app-framework": "file:vendor/webcodingcat/wp-app-framework" and run npm install.

Replace Saij\WpAppFramework\ with WebCodingCat\WpAppFramework\ in your PHP code, Twig templates and PHPStan configuration, also where the backslashes are escaped (Saij\\WpAppFramework\\). The old names no longer exist, so PHP, PHPStan or the build reports every place you missed.

Replace @saij/wp-app-framework with @webcodingcat/wp-app-framework in your scripts, webpack.config.js and ESLint configuration. The build of your scripts fails on every import of the old name.

In the workflow that calls consumer-release.yml, use webcodingcat/wp-app-framework/.github/workflows/consumer-release.yml@v0.20.0.

The documentation moved to webcodingcat.github.io/wp-app-framework; the starter is webcodingcat/wp-app-starter.

0.19

The Text Domain header is required. The framework translates the texts of attributes – titles of blocks, labels of post types and values – with the text domain of the theme or plugin (see Translations). A theme or plugin without a Text Domain header in style.css or its main file is a build error now; add the header, usually with the slug as value. Projects created with wp-app-starter have it.

0.16

delete() moves posts of every type to the trash. AbstractPost::delete() used to call wp_delete_post(), which moves only posts and pages to the trash and deletes posts of other types permanently. Now delete() moves every post to the trash, so an editor can restore it (see Posts). Code that relied on permanent deletion of its own post types calls delete(true). A post already in the trash, and every post while the trash is disabled, is still deleted permanently.

RestException rejects a status in its data. The response always sets status to the status of the exception, so a key status in data was lost while getData() still returned it. It is now an InvalidArgumentException; pass the status as the third argument and remove the key from the data.

0.15

0.15 is the last review of the API before 1.0. It renames and tightens what would otherwise stay inconsistent for the whole 1.x series.

The field markers moved to Saij\WpAppFramework\Value. #[PlainText], #[RichText], #[Image], #[Label], #[Hidden], #[Content] and the interface Labeled are not only for blocks: settings groups, meta classes and value classes use them too. They now live next to #[ListOf], #[Url] and the references. Replace Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\ with Saij\WpAppFramework\Value\ in the use lines of these seven names; the old names no longer exist, so PHP or the build reports every place you missed.

#[CronTask] takes a name. The name of a task used to come from the short name of its class, so renaming the class silently dropped the planned tasks. Now you name it, like a recurring event: #[CronTask('send-reminder')] (see Cron events and tasks). To keep tasks that are already planned, use the name the framework derived before: the short class name in kebab case (SendReminder → send-reminder, HTMLExport → html-export). A #[CronTask] without a name is a build error.

The arguments of #[Variation] follow #[Block]. The order is now name, title, icon, description, keywords, …, as in #[Block]; icon and description swapped places. Only a variation that passes description or icon positionally is affected; name these arguments (icon: 'columns'), because the build cannot tell the two strings apart.

@saij/wp-app-framework is the editor API only. The import used to resolve to the whole global wpAppFramework[slug], so internal parts such as config were importable. It now resolves to wpAppFramework[slug].api, which holds registerControl(), registerSupportControl(), registerPanel(), registerToolbarButton(), loadScript() and getData() (see Editor). Code that imports only these needs no change. Code that called them on the global, window.wpAppFramework[slug].registerPanel(…), calls them on window.wpAppFramework[slug].api now. loadScript() of both imports takes two arguments, the URL and the attributes.

The webpack helper is @saij/wp-app-framework/webpack. The package declares its entry points now, with TypeScript declarations for both imports that your IDE picks up. Replace require( './vendor/saij/wp-app-framework/webpack.config.js' ) in your webpack.config.js with require( '@saij/wp-app-framework/webpack' ); the old path still works.

The release workflow input cli-tests is now cli. It goes with e2e (see Releases and CI). Rename it in the workflow of your project that calls consumer-release.yml.

Internal services cannot be injected. The render context of the editor (Editor\RenderContext) and the post store (Post\PostStore) are internal to the framework. A class of your theme or plugin that injects one of them is now a build error. Use the template functions is_editor(), field() and inner_blocks() in templates, and Event::get(), find() and query() for posts.

The framework is on Packagist. Composer finds saij/wp-app-framework without a repositories entry now. Remove the vcs entry for the framework from your composer.json and run composer update saij/wp-app-framework (see Releases and CI); a project that keeps the entry still works.

The framework is licensed under the GPL-2.0-or-later. Releases before 0.15 declared a proprietary license. A theme or plugin that ships the framework must be under a GPL-compatible license; this is also what the plugin directory of WordPress.org requires (see Distribution).

0.14

The release workflow tests in wp-test-env. consumer-release.yml used to install the release into the release site of wp-dev-env. Since 0.14 it uses wp-test-env, which starts a fresh WordPress for every test run and runs the browser tests with one Playwright worker per instance (see Releases and CI). Three things change in your project:

The input wp-dev-env-ref is now wp-test-env-ref. Rename it if your workflow sets it.

Your Playwright configuration receives the instance URLs in WP_BASE_URLS instead of one URL in WP_BASE_URL, and no E2E_BROWSER_HOST_RULES any more. Set workers to the number of URLs, pick the URL of each worker by TEST_PARALLEL_INDEX, and log in per worker instead of in a global setup. The configuration and fixtures.js of theme-dev-test show how.

tests/cli/run gets the name of a wp-test-env instance instead of a Compose service of wp-dev-env, and runs WP-CLI with ../wp-test-env/bin/wp <instance> … instead of docker compose exec.

0.13

The stylesheet moved to assets/styles.css. Each project now has an assets/ directory for everything that belongs to no PHP class (see Concepts), and the Tailwind stylesheet is the first file there. Move src/styles.css to assets/styles.css and make the paths in it relative to the new place: @source "./**/*.twig" becomes @source "../src/**/*.twig", and url(…) to files in src/ gets a ../src/ in front. A file left at src/styles.css is a build error in the manifest build and in the webpack helper, so it cannot be forgotten.

asset_url, asset_image and asset_svg are framework functions. 0.13 adds them for static assets. A template function of your own with one of these names is now a build error; rename it.

Scripts in src/ need a block or block support. An *.editor.js or *.view.js in src/ without a block or block support class of the same name next to it is now a build error. Before 0.13 the webpack helper built such a file, but the framework never loaded it.

0.12

Deleting a plugin deletes its data. Before 0.12, the framework left everything behind when a plugin was deleted. Since 0.12 it removes the posts of the plugin's post types, its terms, meta keys, settings, tables, cron events, technical options and caches (see Activation, deactivation and uninstallation). Back up the data before you delete a plugin whose data you want to keep.

A plugin must not have an uninstall.php. WordPress runs this file instead of the uninstall hook of the framework, so it is now a build error. Move its code into a method with #[OnUninstall].

0.11

link_attributes is a framework function. 0.11 adds the template function link_attributes() for links. A template function of your own with this name is now a build error; rename it.

Field classes name the class they belong to class. Since 0.11 fields describe the columns of tables as well as meta fields, so the first parameter of their constructors is called $class instead of $metaClass, and the getter getMetaClass() is now getClass(). Field classes written by hand or generated by wp-app-framework meta-fields pass the class positionally and keep working. Change the code only where it names the argument (new IntField(metaClass: EventDetails::class, …) becomes new IntField(class: EventDetails::class, …)) or calls getMetaClass().

0.10

Inner blocks are declared with #[InnerBlocks]. Before 0.10, #[Block] had one argument for containers, allowedBlocks, with block names as strings. 0.10 adds templates, locks and more for containers (see Container blocks); they live in an attribute of their own, #[InnerBlocks], and allowedBlocks moved there as allowed. Blocks are named so that your IDE can resolve them: blocks of your own by class, core blocks by CoreBlock.

Before	Since 0.10
#[Block('section', …, allowedBlocks: ['hero', 'core/paragraph'])]	#[Block('section', …)] and #[InnerBlocks(allowed: [Hero::class, CoreBlock::Paragraph])]
usesContext: ['sections/…'] for context of your own blocks	#[ProvidesContext] on the attribute and a render() parameter with #[Context(Block::class, 'attribute')]

allowedBlocks is removed without alias, so PHP reports the unknown argument. The build reports a block name in your own namespace (name the block by class) and a core block named as string. Other blocks stay strings with their full name.

field() checks its path only in the editor. Before 0.10, a wrong path also threw on the front end. Since 0.10 field() returns an empty string outside the editor without looking at the path, so it costs nothing on the front end. A wrong path still fails when the block renders in the editor.

Every block has an inserter preview. Without #[Example] the inserter now previews a block with its default attributes. Add #[Example(false)] to a block that should show none.

0.9

Each theme and plugin declares a namespace. Before 0.9, block names carried their namespace in #[Block] (sections/hero), REST controllers named their full REST namespace (sections/v1), and settings options were named after the slug, the directory name of the theme or plugin. The directory name changes when a theme is installed under another name, and its settings would be lost with it. Since 0.9 the namespace in composer.json names everything content and data refer to (see Concepts).

Add the namespace to composer.json. Use the namespace your blocks already have, so posts, templates and patterns keep working unchanged:

"extra": { "wp-app-framework": { "namespace": "sections" } }

Then change your code:

Before	Since 0.9
#[Block('sections/hero', …)]	#[Block('hero', …)]
allowedBlocks: ['sections/hero', 'core/paragraph']	allowedBlocks: ['hero', 'core/paragraph']
registerControl( 'sections/hero', … ), also registerPanel() and registerToolbarButton()	registerControl( 'hero', … )
#[RestController('sections/v1', …)]	#[RestController('v1', …)]

The build reports a missing namespace, a block name with / and an unknown own block in allowedBlocks; the register functions warn in the console about names with a namespace. Block markup in templates, parts and patterns keeps the full names.

Settings options are named after the namespace. The option of a settings group is now {namespace}_{name} instead of {slug}_{name}, with _ instead of -. If the two differ – the theme my-theme with the namespace sections stores the group general in sections_general instead of my_theme_general – the saved settings are not moved. Copy them once, for example with WP-CLI: wp option get my_theme_general --format=json | wp option update sections_general --format=json.

0.8

The build checks block templates, template parts and patterns. Before 0.8 the build looked at your PHP classes only. Mistakes in the block markup of your theme – a misspelled attribute, a value outside an enum, HTML in a block without a postContent field – went unnoticed, and WordPress dropped what it could not use. Since 0.8 the build checks these files against your blocks (see Checking templates, parts and patterns).

A theme or child theme that built fine with 0.7 may now fail with errors in templates/, parts/ or patterns/. Each error names the file, the line and the block; fix the markup as the message says. Two errors need more than a fix in place: PHP code inside the block comment of one of your blocks in a pattern (write the attributes as plain JSON), and a container of your theme without content that holds content blocks in a template part or a pattern with a single top-level block (give it #[Supports(contentRole: true)]).

0.7

Template functions that wrap WordPress functions start with wp_. Before 0.7 a template could call post_title() or attachment_image(), and nothing showed that these were WordPress functions rather than framework functions or functions of the theme. 0.7 gives all of them the prefix wp_ and adds many more (see WordPress functions).

The old names are removed without aliases. A template that still uses one fails to compile with an unknown function, so you won't miss any. Rename them in your templates:

Before	Since 0.7
attachment_image()	wp_attachment_image()
post_url()	wp_post_url()
post_title()	wp_post_title()
term_url()	wp_term_url()
term_name()	wp_term_name()
user_name()	wp_user_name()

If your own template functions use one of the new wp_ names, rename them as well: a name the framework already uses is a build error.

0.3

Child themes override theme templates in overrides/{theme}/ instead of src/. Since 0.3 a child theme can have code of its own and boot its own framework instance with ChildTheme::boot() (see Child themes). Its src/ directory now belongs to that instance and can no longer hold overrides of the parent theme.

Move each override from the child theme's src/ to overrides/{theme}/, keeping the path. For the parent theme my-theme, src/Block/Hero/Hero.twig becomes overrides/my-theme/Block/Hero/Hero.twig (see Twig templates).

0.2

The init action is named after the consumer. Since 0.2 plugins can use the framework next to a theme, and each runs its own instance. The single action wp_app_framework/init could not tell them apart, so it became wp_app_framework/init/{slug} (see Boot and modes).

Replace add_action('wp_app_framework/init', …) with the action of the instance you mean, for example wp_app_framework/init/my-theme.
description: From 1.0 on, the consumer API only grows within a major version: nothing is renamed, removed or changed in behavior, and a theme built against 1.0 keeps working with 1.9. Before 1.0, a minor version may still break the API. This page lists every such change, why it was made, and what you need to change in your theme or plugin. The documentation is published for each minor version. The version switcher in the navigation bar shows the documentation of other versions, so you can compare the old and the new state.
